dwell house which be appoint for such as be know to be sure and trusty to the emperor chap. 28. or the private behaviour or quality of the ruff people constitution of their body the private behaviour and quality of the ruff people may partly be understand by that which have be say concern the public state and usage of the country as touch the natural habit of their body they be for the most part of a large size and of very fleshly body account it a grace to be somewhat gross and burley and therefore they nourish and spread their beard to have they long and broad but for the most part they be very unwieldy and unactive withal which may be think to come partly of the climate and the numbness which they get by the cold in winter and partly of their diet that stand most of root onion garlic cabbage and such like thing that breed gross humour which they use to eat alone and with their other meat their diet be rather much then curious their diet at their meal they begin common with a chark or small cup of aquavitae which they call Russee wine and then drink not till towards the end of their meal take it in large and all together with kiss one another at every pledge and therefore after dinner there be no talk with they drink and kiss sleep but every man go to his bench to take his afternoon sleep which be as ordinary with they as their night rest when they exceed and have variety of dish the first be their bake meat for roast meat they use little and then their broth or pottage to drink drink be a ordinary matter with they every day in the week their common drink be mead the poor sort use water and a thin drink call quasse which be nothing else as we say but water turn out of his wit with a little bran meash with it this diet will breed in they many disease but that they use bath-stove or hothouse in stead of all physic common twice or thrice every week all the winter time bath-stove and almost the whole summer they heat their peach which be make like the German bath-stove and their potlad like oven that so warm the house that a stranger at the first shall hardly like of it these two extremity special in the winter of heat within their house and of extreme cold without together with their diet make they of a dark and sallow complexion their skin be tan and parch both with cold and with heat special the woman that for the great part be of far worse complexion than the man whereof the cause I take to be their keep within the hothouse and busy themselves about the heat and use of their bath-stove and peach the ruff because that he be use to both these extremity of heat and of cold can bear they both a great deal more patient than stranger can do extremity you shall see they sometime to season their body come out of their bath-stove all on a froth and fume as hot almost as a pig at a spit and present to leap into the river stark naked or to pour cold water all over their body and that in the cold of all the winter time the woman to mend the bad hue of their skin use to paint their face with white and red colour women-dawbers so visible that every man may perceive it which be make no matter because it be common and like well by their husband who make their wife and daughter a ordinary allowance to buy they colour to paint their face withal and delight themselves much to see they of foul woman to become such fair image this parch the skin and help to deform they when their paint be of they apparel themselves after the greek manner the nobleman attire be on this fashion first a Taffia or little night cap on his head that cover little more than his crown common very rich wrought of silk and gold thread and set with pearl and precious stone the nobleman attire his head he keep shave close to the very skin except he be in some displeasure with the emperor then he suffer his hair to grow and hang down upon his shoulder cover his face as ugly and deform as he can over the Taffia he wear a wide cap of black fox which they account for the best fur with a Tiara or long bonnet put within it stand up like a persian or babylonian Hat about his neck which be see all bare be a choler set with pearl and precious stone about three or foure-finger broad next over his shirt which be curious wrought because he strip himself into it in the sommer-time while he be within the house be a shepon or light garment of silk make down to the knee button before and then a Caftan or a close coat button and gird to he with a persian girdle whereat he hang his knife and spoon this common be of cloth of gold and hang down as low as his ankle over that he wear a loose garment of some rich silk fur and face about with some gold lace call a Ferris another over that of chamblet or like Stuffe call a Alkaben sleeve and hang low and the cape common brooch and set all with pearl when he go abroad he cast over all these which be but sleight though they seem to be many another garment call a honoratkey like to the Alkaben save that it be make without a choler for the neck and this be common of fine cloth or camel hair his buskin which he wear in stead of hose with linen under they in stead of boot-hose be make of a persian leather call saphian embroider with pearl his upper stock common be of cloth of Gold when he go abroad he mount on horseback though it be but to the next door which be the manner also of the Boiarskey or gentleman the Boiarskey or gentleman attire be of the same fashion but differ in Stuffe and yet he will have his caftan or vnder-coat sometime of cloth of gold the rest of cloth or silk the gentleman apparel the noblewomans attire vhe noble woman call china Boiarshena wear on her head first a cawl of some soft silk which be common call red and over it a fruntlet call Obrosa of white colour over the fleming and dane be to the northwards as aforesaid which do yearly hinder the company ship from make a voyage @. 3 the description of the several sort of whale with the manner of kill they whereto be add the description of greenland the whale be a fish or sea-beast of a huge bigness about sixty five * * the ordinary grow whale fin foot long and thirty five foot thick his head be a three part of all his body quantity his spacious mouth contain a very great tongue and all his fin which we call whale fin these fin be fasten or root in his upper chap and spread over his tongue on both side his mouth be in number about two hundred and fifty on one side and as many on the other side the long fin be place in the midst of his mouth and the rest do shorten by their proportionable degree backward and forward from ten or eleven foot long to four inch in length small eye some kind have great stow mention one take on tenet shore the eye of which be a cart-loade a man may stand in the hole upright the like we may guess of the throat etc. nature be herein luxuriant and diversify his eye be not much big than a ox eye his body be in fashion almost round forward grow on still narrow towards his tail from his belly his tayl^ be about twenty foot broad and of a tough solid substance which we use for block to chop the blubber on which yield oil and of like nature be his two swim fin and they grow forward on he this creature come oftentimes above water spout eight or nine time before he go down again whereby he may be descry two or three league off then our whale-killer present row forth from the place where they stand to watch for he make what haste they can to meet he but common before they come near he he will be go down again and continue a good while before he rise so that sometime they row past he yet be they very circumspect ever look round where they may espy he rise or discern his way under water which they call his walk when he be up and the shallop near he they row towards he very resolute as if they will force the shallop upon he if he go down under water but the Harponyre who stand up in the head of the boat dart his harpingiron at the whale with both his hand so soon as he come within his reach wherewith the whale be strike present descend to the bottom and therefore do they rear out a rope of two hundred fathom which be fasten to the harpingiron and lie coil in the boat and they let he have as much of the rope as reach to the bottom and when they perceive he rise they hale in the rope to get near he and when the whale come up above water then do the man lance he with their lance either out of one shallop or the other for most common there be two shallop about the kill of one whale in lance he they strike near to the fin he swim withal and as low under water near his belly as convenient they can you may see this story of the whale-killing present lively in the map which captain edge have liberal add to this relation but when he be lance he frisk and strike with his tail so forcible that many time when he hit a shallop he split she in piece so that the man be relieve and take in by another shallop and sometime he strike so full upon they that some of the man be either maim or kill with his stroke therefore they who undertake this business which be the principal thing in the voyage must not only be bold and resolute but also discreet and wary otherwise their rash forwardness may prevent they of their expect conquest consider they have no shield to withstand the offend beast their enemy but only by a heedful wariness to avoid the receive of his dangerous stroke swim be also requisite for a whale-killer to be expert in for it may be a mean to save his life when he have lose his boat and another be not near present to help he the whale have receive his deadly wound than he spout blood whereas former he cast forth water and his strength begin to fail he but before he die he will sometime draw the shallop three or four mile from the place where he be first strike and as he be a die he turn his belly upward which lie uppermost be dead then they fasten a rope to his tail and with the shallop one make fast to another they tow he towards the ship with his tail foremost then do they lay he cross the stern of the ship where he be cut up in this manner two or three man in a boat or shallop come close to the side of the whale and hold the boat fast there with a boat-hooke and another stand either in the boat or most common upon the whale cut the fat which we call blubber in square piece with a cut knife three or four foot long then to raze it from the flesh there be a crane or Capsten place purposely upon the poop of the ship from whence there descend a rope with a hook in it this hook be make to take hold on a piece of blubber and as the man wind the Capsten so the cutter with his long knife lose the fat from the flesh even as if the lard of a swine be to be cut off from the lean when a piece be in order cut off then let they lower the crane and let down the blubber to float upon the water and make a hole in some part of it put a rope through it and so they proceed to cut off more fasten ten or twenty piece together to be tow a shore at one time be make fast to the stern of a boat or shallop these piece be thus bring unto the shore side they be draw by one and one upon the shore with a high crane or carry up by two man on a barrow unto a stage there to be cut into small piece about a foot long but thin than it be carry unto the chopper by two boy with two little hand-hooke take in each hand a piece and so they put it into half-tub which stand behind the chopper out of which the chopper take it up who stand at the side of a boat which be raise of a equal height fit for the furnace and the boat be fit with all thing necessary for the chopper they place the chap block which they make of the whale tail and the blubber be lay ready for they as they use it in small piece upon the board whereon they stand then the chopper take it up with hand-hooke and lay it on their block and chop it in thin piece the thin he cut it the better it be and when it be chap they put it off the block down into the shallop with a short paddle make like a colerake and thus do six or eight man stand chap on the one side of the boat and on the other side of the boat about two or three yard distant be the furnace and copper place and heat then between the chap boat and the copper be lay a broad thick plank on which stand a hogshead which contain as much as be put into the copper at one time for one boil and the tub be empty be make to slide unto the chap boat again be there fill with a copper ladle again and put into another copper when it be boil enough the small piece of blubber which we call fritter will look brown as if they be fry then be they take out with copper ladle and some of the oil also with they and put into a barrow make close to dreyne the oil which stand over another shallop that be set on the backside of the furnace to receive the oil in and as soon as the fritter be take clean out of the copper then present be the tub of small blubber empty into the copper again to be also boil the boat into which the hot oil be put out of the copper be ever keep half full of water which do not only cool the oil before it run into the cask but also be a cleanser of it from dross which descend to the bottom of the Boat out of the oyle-boat do the oil run thirty or forty yard in trough or gutter and so into butt or hogshead which be fill be roll off to cool and another cask lay to fill and when there be any quantity of oil make it be carry aboard the ship in raft in this manner be the oil save and prepare now concern the whale fin whale fin the whale head be cut off from the body as he float at the stern of the ship where he be cut up be tow by a boat as near the shore as it will come but it be aground in twelve or thirteen foot water then by crab which be place on land it be draw on land at several time when the water be at high so near the dry shore that man at a low water with their boat on cut off the blubber and fin which by the crab be draw on shore and the fin be with axe one sever from another and be make clean be pack up by fifty in a bundle and so ship there be eight several kind of whale and differ the one from the other in goodness quantity and quality eight kind of whale know the first sort of whale be call the grand-bay take his name from grand-bay in newfoundland as have there be first kill he be black of colour with a smooth skin 1. bay whale and white underneath the chap this whale be the best for oil and fin of all the rest and do yield most the elder it grow this sort of whale do yield about a hundred hogshead of oil and some five hundred fin the second sort of whale be call Sarda of the same colour as the former 2. Sarda but somewhat lesser and the fin likewise lesser and yield in oil according to his bigness sometime seventy hogshead or eighty hogshead this whale have natural grow upon his back white thing like unto barnacle the three sort of whale be call Trumpa be as long as the first but thick forward 3. Trumpa of colour more gray than the former have but one spout in his head and the rest have all two he have in his mouth tooth about a span long and as thick as a man wrist but no fin his head be big than the two former and in proportion far big than his body in the head of this whale be the permesitie which lie there in a hole like a well spermacoete this be the whale that be suppose to yield the ambergris there take about forty hogshead of oil beside the permesitie the four sort of whale be call Otta Sotta and be of the same colour of the Trumpa 4. Otta Sotta have fin in his mouth all white but not above half a yard long be thick than the Trumpa but not so long he yield the best oil but not above thirty hogshead the five sort of whale be call Gibarta of colour black like the two first 5. save that it have stand upon the top of his back a fin half a yard long this whale be as big as the first his fin little or nothing worth be not above half a yard long and he yield about twelve hogshead of oil all which his back yield as for his belly it yield nothing at all 6. Sedeva the six ^ort be call Sedeva be of a whit colour and big than any of the former the fin not above one foot long and he yield little or no oil 7. negro the seven be call Sedeva negro of colour black with a bumpe on his back this whale yield neither oil fin nor tooth and yet he be of a great bigness 8. Sewria the eight sort be call Sewria of colour as white as snow of the bigness of a wherrie he yield not above one hogshead or two of oil nor any fin and be good meat to be eat the description of greenland antiphrastical appellation I have find this description of greenland with other note write by ro. Fotherbie dear GReenland be a place in nature nothing like unto the name for certain there be no place in the world yet know and discover that be less green than it it be cover with snow both the mountain and the low land till about the begin of june be very mountainous and bear neither grass nor tree save only such as grow upon the moor and heathie ground in the north part of England which we call heath or ling. this grow when the snow melt and when the ground begin to be uncover and on this do the deer feed in the summer time and become very fat therewithal in a month space but how they live in the winter time it be not easy to be imagine for see at the end of may we find the ground all cover with snow it be very like that in the time of winter there be no part bare where any thing can grow especial during the time that the sun be altogether depress under the horizon which in the latitude of 77. degree continue from the eighteen of October till the four of February this country by all probability have never be inhabit by any people notwithstanding I think man may live there carry thither good store of provision of victual and other thing necessary against the cold which perhaps will be vehement in the winter time by the former reason namely because the sun remain so long under the horizon nevertheless there will not be any continuance of darkness because the sun in his great declination will be but 10. degree under the horizon at this time of his be in the south of the meridian in the former latitude of 77. degree which be once in four and twenty hour and therefore the time of their noon will be much light than our night here in England when the day be at the long for than be the sun 15. degree under the horizon at midnight and yet the great darkness be but like twilight and although it be a general say and a common receive opinion that the further north the great cold yet experience teach that it be not always true for at M^sco and thereabouts in the winter time there be extreme frost and cold weather insomuch that oftentimes man be bring home dead be starve with cold and many have their nose and ear cause to fall off through the extremity of the pierce air yet at Edenborrow which be more northerly by one degree and a half and in all place near unto it the air be temperate and the cold tolerable the snow never lie any long time on the ground after it be fall notwithstanding we have snow remain all the year long in diverse place of England but the reason of this be because the air be ever warm near unto the sea shore yet in China even near the sea and far near the sun betwixt 30. and 40. the winter be extreme ^ Foth as Edenborrow stand and contrariwise the cold be most vehement in place which be far remote from the sea as Moscow be situate all the creature that appear unto we upon the land be dear bear and fox and sundry sort of wild fowl as Cuthbert duck willocke stint sea-pigeon sea-parrets gull noddy etc. the author employ therein chap. 3 the first navigation of WILLIAM barent alias Bernard into the north sea write by G^RAT veer it be a most certain and a assure assertion that nothing do more benefit and further the commonwealth special these country than the art and knowledge of navigation in regard that such country and nation as be strong and mighty at sea have the mean and ready way to draw fetch and bring unto they for their maintenance all the princpal commodity and fruit of the earth in these navigation we must not be dismay if some mislike or if we can perfect a discovery in the first second or three voyage Alexander Magnus after he have win all Grecia a thing not continue can be effect all thing be effect in convenient time and from thence enter into little and great Asia and come to the far part of India there find some difficulty to pass say if we have not go forward and persist in our intent which other man esteem and hold to be impossible we have still remain and stay in the entry of Cicilia where as now we have overrun and pass through all those large and spacious country for nothing be find and effect all at one time neither be any thing that be put in practice present bring to a end to the which end cicero wise say God have give we some thing and not all thing that our successor also may have somewhat to do therefore we must not leave off nor stay our pretence in the middle of our proceed as long as there be any commodity to be hope and in time to be obtain for that the great and rich treasure be hardly to be find I think good to set down in regard that I have undertake to describe the three voyage make into the north sea in three year one after the other behind Norwary and along and about Muscovia towards the kingdom of Cathaia and China whereof the two last I myself help to effect and yet bring they not to the desire end that we well hope first to show our diligent and most toilsome labour and pain take the first find be hard but the second attempt be easy to find out the right course which we can not bring to pass as we well hope wish and desire and possible may have find it by cross the sea if we have take the right course if the ice and the shortness of time and bad cross have not hinder we we have assure find that the only and most hindrance to our voyage be the ice that we find about Zembla under 73.74.75 and 76. degree and not so much upon the sea between both the land whereby it appear that not the nearness of the north-pole but the ice that come in and out from the tartarian sea about Zembla cause we to feel the great cold therefore in regard that the nearness of the pole be not the cause of the great cold that we feel if we have have the mean to have hold our appoint and intend course into the north-east we have peradventure find some entrance which course we can not hold from Zembla because that there we enter among great store of ice and how it be about Zembla we can not tell before we have seek it and when we have seek it we can not then alter our course although also it be uncertain what we shall have do if we have continue in our north-east course because it be not yet find out but it be true that in the country lie under 80. degree which we esteem to be greenland there be both leave and grass to be see wherein such beast as feed of leave and grass as heart hind and such like beast live whereas to the contrary in Zembla there grow neither leave nor grass and there be no beast therein but such as eat flesh as bear and fox etc. although Zembla lie 4.5 and 6. degree more southerly from the pole a comparison of the heat under the line with the cold under the north Pole than the other land aforesaid it be also manifest that upon the south and north-side of the line of the sun on both side between both the tropic under 23. degree and a half yet it be as hot as it be right under the line what wonder then shall it be that about the north-pole also and as many degree on both side it shall not be cold than right under the pole it be not the sea nor the nearness unto the pole but the ice about the land that let and hinder we as I say before for that assoon as we make from the land and put more into the sea although it be much further northward present we feel more warmth the resolute intent and opinion of William barent and in that opinion our pilot William barent die who notwithstanding the fearful and intolerable cold that he endure yet he be not discourage but offer to lay wager with diverse of we that by God help he will bring that pretend voyage to a end if he hold his course north-east from the north cape but I will leave that and show you of the three voyage aforesaid begin and set forth by the permission and furtherance of the general state of the unite declaration of barent his second navigation make in 1595. behind Norway Muscovia and Tartary write by veer the four ship aforesaid be return home about harvest-time in 1594. they be in good hope that the voyage aforesaid will be do by pass along the straits of weygate and special by the report make by the two ship of Zelandt and enckhuysen wherein John of Linschoten be committee who declare the manner of their travel in such sort that the general state and prince Maurice resolve in the begin of the next year to prepare certain ship not only as they go before to discover the passage but to send certain ware and merchandize thither wherein the merchant may lade what ware they will with certain factor to sell the say ware in such place as they shall arrive neither pay freight nor custom Peter Plantius a learned cosmographer be a great furtherer and setter forward of this voyage and be their chief instructor therein set down the situation of the coast of Tartary Cathaia and China but how they lie it be not yet sufficient discover for that the course and rule by he set down be not full effect by mean of some inconvenience that fall out which by reason of the shortness of time can not be holpen in 1595. the general state of the unite province and prince Maurice cause seven ship to be prepare to sail through the weygate or the straits of Nassaw to the kingdom of Cathaia and China two out of Amsterdam two out of Zelandt two out of enckhuysen and one out of Rotterdam six of they lade with diverse kind of ware merchandize and with money and factor to sell the say ware the seven be a pinnace that have commission when the other ship be pass about the cape Tabin which be the further point of Tartary or so far that they may sail forth southward without any let or hindrance of the ice to turn back again and to bring news thereof and I be in William barent ship that be our chief pilot james Hemskerke famous for the Gibraltar exploit and james Hemskerke chief factor think good to write down the same in order as it be hereafter declare as I do the first voyage according to the course and stretch of the land as it lie first after we have be muster at Amsterdam and every man take a oath that be then purposely minister unto we upon the eighteen of june we sail to the texel from thence to put to sea with other ship that be appoint to meet we at a certain day and so to begin our voyage in the name of God the second of july we set sail out of the texel the five of August the north cape lie about two mile east from we and when the sun be northwest the mother and her samoy apparel the manner of their apparel be like as we use to paint wildman but they be not wild for they be of reasonable judgement they be apparel in heart skin from the head to the foot unless it they be for the most part all short and low of stature with broad flat face small eye short leg their knee stand outward and be very quick to go and leap they trust not stranger for although that we show they all the courtesy and friendship that we can yet they trust we not much which we perceive hereby that as upon the first of September we go again on land to they and that one of our man desire at last one of our man go near to one of the sentinel to speak with he and offer he great friendship according to their accustom manner withal give he a biscuit which he with great thanks take and in they that our horse be not able to follow they one of our man shoot a musket towards the sea wherewith they be in so great fear that they run and leap like mad man yet at last they satisfy themselves when they perceive that it be not malicious do to hurt they and we tell they by our interpreter that we use our piece in stead of bow whereat they wonder because of the great blow and noise that it give and make and to show they what we can do therewith one of our man take a flat stone about half a handful broad and set it upon a hill a good way off from he which they perceive and think that we mean somewhat thereby fifty or sixty of they gather round about we and yet somewhat far off wherewith he that have the piece shoot it off and with the bullet smite the stone in sunder whereat they wonder much more than before departure after that we take our leaf one of the other with great friendship on both side and when we be in our pinnace we all put off our hat and bow our head unto the other two come close to the ship which we perceive make our piece ready to shoot at they at which time there stand a tub full of beef upon the ice which lie in the water to be season for that close by the ship there be no water one of the bear go unto it and put in his head to take out a piece of the beef but she fare therewith as the dog do with the pudding for as she be snatch at the beef she be shoot into the head wherewith she fall down dead and never stir the other bear stand still and look upon her fellow and when she have stand a good while she smell her fellow and perceive that she be dead she run away but we take halber^s and other arm with we and follow she and at last she come again towards we and we prepare ourselves to withstand she wherewith she rise up upon her hinder foot think to ramp at we but while she rear herself up one of our man shoot she into the belly and with that she fall upon her fore-feet again and roar as loud as she can run away then we take the dead bear and rip her belly open and take out her gut we set she upon her fore-feet that so she may freeze as she stand intend to carry she with we into Holland if we may get our ship loose and that time it freeze two finger thick in the salt water and it be exceed cold the wind blow north-east the sixteen the sun shine but towards the evening it be misty the wind be easterly at which time east and east north-east that day our carpenter be of Pur^e^aet die as we come aboard about evening the four and twenty we bury he under the sedge in the cleft of a hill hard by the water for we can not dig up the earth by reason of the great frost and cold and that day we go twice with our sled to fetch wood the five and twenty it be dark wether the wind blow west and west south-west house build and south-west and the ice begin somewhat to open and drive away but it continue not long for that have drive about the length of the shot of a great piece it lay three fathom deep upon the ground and where we lie the ice drive not for we lie in the middle of the ice but if we have lie in the main sea we will have hoist sail although it be then late in the year the same day we raise up the principle of our house and begin to work hard thereon but if the ship have be loose we will have leave our build and have make our after Steven of our ship that we may have be ready to sail away if it have be possible the six and twenty we have a west wind and a open sea but our ship lie fast wherewith we be not a little grieve but it be god will which we most patient bare and we begin to make up our house part of our man fetch wood to burn the rest play the carpenter and be busy about the house as than we be sixteen man in all for our carpenter be dead and of our sixteen man there be still one or other sick the seven and twenty it blow hard north-east and it freeze so hard that as we put a nail into our mouth as when man work carpenter work they use to do there will ice hang thereon when we take it out again and make the blood follow hard and violent frost the same day there come a old bear and a young one towards we as we be go to our house be all together for we dare not go alone which we think to shoot at but she run away at which time the ice come forcible drive in and it be fair sunshine weather but so extreme cold that we can hardly work but extremity force we thereunto the eight and twenty it be fair weather and the sun shine the wind be west and very calm the sea as then be open but our ship lie fast in the ice and stir not the same day there come a bear to the ship but when she espy we she run away and we make as much haste as we can to build our house the nine and twenty in the morning the wind be west and afternoon it blow northerly and then we see three bear between we and the house a old one and two young but we notwithstanding draw our good from the ship to the house and so get before the bear and yet they follow we nevertheless we will not shun the way for they but hollow out as loud as we can think that they will have go away but they will not once go out of their footpath but get before we wherewith we and they that be at the house make a great noise which make the bear run away and we be not a little glad thereof the thirty the wind be east and east southeast and all that night and the next day it snow so fast that our man can fetch no wood it lay so close and high one upon the other then we make a great fire without the house therewith to thaw the ground that so we may lay it about the house that it may be the close ground not to be thaw but it be all lose labour for the earth be so hard and freeze so deep into the ground that we can not thaw it and it will have cost we too much wood and therefore we be force to leave off that labour @. 2 their cold comfortless dark and dreadful winter the sun absence moon light sun unexpected return with miraculous speed of bear fox and many many wonder the first of October the wind blow stiff north-east and afternoon it blow north with a great storm and drift of snow whereby we can hardly go in the wind and a man can hardly draw his breath the snow drive so hard in our face at which time we can not see two ship length from we the second before noon the sun shine and after noon it be cloudy again and it snow but the weather be still the wind be north maypole of snow and not work at that time we bring our anchor upon the ice to lie the fast when we lie but a arrow shoot from the water the ice be so much drive away the five it blow hard northwest and the sea be very great cold the seven it be indifferent good weather but yet very cold and we calk our house and break the ground about it at the foot thereof extreme snow that day the wind go round about the compass the eight all the night before it blow so hard and the same day also and snow so fast that we shall have smother if we have go out into the air and to speak truth it have not be possible for any man to have go one ship length though his life have lie thereon for it be not possible for we to go out of the house or ship the nine the wind still continue north hence it may seem that the course of the tide and sea be from the north. and blue and snow hard all that day the wind as then blow from the land so that all that day we be force to stay in the ship the weather be so foul the ten the weather be somewhat fair and the wind calm and blue south-west and west and south-west and that time the water flow two foot high than ordinary which we guess to proceed from the first northwind which as then have blow the same day the weather begin to be somewhat better so that we begin to go out of our ship again and as one of our man go out he chance to meet a bear and be almost at he before he know it but present he run back again towards the ship and the bear after he but the bear come to the place where before we have kill another bear and set she upright and there let she freeze which be cover over with ice and yet one of her paw reach about it she stand still whereby our man get before she and climb up into the ship in great fear cry a bear a bear which we hear come above hatch to look on but by reason of the cold and snowy weather we be constrain to do it if we will save our life for aloft in the ship we must undoubted have die the bear stay not long there but run away the wind then blue north and somewhat westerly and then half of our man keep in the house and that be the first time that we lie in it but we endure great cold because our cabin be not make and beside that we have but a few clothes in it the fourteen as we come out of the ship we find the barrel of beer stand upon the sled but it be fast freeze at the head yet by reason of the great cold the beer that purge out there be scant any unfrozen beer in the barrel beer melt but in that thick yeast that be unfrozen lie the strength of the beer so that it be too strong to drink alone and that which be freeze taste like water and be melt we mix one with the other and so drink it but it have neither strength nor taste the fifteen the wind blue north and east and east southeast that day we make place to set up our Decem. which be the further sign that the sun pass on the southside of the line and from thence it turn northward again the four and twenty be Christmas eeven it be fair weather than we open our door ill sign because we can not take they to put they into the pot or roast they for that have be a very good sign for we the six and twenty it be foul weather the wind northwest and it be so cold that we can not warm we although we use all the mean we can with great fire cold invincible good store of clothes and with hot stone and billet lay upon our foot and upon our body as we lie in our cabin but notwithstanding all this in the morning our cabin be freeze which make we behold one the other with sad countenance but yet we comfort ourselves again as well as we can that the sun be then as low as it can go and that it now begin to come to we again and we find it to be true for that the day beginning to lengthen the cold begin to strengthen but hope put we in good comfort and ease our pain the seven and twenty it be still foul weather with a northwest wind so that as than we have not be out in three day together nor dare not thrust our head out of door and within the house it be so extreme cold burn before freeze behind that as we sit before a great fire and seem to burn on the fore-side we freeze behind at our back and be all white as the countryman use to be when they come in at the gate of the town in Holland with their sled and have go all night the eight and twenty it be still foul weather with a west wind but about eevening it begin to clear up at which time one of our man make a hole open at one of our door and go out to see what news abroad snow high than the house but find it so hard weather that he stay not long and tell we that it have snow so much that the snow lie high than our house and that if he have stay out long his ear will undoubted have be freeze off the nine and twenty it be calm weather and a pleasant air the wind be southward that day he who turn it be open the door and dig a hole through the snow where we go out of the house upon step snow-step as if it have be out of a cellar at least seven or eight step high each step a foot from the other and then we make clean our spring for the fox whereof for certain day we have not take any and as we make they clean one of our man find a dead fox in one of they that be freeze as hard as a stone which he bring into the house and thaw it before the fire and after flay it some of our man eat it the thirty it be foul weather again with a storm out of the west and great store of snow so that all the labour and pain that we have take the day before to make step to go out of our house and to cleanse our spring be all in vain for it be all cover over with snow again high than it be before the one and thirty it be still foul weather with a storm out of the northwest whereby we be so fast shut up into the house as if we have be prisoner and it be so extreme cold that the fire almost cast no heat fire conquer heat smell before feel for as we put our foot to the fire we burn our hose before we can feel the heat so that we have work enough to do to patch our hose and which be more if we have not soon smell then feel they we shall have burn they ere we have know it after that with great cold danger and disease we have bring this year unto a end we enter into the year of our lord God 1597. the beginning whereof be in the same manner as the end of 1596. have be an. dom. 1597. for the weather continue as cold foul and snowy january as it be before so that upon the first of january we be enclose in the house the wind then be west at the same time we agree to share our wine every man a small measure full and that but once in two day and as we be in great care and fear that it second it blow hard with a west wind and a great storm with both snow and frost so that in four or five day we dare not put our head out of the door and as then by reason of the great cold we have almost burn all our wood notwithstanding we dare not go out to fetch more wood because it freeze so hard and there be no be without the door but seek about we find some piece of wood that lie over the good reckon you must understand that when we first see the sun it be in the five degr. and 25. min. of Aquarius and it shall have stay according to our first guess till it have enter into the 16. deg. be freeze we use our hourglass of twelve hour long whereupon we argue with ourselves in diverse wise to know how we shall find out that difference and leave the truth of the time which to try we agree to look into the ephemeris make by josephus Sch^la print in Venice for the year of our lord 1589. till a. 1600. and we find therein that upon the four and twenty day of january when the sun first appear unto we that at Venice the clock be one in the night time the moon and jupiter be in conjunction whereupon we seek to know when the same conjunction shall be over or about the house where we than be and at last we find that the four and twenty day of january be the same day whereon the conjunction aforesaid happen in Venice difference of longitude betwixt Venice and their winter place at one of the clock in the night and with we in the morning when the sun be in the east for we see manifest that the two planet aforesaid approach near unto each other until such time as the moon and jupiter stand one just over the other both in the sign of Taurus and that be at six of the clock in the morning at which time the moon and jupiter be find by our compass to be in conjunction over our house in the north and by east-point and the south part of the compass be south south-west and there we have it right south the moon be eight day old whereby it appear that the sun and the moon be eight point different and this be about six of the clock in the morning this place differ from Venice five hour in longitude whereby we may guess how much we be near east than the city of Venice which be five hour each hour be 15. degree which be in all 75. degree that we be more easterly than Venice by all which it be manifest to be see that we have not fail in our account and that also we have find our right longitude by the two planet aforesaid for the town of Venice lie under 37. degree and 25. minute in longitude and her declination be 46. degree and 5. minute whereby it follow that our place of Zembla lie under 112. degree and 25. minute in longitude and the height of the pole 76. degree and so you have the right longitude and latitude but from the uttermost point of Zembla to the point of cape Tabin the uttermost point of Tarta^ia where it wind southward the longitude differ 60. degree but you must understand note for deg. of longitude that the degree be not so great as they be under the equinoctial line for right under the line a degree be fifteen mile but when you leave the line either northward or southward than the degree in longitude do lessen so that the near that a and be in great haste and fear can not bar it with the piece of wood that we use thereunto but the bear see that the door be shut she go back again and within two hour after she come again and go fourteen it be fair clear weather with a west wind than we see great hill of ice round about the ship than over we have see before which be a fearful thing to behold and much to be wonder at that the ship be not smite in piece the fifteen it be fair calm weather with a north wind than seven of we go aboard the ship to see in what case it be and find it to be all in one sort and as we come back again there come a great bear towards we against who we begin to make defence but she perceive that make away from we and we go to the place from whence she come to see her den bear den. where we find a great hole make in the ice about a man length in depth the entry thereof be very narrow and within wide there we thrust in our pike to feel if there be any thing within it but perceive it be empty one of our man creep into it but not too far for it be fearful to behold after that we go along by the seaside and there we see that in the end of march and the beginning of April the ice be in such wonderful manner rise and pile up one upon the other that it be wonderful in such manner as if there have be whole town make of ice with tower and bulwark round about they the sixteen it be foul house we can not do it because we be too weak wherewith we become whole out of heart doubt that we shall not be able to go forward with our labour but the master encourage we bid we strive to do more than we be able say that both our life and our welfare consist therein and that if we can not get the scute from thence and make it ready than he say we must dwell there as burgher of Zembla burgher of Zembla and make our grave in that place but there want no goodwill in we but only strength which make we for that time to leave off work and let the scute lie still which be no small grief unto we and trouble to think what be best for we to do but after noon be thus comfortless come home we take heart again and determine to turn the boat that lie by the house with her keel upward and to amend it that it may be the fit to carry we over the sea for we make full account that we have a long troublesome voyage in hand wherein we may have many cross and wherein we shall not be sufficient provide for all thing necessary although we take never so much care and while we be busy about our work there come a great bear unto we wherewith we go into our house and stand to watch she in our three door with harquebuse and one stand in the chimney with a musket this bear come bold unto we then ever any have do before for she come to the neither step that go to one of our door and the man that stand in the door see she not because he look towards the other door but they that stand within see she and in great fear call to he wherewith he turn about and although he be in a maze he shoot at she and the bullet past clean through her body whereupon she run away yet it be a fearful thing to see for the bear be almost upon he before he see she so that if the piece have fail to give fire as oftentimes they do it have cost he his life and it may be that the bear will have get into the house the bear be go somewhat from the house lie down wherewith we go all arm and kill she out right and when we have rip open her belly buck we find a piece of a buck therein with hair skin and all which not long before she have tear and devour the one and thirty of May it be fair weather but somewhat cold than before the wind be south-west whereby the ice drive away and we wrought hard about our boat but when we be in the chief part of work there come another bear as if they have smell that we will be go and that therefore they desire to taste a piece of some of we for that be the three day one after the other that they set so fierce upon we so that we be force to leave our work and go into the house and she follow we but we stand with our piece to watch she and shoot three piece at she two from our door and one out of the chimney which all three hit she but her death do we more hurt than her life for after we rip her belly we dress her liver and eat it which in the taste like we well but it make we all sick special three that be exceed sick bear liver venomous and we very think that we shall have lose they for all their skin come off from the foot to the head but yet they recover again june the three of june in the morning it be fair clear weather the wind west and then we be somewhat better and take great pain with the boat that at last we get it ready after we have wrought six day upon it about evening it begin to blow hard and therewith the water be very open which wild desert irksome fearful and cold country the five it be foul weather with great store of hail and snow the wind west which make a open water but as then we can do nothing without the house but fall not out so unfortunate the twelve it be indifferent fair weather than we go with hatchet halberd shovel and other instrument to make the way plain where we shall draw the scute and the boat to the water side along the way that lay full of knob and hill of ice where we wrought sore with our hatchet and other instrument and while we be in the chief of our work there come a great lean bear out of the sea upon the ice towards we which we judge to come out of Tartary for we have see of they twenty or thirty mile within the sea and for that we have no musket but only one which our surgeon carry I run in great haste towards the ship to fetch one or two which the bear perceive run after i and be very likely to have over take i but our company see that leave their work and run after she which make the bear turn towards they and leave i but when she run towards they she be shoot into the body by the surgeon and run away but because the ice be so uneven and hilly she can not go far but be by we overtake we kill she out right and smite her tooth out of her head while she be yet live bear slay the thirteen it be fair weather than the master and the carpenter go to the ship and there come back to the house again and there he speak unto William barent that have be long sick and show he that he think it good they depart see it be a fit time to go from thence and so will the company to drive the boat and the scute down to the water side and in the name of God to begin our voyage to sail from Zembla then William barent write a letter which he put in a musket charge and hang it up in the chimney show how he come out of Holland to sail to the kingdom of China and what have happen unto we be there on land with all our cross that if any man chance to come thither they may know what have happen unto we and how we have be force in our extremity to make that house and have dwell ten month therein and for that we be put to sea in two small open boat and to undertake a dangerous and adventurous voyage in hand the master write two letter which most of we subscribe unto signify how we have stay there upon the land in great trouble and misery in hope that our ship will be free from the ice and that we shall sail away with it again and how it fall out to the contrary and that the ship lie fast in the ice so that in the end the time pass away and our victual begin to fail we we be force for the save of our own life to leave the ship and to sail away in our open boat and so to commit ourselves into the hand of God which do he put into each of our scute a letter that if we chance to lose one another or that by storm or any other misadventure we happen to be cast away that then by the scute that escape man may know how we leave each other and so have finish all thing as stone upon the cliff the sixteen we set sail again and get to the island of orange with a south wind which be eight mile distant from the point of desire there we go on land with two small barrel and a kettle to melt snow and to put the water into the barrel as also to seek for bird and egg to make meat for our sick man we put to the sea again with a southeast wind and drowsy misel weather whereby we be all dankish and wet for we have no shelter in our open scute and sail west and west and by south to the ice-point and we make our scute fast to a great piece of ice and there eat somewhat but the weather be still foul and foul so that we be once again enclose with ice and force to stay there the seventeen in the morning when we have break our fast the ice come so fast upon we that it make our hair stare upright upon our head it be so fearful to behold by which mean we can not make fast our scute so that we think very that it be a foreshow of our last end for we drive away so hard with the ice and be so sore press between a flake of ice that we think very the scute will burst in a hundred piece at last be in this discomfort and extreme necessity the master say if we can take hold with a rope upon the fast ice we may therewith draw the scute up and so get it out of the great drift of ice but as this counsel be good yet it be so full of danger that it be the hazard of his life that shall take upon he to do it and without do it be it most certain that it will cost we all our life this counsel as I say be good but no man like to the tale of the mouse dare hang the bell about the cat neck fear to be drown yet necessity require to have it do and the most danger make we choose the least so that be in that perplexity I be the light of all our company dangerous attempt to draw the boat over the ice take on i to fasten a rope upon the fast ice and so creep from one piece of drive ice to another by god help get to the fast ice where I make a rope fast to a high Howell and they that be in the scute draw it thereby unto the say fast ice and then one man alone can draw more than all of they can have do before and when we have get thither in all haste we take our sick man out and lay they upon the ice lay clothes and other thing under they and then take all our good out of the scute and so draw they upon the ice whereby for that time we be deliver from that great danger make account that we have escape out of death claw as it be most true the eighteen we repair and amend our scute again be much bruise and crush with the rack of the ice and be force to drive all the nail fast again and to piece many thing about they God send we wood wherewith we melt our pitch and do all other thing that belong thereunto that do some of we go upon the land to seek for egg which the sick man long for but we can find none but we find four bird not without great danger of our life between the ice and the firm land wherein we often fall and be in no small danger the nineteen it be indifferent weather the wind northwest and west south-west but we be still shut up in the ice and see no open which make we think that there will be our last abode and that we shall never get from thence w. barent die the twenty claes Adrianson and William barent die the death of William barent put we in no small discomfort as be the chief guide and only pilot on who we repose our self next under God the two and twenty in the morning it blow a good gale out of the southeast and then the sea be reasonable open but we be force to draw our scute over the ice to get unto it and after draw they at the least a hundred pace more over the ice before we can bring they to a good place where we may easy get out and be get unto the open water we commit ourselves to God and set our good fall into the water but we with great diligence draw our scute further upon the ice towards the land where we think to be better defend from the drive of the ice and as we go to fetch our good we fall into the great trouble that ever we have before for that we endure so great danger in the save thereof that as we lay hold upon one piece thereof the rest sink down with the ice and many time the ice break under our own foot whereby we be whole discomfort and in a manner clean out of all hope expect no issue thereof in such sort that our trouble at that time surmount all our former care and impeachment and when we think to draw up our boat upon the ice the ice break under we and we be carry away with the scute and all by the drive ice and when we think to save the good the ice break under our foot and with that the scute break in many place especial that which we have mend as the mast the mast plank and almost all the scute wherein one of our man that be sick and a chest of and our leg at which time think that we have be clean quit of our scute we behold each other in pitiful manner know not what we shall do our life depend thereon but God make so good provision for we that the piece of ice drive from each other wherewith we run in great haste unto the scute and draw it to we again in such case as it be and lay it upon the fast ice by the boat where it be in more security which put we unto a exceed and great and dangerous labour from the time that the sun be southeast until it be west south-west and in all that time we rest not which make we extreme weary and scute up we spread our sail upon they to shelter we under they for it be still misty and rainy weather much desire to hear some news of our man that be go to Coola with the Laplander the nine and twenty we spy the Laplander come alone without our man whereat we wonder and be somewhat in doubt but when he come unto we he show we a letter that be write unto our master which he open before we the content thereof be that he that have write the letter wonder much at our arrival in that place and that long since he very think that we have be all cast away be exceed glad of our happy fortune and how that he will present come unto we with victual and all other necessary to succour we withal we be in no small admiration who it may be that show we so great favour and friendship can not imagine what he be for it appear by the letter that he know we well and although the letter be subscribe by i John Cornelison rip yet we can not be persuade that it be the same John Cornelison who the year before have be set out in the other ship with we and leave we about the bear island for those good news we pay the Laplander his high and beside that give he hose breeches and other furniture so that he be apparel like a Hollander for as then we think ourselves to be whole out of danger and so be of good comfort we lay we down to rest here I can choose but show you how fast the Laplander go for when he go to Coola as our companion tell we they be two day and two night on the way and yet go apace and when he come back again he be but a day and a night come to we which be wonderful it be but half the time so that we say and very think that he be half a conjurer and he bring we a partridge which he have kill by the way as he go the thirty we see a russian jowl come row with John Cornelison and our companion that we have send to Coola who be land we receive and welcome each other with great joy and exceed gladness as if either of we on both side have see each other rise from death to life again for we esteem he and he we to be dead long since he bring we a barrel of Roswicke beer wine vit^ bread flesh Bacon salmon sugar and other thing which comfort and relieve we much and we rejoice together for our so unexpected meeting at that time give God great thanks for his mercy show unto we the first of September in the morning with the east sun September we get to the westside of the river of Coola and enter into it where we row till the flood be past and then we cast the stone that serve we for anchor upon the ground at a point of land till the flood come in again and when the sun be south we set sail again with the flood and so sail and row till midnight and then we cast anchor again till morning the second tree a rare sight in the morning we row up the river and as we pass along we see some tree on the river side which comfort we and make we glad as if we have then come into a new world for in all the time that we have be out we have not see any tree and when we be by the salt kettles which be about three mile from Coola we stay there a while and make merry Coola and then go forward again and with the west northwest sun get to John Cornelisons ship wherein we enter and drink there we begin to make merry again with the sailor that be therein and that have be in the voyage with John Cornelison the year before and bad each other welcome then we row forward and late in the eevening get to Coola where some of we go on land and some stay in the scute to look to the good to who we send milk and other thing to comfort and refresh they and we be all exceed glad that God of his mercy have deliver we out of so many danger and trouble and have bring we thither in safety the three we unlade all our good and there refresh ourselves after our toilsome and weary journey and the great hunger we have endure thereby to recover our health and strength again the eleven by leave and consent of the Bayart th^ir scute and boat lay up for a monument how much more worthy than the old world Argo governor of the great prince of Moscovia we bring our scute and our boat into the merchant house and there let they stand for a remembrance of our long far and never before sail way and that we have sail in those open scute almost four hundred dutch mile through and along by the sea coast to the town of Coola the seventeen of September John Cornelison and our master be come aboard the next day about the east sun we set sail out of the river Coola and with God grace put to sea to sail homeward and be out of the river we sail along by the land northwest Michael the archangel which fall into the white Sea this oneeko be rich as be say have also many child God have large bless and provide he with plenty of all thing yet nevertheless he have a earnest desire and affection to know what country be possess and inhabit by those people which yearly come into Russia to traffic bring with they costly fur and diverse other merchandize much differ in language apparel religion and behaviour call themselves Samoieds and by other unknown name these people come every year down the river Wichida and exchange their commodity with the Russ and moscovite in the town of osel and vstiug on the river Duina which at that time be the receipt and chief mart town of all kind of merchandise but especial of costly fur Oneeko therefore as have be say be most desirous to know from whence these people come or what country they do inhabit easy conjecture that great wealth be there to be get since the fur yearly bring they amount to a great sum of money wherefore secret he get acquaintance and consort himself with diverse of they and send in their company about ten or twelve of his own people into those part enjoin they that through what country so ever they shall travel they shall make diligent search of every particular thing therein and full observe the manner rite dwelling and whole course of life of those nation that at their return they may bring from thence perfect knowledge thereof which they have at length perform he entertain they bountiful at their return and show they all favour but with especial charge to keep silence he likewise keep all these thing close to himself not reveal they to any man the second voyage and the next year follow he send thither a great number of his people join with they certain of his kindred and alliance these carry with they diverse base merchandise as small bell and other like dutch small ware and take diligent notice of every thing in those part and after they have pass many desert and diverse great river they come to the river Obi where make acquaintance and friendship with the many desert and diverse great river river Obi. great wealth to be get by the tr^de to the river of Obi. condition of the people government no Bread shoot apparel house they find that fur be to be have for a small price and that great wealth be there easy to be get and further that this people have not any city but live together in company and peaceable and govern by some of the ancient among they that they be loathsome in their feed and live on the flesh of such beast as they take that they have no knowledge of corn or bread be cunning and skilful archer make their bow of a gentle and flexible kind of wood and that their arrow be head with sharpen stone or fish bone with those they kill wild beast which be exceed plentiful in those place that they sow also with bone of fish serve they for needle their thread be make of the sinew of certain small beast and so they sew together the fur wherewith they clothe themselves the furrie side in summer turn outward and in winter inward that they cover their house with the skin of elke and such like beast little esteem among they final these messenger of Oneeko search curious into every matter and return home store with costly fur now when as Oneeko understand by their report that which he so much long to know he together with certain by which customer the town of Pechora be now govern since there be no gentleman send from the Moscow this man give they good entertainment and send up with they a man of his own fear that the people will be amaze at our man sudden and unexpected come our man arrive at town of Pechora people afraid of the English yet as soon as they espy our people they be all exceed afraid diverse of they with their woman flee into the wood until that one of the chief customer have send for they other customer who at that time be all out of town but be meet together master logan show they the privilege of the good which he have leave there and that he do purpose to return again to island with as much speed as can be make subscribe Thomas edge at our come to the island we have three or four day together very fine weather in which time come in reasonable store of morse both at the south Cove and at the north-side and we be in good hope we shall have make a save voyage nevertheless though there be store of beast morse fearful yet by no mean will they go on those beache and place that former they have be kill on but forty or fifty of they together go into little hole within the rock which be so little steep and slippery that as soon as we do approach towards they they will tumble all into the Sea the like whereof by the master and William gourdon report be never do for lie as they do and be so shey as they be it be not possible to do any good upon they moreover to get they off these foresay rock to make they come on shore upon their accustom place the master and our man on both side of the island go to drive they away yet they will not but by often drive of they out of their hole we kill as many as we can in the end the weather grow stormy and cold there be few or none of they leave wherefore see all hope of good to be do of they to be pass we depart from thence the six and twenty of August August 26. 1611. for England we do not perceive any ship of Hull to have be there this summer have touch the chief point of our voyage I think it meet to set down somewhat of the state commodity and trade of Pechora Oust Zilma and Parmia the town of Pechora be small have three church in it and the most part of the people be poor Pechora in the spring and a great part of the summer they live by catch of partridge goose duck and swan of which they every summer take a great number the flesh of these fowl they salt and live of they the most part of the winter but the feather of the say fowl they gather together oustiug and sell to the man of colmogro oustiug and other that come every year out of Russia to buy the same some of they give a little money before hand to the fowler which must be do with great care as the time be now one meafed a man son of Pechora a poud be 37. pound or the three part of a hundred weight a Alteen be five of their penny a groat of we who father be a man of great deal tell i that they sell white partridge feather to man of colmogro for ready money at five altines the poud and duck feather among which be down they sell now for seven or eight altines the poud likewise he tell i that in former time the Russ that use to trade thither before the people of the country know what commodity be worth have common a poud of partridge feather for two penny of their money and a piece of cake soap worth at colmogro ten penny of their money so that the chief commodity and best cheap be feather be buy at Pechora with ready Russee money of the fowler themselves and not of the liger there that use to sell they to we at archangel on the river of Duyna a great fish of salmon begin the first of August moreover one hundred english mile on this side of the town of Pechora be a place call by they the Boluano where they take great store of Salmon but it be always the first of August before they begin to cast out their net and oftentimes towards the late part of the summer they have such store that they be sell ordinary for fourpence a fish and sometime for a penny a fish of their money yea in a plentiful year I have be tell one may buy whole draught of salmon for a very small sum of money the salmon here be fat three fish weigh common a prove and no more the best sort of the people of Pechora use to preserve a great quantity of their salmon with a little salt for they salt eighty or one hundred fish with a prove of salt and many time in plentiful year much fish be cast away for want of salt which they be loath to bestow when salt be dear this salmon be carry by the Pechora man to mezen in sled draw with rein dear but if they be mind to carry the say fish from mezen to Colmogro than they carry the same from thence with sled draw with horse also many man of colmogro Pinega and mezen buy salmon at Pechora and carry it in the winter time to mezen to which place they pay from Pechora for the high of a sled and a rein dear ordinary ten altines be twelve day journey and from mezen to Colmogro be six day journey they pay fourpence a prove at the most the deer that travel from Pechora to Mezen will not draw above seven prove weight this way be travel every winter twice the first be six or eight week before Christmas and the second time be two or three week before Shrovetide which be the time that they very diligent observe to sell the salmon in most part of the man of Pechora have every one his own dear to travel with and some particular man of the better sort have twenty or thirty deer travel dear which they let out to high in the winter time and in the summer time they put they forth to the samoyed to keep diverse other place into the country of Russia all which they do in a summer time chap. x. the voyage of master Josias logan to Pechora and his winter there with master WILLIAM PURSGLOVE and marmaduke Wilson 1611. the first of july William gurdon Richard Finch and William Pursglove the former part of the voyage be omit to avoid tedious repetition go on shore at Suatinose where two cross stand the second we weigh anchor again and stand into the bay because of the ice and that night we go on shore again the three we weigh anchor and stand it about Suatinose the five we stand to the eastward five league more and about twelve of the clock at night we be thwart of the island of toxar the ten at eight of the clock at night we weigh and go over a bar at two fathom and come into harbour where we anchor at ten of the clock in the morning in five fathom have sand round about we be land-locked the eleven myself William gurdon and William Pursglove with six of our man more depart from the ship with our shallop to go up to the town of Pustozer the fourteen we arrive at the fish house of one Vasiliou see Pustozera where the people be afraid of we and be ready to run away but we speak to they and give they some biscuit and and they sod we some fish and show we our way to another fishery but they run away from we so we depart on our way the fifteen day at four of the clock in the afternoon we meet with a ruff that be bear at vstiug who give we milk and such thing as he have and we give he some biscuit and some and he direct we unto another fishery about some five mile from that place where we arrive about six of the clock the same night but come ashore we find not any save one man who after some conference have with we and give he some bread and some of our he tell we that the master of the house with three of his son be hunt of duck and that their wife be afraid and be run into the wood to hide themselves leave a young child behind they for haste so he bring we into the house where by that time that we have stay a hour because there be so many which be like unto a Midge and sting most horrible so that we be not able to stay without the master of the house and his son come thither who at the first be afraid think we come to rob they and they be about to shoot our man in the boat but one of our man hold up a biscuit cake they then come to they and speak unto they but our man not understand they make they sign to the house where myself William gurdon and William Pursglove be who when they come into the house be yet afraid they come in one after another now when we have salute they after the ruff manner they ask we of whence we be and for what cause we come thither whereunto I make answer that we be englishman who because of the trouble in Russia come thither to seek a trade have hear diverse time of the fame of those part then he reply that in time past those place have be good for trade but now by reason of a bad governor in those troublesome time upon a spleen he have fire the town and burn above a hundred house and so by that mean they be fall into poverty and trade decay by reason of his great exaction yet he say that they have great store of salmon july and that the last year they get above 15000. salmon and in the winter be their chief mart. for then the samoyed come thither from diverse place and bring sable and beaver white fox rosamacke feather and some squirrel so have sup with he we give he a gallon of our and some forty cake of our white biscuit and three or four pound of raisin for we hear that he be one of the princpal man in the town then desire his favour he help we to a man to go with we up to the town because of the fearfulness of the people which they conceive through the war of the pole and so we depart from thence that night to the town the sixteen in the afternoon we arrive at the town of Pustozera where we find not many people consider the number of house there which be betwixt fourscore and a hundred be of wood build after the russian manner and they be subject unto the ruff observe all their rite as do the Russ the people be all abroad some in get of morse oil and belougaes oil and some fish of a fish call Ometta which be a very sweet fish and some hunt duck save the customer and three or four more who be likewise afraid of we although we have one of their own people with we and be ready to flee away so we see their fearfulness cause their man to go first on shore with we three above mention not permit the rest of our man to come on land as yet then he call to they they stay still peep from behind the corner of their house until at the last there be a ruff one of colmogro that have winter with they who know i and have see i some two year before at Cola in Lappia at his uncle house and so he encourage they speak great in our commendation Cola in Lappia show they that I be a merchant and come to trade with they and not with any intent of harm for he know i very well and tell they that I be at Cola four or five year together and lay at his uncle house so he come to i and take i by the hand ask i how I do and tell i his name and how he have see i with his uncle at cola. then I call to mind that I have see he there and so we grow acquaint and he go with we to the customhouse where stay a hour at length the customer come and after many question have concern our come thither I crave licence that four of we may winter with they which they deny allege that they dare not without the emperor of Russia his licence whereupon I answer that the emperor majesty when he be reign be very gracious unto our nation above all other stranger and show what great privilege he have bestow on our people and how by the englishman mean at the first what a trade be now at Arkania Arkania and what profit come not only into his majesty treasury but also into all part of his dominion which in time may be bring hither and withal show the emperor privilege wherefore then they begin to put away fear and will we to stay five or six day until he have send for the chief man of the townsman who be abroad and then they will give we a answer then I desire that we may have a house to be in and not to stay without door so he give liberty to any that will to entertain we whereto there be one that make answer that he will whereupon we go with he and be in a Ambar of his until we receive answer from they in the mean time we make much of they and feast they with our biscuit and fig that we may the better obtain their love the four and twenty the customer come to give we our answer and tell we that they have conclude that we may stay if we will but they must write up to the Musko of our be here so we thank they and give they such entertainment as we can and send present to six of they of the chief which they take very thankful and promise what favour they can so this night I make ready my letter to send for England the four of August five and twenty Lodyas arrive at the town lade with meal and other which be bind for Molgomsey but by reason of contrary wind they be force into Pechora Molgomsey and come up to the town of Pustozer and unlade to make sale Pole baptize Russee the six and twenty we remove from the house where we be at the first unto a pole house who be christen Russee where we be to remain all the winter the nine and twenty the frost be so strong that the Ozera be freeze over and the ice drive in the river to and again frost in August break all the net so that they get no salmon no not so much as for their own victual the second of September the frost break up of josias logan from Pechora to master hakluyt prebend of Westminster there use to come hither in the winter about two thousand Samoieds with their commodity which may be such as we dream not on yet of all goodness jul. 24. 1611. in another letter from Pechora August 16. there come two or three thousand Samoieds hither to trade with their sable beavers black fox squirrel wolf rosomack ermine and and that they find write table in one of their pocket and other small trifle which they take away the vaygat be sometime open and sometime shut and upon they grow crystal of the Mount the Russ and
