come to a Voloc or neck of land which continue but three verst over which they draw their boat and good and so come to another river call Zelena Reca or the green river which bring they into Obi into which on the easter side the river fall make but one mouth with the river Obi be shall and they report it to be as broad towards the mouth as a man can discern over have many land therein moreover there be another great river call Yenissey beyond which they say be rather big and deep than Obi and it run up into the land no man know how far although they have discover some fourteen day row up therein neither can they learn of the inhabitant thereof how far it stretch a people a white city great ring of bels. who they call Tingussey who be a proper people of themselves and the report that they have travel so far that they come within sight of a white city or town which shall seem to be build of stone for they dare not go to make trial and they hear great ring of bels. also they say that they see beast but they be not like their deer for they have a great mane a long tail no horn and their foot be round not cleave as their deer be and they use to ride upon their back and not to draw in sled as their dear use to do these I assure myself be horse horse people in armour they be not far from Cataia and China and further they report that there come people unto they all make of iron their head arm hand and leg so that neither arrow sword nor spear can enter which as I conjecture be people in armour for they say that two hundred of they they think be able to conquer all their realm by this you may gather that they be not far from Cataia and China thus have I show ^nto you the great secret and the near to the truth that I know request you if you think it meet that the right honourable the earl of Salisbury may have a copy thereof thus wish you health and prosperity in this world and felicity in the world to come I cease chap. 11 a brief relation of a voyage to Pechora and winter there begin in the year 1611. write by WILLIAM PURSGLOVE master josias logan and William Gourdon have receive direction from the right worshipful company of english merchant trade Russia the eleven of April 1611. depart from blackewall in the river of Thames in a good ship call the amity whereof james Vndum of rederiffe be master the sixteen of july we arrive at Pustozera be much wonder at by the inhabitant a Permac receive we into his house and let we have a Warehouse for our good we all continue there until the five and twenty of july they be first receive into a permacks house then we return in our shallop again to our ship have a small Russee boat in our company to carry some of the feather and down which we bring there our own boat not be able to carry all be pester with our provision and some feather and white fox we come aboard our ship the seven and twenty of july where we deliver those white fox feather and down and a exceed rich black fox skin have lade the ruff boat with part of our good the rest of our good they lay upon the sand to be send up afterward leave i and Marmaduke Wilson and a hire ruff with they where we attend to hear of (@) from the town but master logan not hear of any above a ton and a half can not get any to come down to we because they fear to go over the dry or shall sea in their little boat be lade the one and thirty our ship depart over the bar purpose to make their voyage in Zembla or some land not far distant from thence at their departure there be five and twenty coach or Soymas in that road of Pechora with at least two hundred man in they bind for Molgomsey but hinder by contrary wind and ice our ship be over the bar they all come on shore to we some threaten other flatter we but after I have bestow two bottle of beer among some of the best of they they all go up to Pustozera where most of they that have any good to sell stay all winter and sell their commodity in barter with the inhabitant and when they can happen secret upon any Samoieds they will be trade with they also which be contrary to the privilege grant by the emperor to the pustozerit their winter there be no little hindrance to we for the sale of our good we arrive at the town the seven of August in my absence master logan have hire part of a house of one call Tiffon Vriawich a polonian who be turn Russee August the three and twenty of November I depart from Pustozera to go for Russia November his voyage over-land to Slobotca and Colmogro mountain and Cameni or rock at three of the clock in the afternoon in the company of certain Russ permack and Samoieds which Samoieds be our guide over the mountain and one day journey over the rock which they call Cameni which be not rocky hill as in Norway but high land yet in most place smooth and most marish ground full of little hillock which be cover with snow and freeze do not much annoy we our Argeshey or Caravan be about two hundred and ten sled draw the most part with two dear in a sled they have also about two hundred spare dear to ease the weary we keep company until the four of December together have pass two three part of our way to Slobotca be the first town in the country of Mesen that we see and then in company of four sled have each two choice buck with a samoy in the five for our guide we leave the Argeshey and rid post for he arrive at Slobotca the 9 of December in 16. day Thomas ligon where we arrive the nine of December at ten of the clock at night in this town I find one Thomas ligon a Englishman who have serve master Richard cock of London who salute i in english marvel much to meet i there and carry i from the rest of my company to his lodging and give i there very kind entertainment the next morning I depart thence in his sled have over night hire a horse to the next town which be fifteen verst off and so travel day and night change horse at every convenient place I come to Colmogro the twelve of December he arrive at colmogro the 12. of decemb. and deliver my letter from master josias logan our factor in Pustozera to master Fabian smith than agent for the english company have rest myself four day there and receive certain money to help to put off some of our good at Pechora I depart from Colmogro the seventeen of December and come to Slobotca the nineteen day the height of the pole be there some sixty five degree I stay there till the two and twenty of the say month by which time the permack and the inhabitant of Pustozera be ready to return to Pechora with their good be rye malt hops salt and some course Cloth moreover diverse Russ have their son or kinsman leiger there in winter do send cloth and money over Land have make my provision for my journey and take my leave of master Thomas ligon we set forward that night and rid not above five and twenty verst to a place where we find the Argeshey which set out from Slobotca the two and twenty day in the morning by break of day we have better passage in our return than we have in our journey from Pustozera by reason of much snow fall in the time of our be in Russia snow better their travel and freeze so hard that it bear both dear and sled in all place we keep together with the Argeshey be then two hundred and fifty sled till we have pass more than two three of our way over the mountain and then long before day have choose buck of the best the four of januarie we depart the four of januarie be eight sled in company and rid post all that day and night follow be moonlight save sometime for the space of a hour that we stay where the samoy our guide know there be good store of moss moss food for the dear which be white to refresh our deer the five of januarie we come to Pustozera have in forty hour travel three hundred and fifty verst with our choice buck our Argeshey or Caravan arrive there after we the twelve of januarie the manner of travel with the the Samoieds be the only guide in winter either from Pustozera to Slobotca or to any other place eastward as Ougoria siberia or Molgomsey know by their continual travel the way though it be never so thick weather as also where most store of white moss be grow and according as they find themselves near unto some mossy place be it something before night or within night four or five hour before they can come thither there for that night they pitch their tent be for the most part make of dear and elke skin we have in our company four great tent set up their tent and some twenty under each tent. this work of pitch the tent belong unto the woman in the mean time the man unyoake the deer and turn they loose to dig through the snow be it never so deep for their food and sustenance then the of every tent one out of the next wood provide as much fuel as shall (...) turn for their abode there first they set on kettle full of snow water which be melt they drink thereof every one a good draught then they see their supper use as before snow water melt for their drink hard-soft lodging our lodging be upon the snow within our tent round about the fire have under we for our bed the skin of deer cover with our day apparel for all the time of our journey the merchant whether stranger Russee or Permac according to the number of they make provision of victual to feed the whole family in every tent poor Samoieds every man his day about together with the their wife and child who carry all their household every where with they and out of their son and daughter they appoint a watch over their deer dangerous wolf for fear of the wolf and other beast which notwithstanding their watch sometime kill in a night one or two of their deer as it fall out two night in our journey to Slobotca this Slobotca be a pretty town have in December and januarie great resort of people repair thither as well rich Russ out of many place with money to buy fur as other with provision of meal and malt and other commodity to furnish the pustozerit as also to buy fish to wit salmon oil of Bealugos dear skin and fur of they trade with the of Ougoria eight or nine hundred Samoieds come to Pustozera the ten of january the inhabitant of Pustozera return from trade with the of Ougoria on which journey they set forward the five and twenty of November and within three day after come betwixt eight or nine hundred Samoieds with a small quantity of their commodity in respect of former year by reason of war between the Samoieds of Ougoria and Molgomsey who be wont to trade one with another and not to war one against another so sable and other commodity be scant the inhabitant sell they very dear yet notwithstanding the Russ buy up all strive one to have they before another so that after that little money which we have be bestow we can not do any thing in barter moreover the Russ do not only inform against we to the inhabitant to stir they up against we the false suggestion of the Russ against we but also use the like mean to the to dissuade they from trade with we either in their own country or elsewhere allege that we will betray they and not only carry they away to make they slave and rob they but also will murder and destroy all the rest wheresoever we shall come the inhabitant also of Pustozera be incense by the Russ doubt we will enter far into their trade eastward begin also to hinder and forbid the to come to we yet by mean of our host be a Polac bear we speak with diverse of the principal of the he be our interpreter and we ourselves understand certain Samoieds speak break Russee and by these mean we find out more at large the despitefulness of the Russ and the envy of some of the inhabitant against we as also their fear lest we or any other stranger shall enter into further discovery of their traffic towards the east but especial about the river ob. some say we be send as spy to betray their land to the pole or the Swethen with who they then have war some give counsel to put we under the water other advise to set we upon the sand where we shall have be without all doubt drown in short space other think best to send we up to the nobility and to seize on all our good to the use of the State but diverse of the best in the town with who we keep all friendship that possible we can withstand those bloody practice the lord therefore be bless the five of march the inhabitant of Pustozer go again to Slobotca carry the Russ with their commodity thither March they return home the eleven of April 1612. the one and twenty of April April 1612. water be first see upon the main river Pechora above the ice descend from above oustzilma the twenty of May the ice break up the five and twenty of May may 20. the ice break up certain of the inhabitant of Pustozer go by water unto oustzilma the six and twenty josias logan with our host the polonian hire a boat and go towards oustzilma carry with he certain cloth and copper kettles in hope to sell they well there be entreat in the summer before by one of their townsman to come thither or to send one to winter there allege that they get great store of losh-hyde squirrel sable and bever which some year indeed as we be credible inform fall out according to his report but at his arrival there diverse of the townsman come against he and will not suffer he nor any of his boat to land for the space of ten hour but in the end our man entreat to winter at oustzilma they let he go on shore after as we suppose the inhabitant of Pustozer have buy most of their commodity so that he stay there two day can get but nine losh-hyde and half a timber of course sable in barter for some cloth and copper the principal cause of his go thither be to meet with some of the permack out of Permia who some year come down with rye and rye-meal and think to have give notice to those permack of our be at Pustozer and to have will they to have persuade their countryman to bring thither the next spring follow all their commodity be wax honey losh-hyde and fur which they may do for half the charge that they be at in bring they to archangel on the river Duina oustzilma be a pretty town of some sixty house oustzilma and be three or four day sail with a fair wind against the stream from Pustozer but back again they may sail it in two day the three of june come the first Russ in their cayook by river out of Russia to Pustozer june 3 these cayook be small boat of two ton have two four and twenty the inhabitant of Pustozer fish for Bealugos under the boluan go to fish for Bealugos under the boluan be the high land near unto the dry sea and two day sail from the town the five and twenty I depart after they and arrive there the seven and twenty hope to have provide good store of Bealugos oil but it fall out contrary though there be above fifty boat have in every boat three man and in many four by reason it please God to send such windy and stormy weather that the boat can not go to sea in many day together during their wont time of fish for those beast be till the twenty of july then every man leave that fish and repair to their own fisherie to hunt duck goose and swan which most year they get in abundance and make good profit of their feather and down as also of their flesh which they salt up in cask for winter provision serve they also all the summer for flesh day these Bealugos they catch with harp iron tie fast to a long rope of ninety or a hundred fathom manner of kill they the Russ upon the ice use to kill the Morse as they do their Bealugo but their rope be long and a barre^^ make fast at one end to buoy it poverty Bealugo make meat in Italy with a staff of the length of two yard or somewhat long be put loose into the iron wherewith when the beast come within the reach of he that strike he smite he with the iron leave it in the beast then the rope be lay out clear to veer out the man hold his staff still in his hand but the beast be wound hasten to the bottom where have beat himself near to death they hall in their rope by little and little the beast ascend thereby and if they find he not near death they strike he again and be dead they cut off his skin with the fat on it in many part some the breadth of two hand some more or less then come on shore they take the fat from the skin and cut it in small piece to dissolve it to oil cast away the flesh which be red to the fowl of the sea except some poor samoy come that way who take it though it have lie putrify two or three day and dry it and make good cheer with it with his family this beast be as big as two good sturgeon moreover I be inform by a ancient traveller that the flesh and fat of that beast be cut as beef and salt in cask be a great and rich commodity in Italy which can choose but to be much better than young whale which I have hear that the biskayner use to preserve for good meat with the fat of some one of these beast they will fill three barrel of some lesser two barrel and some yield but one barrel of blubber which they call Shilliga in that summer when I be there by reason of northerly wind blow hard they kill by all their boat not above forty beast with some boat they kill two with other three with some four but with most not one the thirteen of july I receive a letter from master josias logan the effect whereof be that the company of our english merchant of Russia july 13. a boat send by river to Pustozera to fetch home master logan and his company into Russia August the Gloubuc have send a boat out of Russia by river which stand they in fourteen rubbel or mark for we to go in she or by Lodia for Russia for they be purpose not to oil feather down and losh-hyde as soon as it begin to be daylight and that the Russ know we to be upon the main Land the thirty day be somewhat calm and the wind easterly but thick weather still there description of the samoy life the twenty of November I depart from Pustozera to go to Yougorie November 1614 his journey within 30. league of and near to Bersoma the river coy fall into Pechor^ at four in the afternoon and do ride most of the night before we come to the choome go east southeast the one and twenty Mihiloe return to the town and we remove and go our journey fair and little wind the two and twenty little wind north we keep on our course east southeast have go from the town 50. mile at night Mihiloe come to we the three and twenty little wind we go on our journey and at noon pass over a little river call coy fall north into Pechora 14. league below the town and at night come all the Russ from the town have go 24. mile east southeast the four and twenty we remove on our journey be very cold and go not above ten mile east southeast at night we break one of our sled which go lade with victual the five and twenty we go forward very slow at noon I receive a letter from master Copman by Poma creticove this afternoon another have his sled break we go 10. or 12. mile the six and twenty we continue on our journey and at eeven we pass over a river call Shapkina fall south into Pechora half way betwixt Pustozer and oustzilma the river Shapkina fall into Pechora a sled break and mend out of hand go east southeast 15. mile the seven and twenty be Sunday the wind at south-west do blow very hard and snow all the day the snow drive that we can hardly see which way to go yet we keep on east southeast 18. mile the eight and twenty in the morning we pass over Nougorotka river which fall west south-west into Shapkina river six day journey above oustzilma the river Nougorotka fall into Shapkina Habeaga river fall into Pechora the wind south-west and snow all day we keep on still east southeast 15. mile the nine and twenty the wind south with snow all day be not cold we go on east southeast 20. mile the thirty the wind east southeast very cold in the afternoon we pass over Habeaga river which fall into Pechora six day journey above oustzilma go 20. mile the first of December the wind east blow very hard the snow do drive so hard that we can not go forward but stand still all day and do not remove the second December calm and not so cold we go on east southeast 10. mile the three in the morning it be very warm at noon the wind north it be extreme cold the snow drive very thick the river haryena fall into Coluoy in the afternoon we pass over the river haryena which fall into Coluoy southeast have go east southeast 15. mile the four day warm we go east at eeven we come to a river call Coluoy the river Coluoy fall into ouse which fall south into the river ouse where we stay all night have go 20. mile the five in the morning we go on upon the river six or seven mile east and by north and come where it part in two the one keep north-east the other be call sandavet from the southeast we go betwixt they both east and by south 12. mile and take up our lodging upon a plain where no wood be to be see the six be saint Nicholas day which with the Russ be hold a principal day in the morning they cause their image to be bring into the choome saint Nicholas Bay light wax-candle before they make their prayer to they according to their order after which I give they a bottle of wherewith the guide be drink that they can not guide their deer but set i to direct the way by compass which I do all the day although I have but little skill we go southeast and by east 20. mile the seven be very fair weather our guide lay all the day with pohmeall and can not go forward the eight fair and calm we go forward southeast and by east 10. mile a small river fall into sandavet and take up our lodging by a small river which fall into sandavets river the nine very cold that we have much ado to keep ourselves from freeze go on foot all the day over a plain where no wood grow go southeast 15. mile and lay by a wood side all night the ten the frost be so extreme that we lie still and can not proceed the eleven be Sunday the frost continue extreme we remove terrible frost there be few in the company that have not some part of their face freeze and myself although I be something better provide then any of they yet I have something to do to keep myself from freeze go on foot most part southeast and by east 15. mile the twelve the frost be so extreme that there be no look forth but lay still all day the thirteen not altogether so cold we proceed on our journey 20. mile southeast and by east and at night we pass over the river Hoseda the river Hoseda fall into Azua which fall southeast into the river Azua the fourteen the wind south with snow and not so cold we go through wood 20. mile east southeast the fifteen the wind oustzilma the nine of june my servant Marmaduke Wilson come from oustzilma have winter there to buy and sell good bring with he such commodity as the place do afford as sable rosomack wolf ermine Holland but do not depart till the 21. of August and the three and twenty of September give hearty thanks to God we arrive at Dort in Holland now for the manner of the samoit in their journey their upper coat be call a parka apparel of samoyed which be for the most part of deere-skin and some of white fox or woluerin which they wear the hair or fur outward under that they have another coat which be call a Mallek make of young fawne-skin or hare-skin or swan-skin very soft and well dress a cap of beaver double and close to their head with two flappe for their ear tie under their chin a pair of breeches of deere-skin with the hair inward upon their foot they have sock or stocking of deere-skin the hair to their skin upon that long boot which they call pemye make of the leg of deere-skin thus apparel they sit upon their Sled^ crosslegged sled with a deere-skin under they two deer be yoke to a sled they will run with such swiftness and so long to continue as be not to be believe except to those that have see the same dear swiftness for ride post they will ride without rest or sleep two hundred mile in four and twenty hour but with their argish or stuff thirty mile in twelve hour their woman usual do guide their argish which be ten sled and to every sled a buck all make fast one after another woman the man in the way do provide wood for fire and do hunt for all manner of beast and fowl which the woman dress it be the woman labour to set up the choome or tent tent and chapel make one place therein always holy which the woman must not set her foot into neither go about the tent round which if they chance to do they will present remove all superstition for fear of the wolf or bear which they say will devour they if they do not remove their tent or choome be make in this manner first they set up long firre-pole than they have six quarter double of deere-skin which be set up they throw snow round about the edge a yard thickness leave the top open for to vent smoke make a fire in the middle spread deere-skin upon which they lie in which manner it be altogether as warm as the stove in Russia they have no town neither any certain place of abode no town but with their deer they travel from place to place where they find the best moss for their deer their wife they buy for deer and will have if he have ability four or five wife with who he lie by turn every night several marry wife buy and sold. marriage he be the rich man that have most dear or daughter sell they to any that will give most for they in their marriage have agree of price they use not great ceremony only they make a feast to their friend after which the woman be bring to the man that have buy she she be hang with many iron ring and brazen bell all depart out of the tent save they two till the next morning ring and bels. and then he depart but if he be one of wealth they will continue their feast seven day it fall out many time that after they have have their wife half a year or a year they will turn they back to their friend take their deer again pay for the charge of the feast divorce which be always to be make at her father charge and lose the increase of his deer they have not knowledge of the true God but worship block and image of the devil unto which they will strangle tame deer rub the blood on the idol religion and eat the meat themselves when a rich man die because he shall not travel on foot funeral his friend will kill three deer to draw he in the new world and they will strangle a slave to tend on he the deer they kill in this manner to serve the dead man they make a stake sharp which they thrust into the beast fundament with many howl and cry till they be dead the master with the slave they bury the dear they eat as well raw as boil or roast although they use all three their year but half a year if a young child die under fourteen of their year which be seven of we they do hang it by the neck on some tree say it must fly to heaven if any controversy be which can be decide or the truth know than one of the two betwixt who the controversy be judgement or oath must be swear which be in this manner they will make a image of a man of snow bring a wolf nose deliver a sword to he that must swear he rehearse by name all his friend desire that they may all be cut in piece in that manner as he do cut that image of snow then he himself do cut the image of snow all to piece with the sword then after the wolf nose be lay before he he desire that the wolf may destroy all his tame deer and that he may never more take or kill any wild deer after that if he speak not the truth so cut the wolf nose in piece there be no more to be say of that controversy their person the samoit be stout and bold of spirit not very tall but broad breast broad face with hollow eye their ordinary instrument for war be Bowes and arrow very dangerous they have long spear the head be make in Monganzey by another sort of samoit and short sword not much unlike some that I have see bring from east India divination when they will know any thing to come they send for their priest or witch to converse with the devil sit in one side of the tent have before his face a piece of a old shirt of mail hang with bell and piece of brass in his right hand a great tabor make with a wolf skin beat upon the same with a hare foot make a very doleful sound with sing and call for the devil to answer his demand which be end they strangle a dear for a sacrifice make merry with the flesh. woman hardiness the woman be very hard of nature for at their child-bearing the husband must play the midwife and be deliver the child be wash with cold water or snow and the next day the woman able to conduct her argish the Russ have a yearly trade with the merchant of Beghar at a place call tumen in Tartary whither they of Boghar come with camel every year from tumen in Tobal in siberia they come in fourteen day from Tobal they come to Beresova in nine day all down the river ob. from Beresova partly by the river then over a neck of land of half a mile over into the river ouse and down the river ouse into the river Pechora and so to Pustozera in three week at Pustozera the english have winter three year chap. 13 diverse voyage to island in the year 1604. 1605. 1606. 1608. 1609. write by Ionas Poole we set sail * * this be master bennet second I have add at the end of this chapter after pool relation this be set before I see that from London the fifteen of April 1604. in a ship call the God speed of sixty ton with thirteen man and a boy our merchant be one master Thomas welden our master be one Steven bonnit of saint catherins we arrive at Cola in Lapland the first of May where we tarry till the last of the same month at which time we set sail from Cola and go to a harbour call Pechingo which lie between Cola and ward-house in which harbour of Pechingo we continue until the thirty of june at which time we set sail from thence and through contrary wind and foul weather be put into ward-house where we take in fresh water and stay until the six of july the same day the wind come southerly and we steer away northwest and by north about 56. league we observe the sun at twelve of the clock at noon and find ourselves to be in 73. degree 5. minute of northerly latitude the seven of july it be all day calm and we sound but have no ground in two hundred and fifty fathom the eight day we have little wind which be at southeast and foggy weather and at eight of the clock at night we see great flock of sea-fowle which we call willocke some of these fowl have each of they a small fish in their bill and fly towards the northwest and by north. the other without fish some of they fly contrary to the former and some sit in the sea very near our Ship about twelve of the clock at night we sound and have ground at one hundred and twenty fathom we steer away northwest and by north till four of the clock the eight day in the all the better plate they will also strike with their tooth at he that be next they the fight of the Morse but because their tooth grow downward their stroke be of small force and danger after we have open the beast which we have slay we take out the blubber and carry it a mile into the bay where we set up the shallop the reason why we carry it thither be because we think that the fire of our furnace will scare they away for we do boil all their fat to bring it into oil thus we follow our business till the four and twenty of july oil make of the fat of the morse eleven tun of oil at which ship bear from we southeast about four league I have not sail ten mile but the ice be so close and firm that I can not get aboard nor back again for it close with such force that it make the shallop side crack as though they will have meet together we labour very sore to save our boat because it do concern our life and get she into a place where she lie between two piece of ice after this sort we drive with the ice till we have lose sight of our ship which be about a north sun and still we drive be not able otherwise to move till we be above eight league from the island the sixteen day at a east southeast sun the ice begin to open then although my company be in despair and say it be impossible to get out to work we go and by cut off ice and remove of it one piece from another we make way through towards the Land the near to the land we get we find the more open sea and by a north sun we get on shore after we have give God thanks for our deliverance out of such extreme danger we eat some fowl and bear flesh which we sod under a cliff they feed on bear flesh nine fox find there we find nine young fox and kill the old one there also we sleep upon the cold sand which be not pass three inch thick and underneath ice and stay here till a southeast sun the seventeen day the seventeen we go from this place to the cove where we find the Hull man Boat I make a tilt of the shallop sail and sod some bear flesh and fowl and stay about the cove all that day and upon a island common call gull-iland I find three mine of lead Vre three mine of lead find on gull-iland but have no fit tool to break the rock and also because it be in the view of the Hull man tent I be force to let it rest till the ship can get into the cove. the eighteen day we go to the north side of the island and in our way we find good sea-coal to burn good sea-cole find on the island two bear slay some we take with we to try they and find they good and on the north side I slay two bear then we share the bread that be leave and we have but two cake to a man for some of my company while I be asleep or kill of the bear have break open the chest wherein the bread be and have convey some away our beer be spend before this time and we be fain to drink snow water the nineteen we go to the cove the wind be westerly to see if we can espy our ship but we can not neither can she come near the island for ice for all the sea as far as I can see from the top of a high hill be cover with ice a huge compass of ice save that within a quarter of a mile off the shore it be clear round about once in a tide another bear slay the twenty day I go to the north side again and slay a bear thus we spend the time sometime on one side sometime on the other never stay above one day in one place till the ship come in which be the seven and twenty of june on which day I slay another bear another bear slay I slay seven in all who flesh we eat full savourly forget the oily rankness of it for hunger be a savoury sauce their ship get in the second time the seven and twenty our ship come to a anchor on the north side where we than be assoon as we see she we need no bid to go aboard when we be come to the ship side they bid we welcome but whereas we think to have relieve ourselves we find it far otherwise because the ship have a knock with a piece of ice in the stern which break in the corner of a plank under the water so that our bread-roome be full of water and all our bread spoil save about one hundred weight which be but a small quantity for three and forty man the Matthew this day a ship call the Matthew come to a anchor by we then master welden and I go on shore where we find one John Skinner master mate of the Matthew with eleven man by he we set up our tent and tell he there be no voyage for he to make but our necessity be such that we be fain to take four hundred of bread of they upon some condition which I will not speak of here the same day we think to have take a copper aboard which I dig out of the snow but by negligence it be let fall into the sea yet afterward take up again and carry aboard the marie Margarite the same day another ship call the Mary Margarite come into the say cove on the south side the eighteen I go to the cove with the shallop and six man where I find the marie Margarite there pass no great kindness between they and i I slay three morse there where we get foul for in all the time of our be about the island and in the ice they be our chief food the four we weigh and go to the north side where we be trouble with much ice the wound be at west and by north which bring the ice whole upon we so that we be force to weigh again a bear slay the six we come into the cove where master welden slay a bear the eight day he slay another bear and the same day I go to the north side with the shallop and victual for the man which keep on that side another bear slay I stay there till the fourteen of july on which day we have the wound northerly with snow and frost and the island environ round with ice in this time the ship company on the south side do dig some mineral lead snow and frost some mineral lead dig above twenty fox eat and we catch above twenty fox which we do eat as savourly as if they have be venison the fifteen day by a north-east sun we come aboard the ship which lie in the cove with our shallop and all our provision that be on the north side and the lioness prepare to go to saint Nicolas in Russia as it be appoint before in London the sixteen the wind be north-east bring such store of ice to the island that it be compass round close to the shore and fill the cove so full that by no mean possible the ship can get out but rid still shut in for five day the seventeen the ice begin to open at the mouth of the cove and some be willing to go out with their ship but covetousness have like to have bring we all to great misery for each man strive to ride long in the cove suppose that there the morse will come first on shore danger by the ice they find it clean contrary for the wind come southerly and blow all the ice from this side of the island save that which be in the cove which press so sore upon our ship that our anchor can not hold we for the Matthew be put from three anchor and drive with that small tide that run there within her length of a sink rock but a great piece of ice on ground upon the rock do keep she from it and when the flood come again she be drive within half her length of the rock so that they be glad to get most of their victual out of she upon the rock look each minute when she shall split in sunder and though the rest of the ship do not drive as she do yet they have many a sore stroke with the ice for the southerly wind cause a hollow sea to come in so that our ship strike with such force against the ice that we can hardly stand on our foot in they then each man lay to his hand to save his ship by put plank and old cable end and bundle of hoop between their ship and the ice but they be beat all to piece present then we put piece of elm Plancke between the bow of the Paul in which ship I be immediate they also be beat into small piece although they be above four inch thick with the stroke that break the plank the carpenter say the ship side do crack and two timber be break then present we also get out of the ship most of our victual and carry it to the shore there may you see a sorrowful spectacle for all the ship be five in number be so fast in the ice that all the man that be in they all which be one hundred eighty two can not imagine how to save one among the rest we make account that the Matthew will sink ere long because the ice have break nine timber on one side and eleven on the other so that the green sea do come into the ship and her main beam be break at that instant likewise in this sort we continue till the twenty day follow when we look still to be put on the cliff with the force of the ice that press upon our ship so sore that our anchor can not possible hold upon the twenty day it please God to bring the wind westerly than the ice begin to open and to drive out of the cove by little and little to our great comfort but that ice that do not get clean out come back again and run round in a circle so that we have a continual labour to defend the ship from it whereupon we make mean to get out by long l l a warp be a rope common a Hawser use to warp a ship that be with a anchor bend to the Hawser and lay out to hale the ship forward which be do when they want wind to carry out or into a harbour warp as we term they we be fain to let slip one cable and the lioness one the Matthew have but one cable and anchor but they borrow one of we by a northwest sun all the ship get out of the ice to the Coves mouth where we stay for the ebb when the ebb be come the lioness depart on her voyage to saint Nicholas in Russia and present the Matthew and the Mary Margarite set sail and get out then we in the Paul set sail and before our anchor be up it get hold upon one of Matthewes cables that she lose when she drive out and bring we up to a m m a bitter be a turn of the cable about the bit for when they come to anchor they take a turn with it about the bit two main square piece of timber which stand pillar wise in the loose of the ship to make fast the cable unto that they may by little and little veer it out at ease otherwise if a stopper fail the cable will run out end for end that be altogether but thus stop the ship be say to be bring to a bitter the bitter end be that end of the cable within board at the bite bitter so that we be very near the rock but we get off again and ride there till a northwest sun the next day the one and twenty day we weigh and stand to the east side of the island where we find the come to the cove on the south side where we find abundance of morse lie on the ice that be in the cove. I slay one of they and take off his head we can not get to the shore where our victual lay but we make a fire under a cliff in the same cove. the three and twenty day we get to our victual and josias go with it to our ship but I tarry at the cove hope that the beast will come on land when the ice be go as they do afterward there I tarry till the five and twenty of july at what time josias logan come to i with the shallop and a Skiffe load with cask and other provision and tell i that they have slay five or six hundred morse on the north side he tarry with i till the seven and twenty of july now see no beast do come on land because the ice do hang about the cove he go to the north side again but the same day after he be go they begin to come on Land the next day follow be the eight and twenty we slay about eighty and take their blubber and tooth then they begin to come on shore again the thirty day at what time master Bonner be come into the cove to seek his anchor then his man come on shore and we slay about one hundred and fifty beast more but there rise a storm at southeast that bring in such a surge that it wash above sixty beast into the sea so that most of they be lose the next day be the last of july master welden and master jones come to the cove with about twelve man be all very weary for they have leave the shallop in a cove on the northwest side of the island and come over Land then to work we go on all hand and place our copper and by the five day of August we have end our business and the ship come from the north side into the cove. August the six of August I take the Skiffe and seven man to fetch the shallop to the cove that master welden have leave in a cove on the northwest side of the island the last of july when I come to the place consider I be near the north side where we common make our voyage note and also desire by master welden if I can go to do so I go thither and find about five and forty as good head beast for little wind at northwest and by west then see no amendment of the weather we leave the ship of Hull behind we in the island and about six of the clock set sail for England and arrive safe at London the last of August 1609. bless be God a voyage perform to the northwards 1603. in a ship of the burden of fifty ton call the grace and set forth at the cost and charge of the worshipful FRANCIS write by WILLIAM gorden be the first voyage to island which come to my hand since the former or rather late voyage be in the press the ship be ready the ten of April whereof be master Stephen Bennet and for factor and overseer William gorden our direction from the say merchant be first to proceed to Cola and there to make sale of such good as we have and to take in such other as the country of Lappia do afford and then to proceed upon some discovery wherefore omit our journey to Cola as a matter of small importance be so well know before after our affair end we be ready to proceed forward but our man not be hire thereunto will have refuse if there have not be make a agreement by mean of josias logan who be to lie there as factor for master the master and myself partly with promise partly with gift and thus set forward the six of August from the river of Cola be determine to have sail into 80. degree of latitude if nothing do hinder we a island or if we do not light upon some land our determination be hinder by mean of meeting with a island and likewise the year be far spend keep our course from the west end of Kilden to the land of ward-house which we pass the ten of August with little wind then direct our course north northwest the wind at south-west easy wind so that the eleven day we do reckon ourselves to have sail twenty league northwest the twelve day it be most part calm and foggy the thirteen day it be clear and the wind at south and we have sail twenty two league north northwest the fourteen day the wind at east we keep our course and sail ten league and the same day be thick and foggy we have think we have see land about four of the clock in the afternoon bear from we west northwest and northwest by west but sail towards it three hour keep still his form and not alter till the wind increase cause it to fade away for it be no other than a bank of fog after we have sail three league change our course we sail then fifteen day twenty league northwest and by north still have close weather that we can not make any observation the sixteen day in the morning at two of the clock we do see two great high hill which do seem to we above the cloud and do seem very near but we find it otherwise for sail towards it we find it further than we do expect for it be six of the clock at night before we can come near unto the land where we anchor in thirty fathom in which time we can not sail less than eighteen league north and by west that night our master know better what do belong unto those affair will not suffer the boat to go aland till the morning which be the seventeen day of August and before our go aland the master cause a shank of line to be shoot for to toy for fish and then he and myself with four of our company go aland first upon a little island mere adjoin where we have much ado to get to our boat again by reason of the steepness of the rock then we go on shore upon the main where at our come on land we do see two fox one white the other black thus spend most part of the day we return aboard our ship without any profit only one of our man take up a piece of lead and I find a piece of a morse tooth by which we perceive that the sea morse do use thither but the time for that year be past for we do see none after our come aboard have hale the line we find nothing but one but fish thereon wherefore present weigh anchor we sail west to see if we can have any true observation the next day which we have and find ourselves to be in 74. degree 30. minute the same day direct our course for London where we arrive the ten of September by God help in health and safety chap. 14 diverse voyage and northern discovery of that worthy irrecoverable discoverer master HENRY HUDSON his discovery towards the north Pole set forth at grace of God we safe arrive in the range of Dartmouth in Devonshire in the year 1609. chap. 17 a abstract of the journal of master HENRY HUDSON for the discovery of the northwest passage begin the seventeen of April 1610. end with his end be treacherous expose by some of the company April 17. the seventeen of April 1610. we break ground and go down from saint Katherine pool and fall down to blackewall and so ply down with the ship to Lee which be the two and twenty day the two and twenty I cause master Coleburne to be put into a pink bind for London with my letter to the adventurer import the reason wherefore I so put he out of the ship and so ply forth the second of May the wind southerly at eeven we be thwart of flamborough Head may. the isle of orkney the five we be at the isle of orkney and here I set the north end of the needle and the north of the fly all one the six we be in the latitude of 59 degree 22. minute and there perceive that the north end of Scotland note far land 62 degree 24. minute westmony Orney and Shotland be not so northerly as be common set down the eight day we see far land in the latitude of 62. degree 24. minute the eleven day we fall with the easter part of island and then ply along the souther part of the land we come to westmony be the fifteen day and still ply about the main island until the last of May with contrary wind and we get some fowl of diverse sort june the first day of june we put to sea out of a harbour in the westermost part of island and so ply to the westward in the latitude of 66. degree 34. minute and the second day ply and find ourselves in 65. degree 57 minute with little wind easterly the three day we find ourselves in 65. degree 30. minute with wind at north-east a little before this we sail near some ice Groneland the four day we see Groneland over the ice perfect and this night the sun go down due north and rise north north-east so ply the five day we be in 65. degree still encumber with much ice which hang upon the coast of Groneland frobishers straits the nine day we be off frobisher straits with the wind northerly and ply unto the southwestward until the fifteen day the fifteen day we be in sight of the land in latitude 59 degree 27. minute which be call by captain John davis desolation and find the error of the former lay down of that land desolation and then run to the northwestward until the twenty day we find the ship in 60. degree 42. minute and see much ice and many ripling or ouerfals and a strong stream set from east southeast a current west northwest to west northwest the one and twenty two and twenty and three and twenty day with the wind variable we ply to the northwestward in sight of much ice into the height of 62. degree 29. minute east entrance into the straits the four and twenty and five and twenty day sail to the westward about midnight we see land north which be sudden lose again so we run still to the westward in 62. degree 17. minute july the five of july we ply up upon the souther side trouble with much ice in seek the shore until the five day of july and we observe that day in 59 degree 16. minute then we ply off the shore again until the eight day and then find the height of the pole in 60. degree no minute here we see the land from the northwest by west half northerly unto the south-west by west cover with snow a champagne land and call it desire provoke desire provoke we still ply up to the westward as the land and ice will suffer until the eleven day when fear a storm we anchor by three rocky land in uncertain depth between two and nine fathom and find it a harbour unsufficient by reason of sink rock one of which be next morning two fathom above water isle of God mercy we call they the isle of God mercy the water flow here we put to sea for Groneland but to the west we see land as we think for which we bear the best part of a day but it prove but a foggy bank so we give it over and make for gronland which we raise the cover with snow we turn the land on the south side as near as the ice will suffer we our course for the most part be between the west and northwest till we raise the desolation which be a great island in the west part of Groneland on this coast we see store of whale island of desolation store of whale and at one time three of they come close by we so as we can hardly shun they then two pass very near and the three go under our ship we receive no harm by they praise be God from the desolation our master make his way northwest the wind be against he who else will have go more to the north but in this course we see the first great island or mountain of ice whereof after we see store about the latter end of june we raise land to the north of we which our master take to be that island which master davis set down in his chart. on the west side of his straight our master will have go to the north of it but the wind will not suffer he so we fall to the south of it into a great ripple or himself of this ice and stand to the south and then to the west through store of float ice and upon the ice store of seales we gain a clear sea and continue our course till we meet ice first with great land and then with store of the small sort between they we make our course northwest till we meet with ice again but in this our go between the ice we see one of the great land of ice overturn which be a good warning to we not to come nigh they nor within their reach into the ice we put ahead as between two land island of ice overturn the next day we have a storm and the wind bring the ice so fast upon we that in the end we be drive to put she into the chief of the ice and there to let she lie some of our man this day fall sick I will not say it be for fear although I see small sign of other grief the storm cease we stand out of the ice where we see any clear sea to go to which be sometime more danger by ice and sometime less our course be as the ice do lie sometime to the north then to the northwest and then to the west and to the south-west but still enclose with ice which when our master see he make his course to the south think to clear himself of the ice that way but the more he strive the worse he be and the more enclose till we can go no further here our master be in despair and as he tell i after he think he shall never have get out of this ice but there have perish therefore he bring forth his card and show all the company that he be enter above a hundred league further than ever any english be Hudson enter 100 league further than any have be and leave it to their choice whether they will proceed any further yea or nay whereupon some be of one mind and some of another some wish themselves at home and some not care where so they be out of the ice but there be some who then speak word which be remember a great while after there be one who tell the master that if he have a hundred pound he will give fourscore and ten to be at home discontent but the carpenter make answer that if he have a hundred he will not give ten upon any such condition but will think it to be as good money as ever he have any and to bring it as well home by the leave of God after many word to no purpose to work we must on all hand to get ourselves out and to clear our ship after much labour and time spend we gain room to turn our ship in and so by little and little to on Saturday the one and twenty of june at night Wilson and Green their wickedness Wilson the boatswain and Henry Greene come to i lie in my cabin lame and tell i that they and the rest of their associate will shift the company and turn the master and all the sick man into the shallop and let they shift for themselves for there be not fourteen day victual leave for all the company at that poor allowance they be at and that there they lay the master not care to go one way or other and that they have not eat any thing these three day and therefore be resolute either to mend or end and Nicolo arm three bark with which he arrive in Engroneland saint Thomas monastery in greenland hot spring and the strange effect thereof where he find a monastery of friar of the preacher order and a church dedicate to saint Thomas hard by a hill that cast out fire like vesuni^s and Aetna there be a fountain of hot water with which they heat the church of the monastery and the friar chamber it come also into the kitchen so boil hot that they use no other fire to dr^sse their meat and put their bread into brass pot without any water it do bake as it be in a hot oven they have also small garden which be cover over in the winter time and be water with this water be defend from the violence of the frost and cold and bring forth flower in their due season the common people astonish with these strange effect conceive high of those friar and bring they present of flesh and other thing they with this water in the extremity of the cold heat their chamber which also as the other building of the monastery be frame of those burn stone which the mouth of the hill cast forth they cast water on some of they whereby they be dissolve and become excellent white lime and so tough that be contrive in building it last for ever the rest after the fire be out serve in stead of stone to make wall and vault and will not dissolve or break except with some iron tool their winter last nine month and yet there be a fair haven where this water fall into the sea not freeze by mean whereof there be great resort of wild fowl and fish which they take in infinite multitude the fisher boat be make like to a weaver shuttle of the skin of fish fashion with the bone of the same fish and be sow together with many double they be so strong that in foul weather they will shut themselves within the same not fear the force either of sea or wind neither can the hard-hearted rock break these yield vessel they have also as it be a sleeve in the bottom thereof by which with a subtle device they convey the water forth that soak into they the most of these friar speak the latin tongue a little after this Nicolo return and die in Friesland whither his brother Antonio have before resort to he and now succeed both in his good and honour who Zichmui employ in the expedition (@) Estotiland Estotiland which happen upon this occasion six and twenty year before four fisher-boat be apprehend at sea by a mighty and tedious storm wherewith after many day they be bring to Estotiland above a thousand mile west from Friesland upon which one of the boat be cast away and six man that be in it be take and bring to a populous city where one that speak latin and have be cast by chance upon that island in the name of the king ask they what countryman they be and understand their case he acquaint the king therewith they dwell there five year and find it ^o be a island very rich be little less than Iseland but far more fruitful one of they say he see latin book in the king library which they at this present do not understand they have a peculiar language and letter or character to themselves they have mine of gold and other metal and have trade with Engroneland they sow corn and make beer and Ale they build bark but know not the use of the compass and have many city and castle the king send these fisherman with twelve bark southwards to a country which they call Drogio in which voyage escape dreadful tempest at sea they encounter with cannibal at land which devour many of they Drogio these fisher show they the manner of take fish with net escape and for the present which they make of their fish to the chief man of the country be belove and honour one of these more expert it seem then the rest be hold in such account that a great lord make war with their lord to obtain he and so prevail that he and his company be send unto he and in this order be he send to five and twenty lord which have war one with another to get he in thirteen year space whereby he come to know almost all those part which he say be a great country and as it be a new World the people be all rude and void of goodness they go naked neither have they wit to cover their body with the beast skin which they take in hunt from the vehement cold they be fierce and eat their enemy have diverse law and governor their live be by hunt further to the south-west they be more civil and have a more temperate air they have city and temple dedicate to idol where they sacrifice man and after eat they and have also some use of gold and silver he flee away secret and convey himself from one lord to another come at length to Drogio where he dwell three year after this time find there certain boat of Estotiland he go thither with they and grow there very rich furnish a bark of his own and return into Friesland where he make report unto his lord of that wealthy country prepare to send thither but three day before they set forth this fisherman die yet take some of the mariner which come with he in his stead they prosecute the voyage and encounter after many day a island where ten man of diverse language be bring unto they of which they can understand none but one of Iseland he tell they that the island be call icaria and the knight thereof call descend of the ancient pedigree of Dedalus king of scot who conquer that island leave his son there for king and leave they those law which to that present they retain and that they may keep their law inviolate they will receive no stranger only they be content to receive one of our man in regard of the language as they have do those ten interpreter sail hence in four day descry land where they find abundance of fowl and bird egg for their refresh the haven they call cap trin. there be a hill which burn cast out smoke where be a spring from which issue a certain water like pitch which run into the Sea the people of small stature wild and fearful hide themselves in cave build there a city and determine to inhabit send Antonio back again with the most of his people to Friesland this history I have thus insert at large which perhaps not without cause in some thing Abrah. ortel chart. 6.
