Nicolo Diego MICHIEL * * there be also the relation hereof by Quirino himseife extant together with this in R^musio tom. 2. out of which I have here add diverse annotation who be present there here contract it seem to be a convenient duty to make a memorial and not suffer to be bury in oblivion that most lamentable and cruel voyage full of innumerable and extreme misery which befall a venetian ship wherein we carry above seven hundred butt of wine spice cotton and other merchandise of great value furnish in Candia with threescore and eight man to go towards the * * the italian call the sail into the mediterranean the Levant or east and thence into the spanish ocean and these part the or west west the master whereof be master Piero Quirini a venetian gentleman in the year 1431. who after many trouble * * these be particular relate by Quirino the patron or owner they lose their rudder on a rock not far from Cales in Spain and be fain to make thither to repair it and other diast^rs follow misfortune and want befall he after his departure from Candia towards the west on the six of November in the foresay year of the lord by chance come into the mouth of the channel of Flanders and go far beyond they by a storm from the south towards the northwest about one hundred and forty mile run still upon the island of where by agreement we Christoforo Fioravanti and Nicolo Michiel say that at noon we found the bottom of the sea with the lead and find ourselves in five and fifty fathom of water and afterward towards the evening we sound and find ourselves in ninety fathom and more but the storm and fury of the wind be so great that it break five of the hinge off our rudder on the twelve in the morning the storm not cease but increase every hour more and more beat upon our weak rudder with so great violence and fury that it break away all that hold it in such sort that it hang on the one side where for the last remedy we fasten a great cable unto it with the which for three day we draw it after we not be able to do it otherwise in which time in our judgement we think we have run two hundred mile and more against our will afterwards we take away the two rudder and with many piece of timber we make another which may rather be call a shadow then a true rudder and we put it in his place to guide and direct the ship but it can not endure long then till the six and twenty of November when the violence of the sea carry it all away so that then we remain deprive of all hope of government and direction on the four of December the fury of the wind grow so outrageous again that it carry away all this three sail and so be spoil and bereave of sail and rudder we go at adventure until the eight day always wander not know by any mean how to provide for our safety afterwards the wind always increase from the east and with so great violence and fury that the sea begin to swell so high that the wave seem mountain and far great than we have ever see before with the darkness of the extreme long night so that we seem to go in the bottomless depth of hell whereby you may imagine how great the anguish and tremble of our heart be because although we be live yet at that instant we seem to be dead expect death every hour which we see present in this darkness the heaven be sometime see to open with the lightning and sudden flash of fire so bright that they take away the fight of our eye and sometime we seem to touch the star the ship mount so aloft and then again we see ourselves bury in hell insomuch as be all astonish we have lose our strength and force and be in this miserable case we do nothing else but with pity behold one another and run with so great violence for many hour in the end a surge of the sea come over the ship under the wind with such fury that the water enter into it fill it almost half full whereby be now much weaken it be ready to sink and turn up the keel and sure that be the last hour and our end and true we have be swallow up of the sea if our lord jesus Christ have not be who forsake not they that religious call upon he who put such power and strength into our afflict mind that see the ship in so dangerous a case full of water as it can not be cast out by any humane force we determine to cut down the main mast and cast it together with the main yard and tackle into th^ sea and so we do whereby the ship be disburden pause awhile and we then take courage begin to cast out the water which with our great trouble and labour we overcome in the end in this manner we go scour away all that long night now when the day be almost come they agree to make ready the boat and the schiffe with that little provision of victual which be remain equal part and the patron say with your consent I command you Nicolo Michiel the notary that you set down in a note the name of those that be willing to enter into the schiffe and boat so present he give he forty five person in a note who be willing to enter into the schiffe which be capable but of one and twenty man only and therefore it be necessary to cast lot who shall go therein and so it be do and they prepare it and set it in order and do the like to the boat into the which the master with forty seven man enter the one and twenty person to who the lot fall enter the schiffe they leave the ship and a rate be give they according to the proportion of the victual which be remain of biscuit and also of Frisoppi three hundred pound weight of cheese of Candia eighty pound of dry bacon eight pound of tallow to trim their schiffe forty pound of oil about two pound weight and no more but beside we bestow there seven carrattell of tyrian wine which be a kind of malvasy for the pinnace or schiffe will hold no more in like manner forty seven man reckon the master enter into the boat or pinnace unto who rateable fall their proportion of victual add thereto a little green ginger in syrup and syrup of lemon with some small quantity of spice which we have take we be in our judgement distant from the near island or land about five hundred mile or more from the point of land to lee-ward of the north part and we sail with these conserve in a quiet and calm sea that little time of the day together with our one and twenty companion comfort ourselves in that which we have see the beginning of so fair a fortune but when the night come a dark mist rose which be a token of the evil success and end the schiffe lose which our companion of the schiffe be to have of who we have now lose the sight so that we never see they any more the ninteenth day the morning appear and not see any token of the schiffe it make we suspicious of their death whereupon our mind be much trouble doubt what may befall they because the wind rage in such manner that a wave of the sea mount with so great violence into the pinnace behind the poop where we Christopher and Nicholas be set down that through the force of the fury thereof two stay be batter and bend which leave a token of unsupportable trouble and grief by mean that the pinnace be more charge with the weight of the water then with her own burden wherefore to remedy it we run all to lade it out with our hand and be constrain through fear and necessity for the free of she we be fain to cast out all that whether with water or without which come most fit and ready to our hand the pinnace become dry again present in this storm we agree to cast overboard the great part of the wine and we find ourselves in so great extremity that if we will taste thereof to comfort our trouble sense no more than one goblet of wine apiece fall to every man share for the whole day and who so will drink more be constrain to take the sea-water hard diet and this measure and quantity of wine hold out eight day and no more and afterward be drive to great necessity we bring ourselves to a great extremity by restrain our proportion to half a goblet a day and none of we can secure sleep for the diverse doubt and danger wherein we always present stand we continue every day and night four or six of we at the helm and those that be at the pump stand always firm and upright change their course where we endure cold beyond comparison far great than that which not many year since be in Venice great frost a^ Venice when all the channel be freeze so that from Margara to Venice not only man and woman but ox horse cart and wagon go over upon the ice in great multitude to the admiration of all the people because that region be without comparison much cold than the country of Italy now consider what our case be be without clothes to cover we and not have any thing to eat or drink or other necessary thing for the maintenance of man life except a few frisoppi which be leave and the night one and twenty hour long and also dark through the which cold extreme cold we begin to lose the feel of our foot and by little and little the cold become more vehement possess the whole body procure a dogged and rage appetite and hunger so that every one seek to devour that which be hide in a corner and whatsoever he have next at hand wheresoever he can find it as well as he may with that weak and little strength which he have remain afterwards death seize upon they you may see they shake the head and fall down present dead in the which disease of seven and forty man which we find in that case six and twenty yield up the ghost and it be not any wonder the death of six and twenty consider we can not have any succour nay it be a divine miracle that any one remain alive and those few of we that be remain live only to commend to memory and high to exalt the great power of God those six and twenty die from the three and twenty of December until the five of january now one now two and sometime more in one day who we bury in the Sea the one and thirty of December our wine be whole spend and have see the cruel and lamentable experience of our six and twenty companion who die with drink of the sea-water necessity give we a good stomach that be to say to take our own water to quench our thirst now there be some of the company exceed trouble with giddiness great thirst for want the abundant plenty of wine they be not able to endure thirst nor to expel it but they account it a great favour to be able to obtain of their companion whereof there be some who deny it to their dear friend to keep it for themselves it be true that some of we wary mortify it by mingle a little syrup of green ginger or lemon therewith which by chance we have remain during this time until the five of january we be every hour more accustom to great extremity the three of january 1431. we have sight of the first land which give we great hope although it so fall out that it be very far distant sight of Land where we see certain rock to weatherward cover to the top with infinite heap of snow to the which the wind be contrary we be not able to approach with the sail and much less with oar because our arm be exceed weaken wherefore we stro^e to come near they with the wind but pass beyond they through the current of the water we lose sight of they altogether and after difficult escape from the rock sail forward towards a very high rock we have sight of a valley situate between the two next mountain into the which desire to enter about the four hour of the night the cruel and outrageous wind will not suffer we notwithstanding inflame through a exceed great desire to go on land we take courage and strength and through force of the oar and the help of God enter into the say valley at a point of land in the least doubtful and dangerous place as it be at the very beginning and entry thereof in the which as soon as they perceive the pinnace to touch upon the sand five of our company be more desirous of drink hot strong stomach to cold small drink then of any other refresh and recreation leap into the water without any regard although it be very deep and go their way towards the snow and so glut themselves therewith that it be a incredible thing and afterward they bring a great quantity thereof unto we who remain in the pinnace to defend it from the beat of the sea of the which we also with great greediness receive without measure and run according to our judgement as we have run in this pinnace for eighteen day from the day that we depart from the ship until this six of januarie sail always between the north-east and the east and not with less wind than after six mile a hour we have run about two thousand five hundred mile and more without ever see any Land they go on Land island of saint or Santi bear off the coast of Norway see Ortelius his map of scandia he place Santi and Rustene in 74. degree but too northerly than they be from the north cape from which this rock say Quirino bear westward 70. mile other rock not far distant some inhabit some not this be off Rustene three mile in compass and call in their language for the extreme remoteness the arse of the World four die and other after on the six of january at the time of the solemn day of the Epiphanie nineteen of we go on land in this desolate and dry place call the island of the saint in the coast of Norway subject to the crown of Denmark leave two other to look to the weak pinnace that it may not be break with the beat of the Sea and be land there by mean of a oar we endeavour to kindle fire and with a tinder box and steel to strike fire we retire ourselves into the close place from the wind and at the sight of the fire nature thereby receive a little strength find this island not inhabit and seek to go in the pinnace to another island five mile off she so leak that part of we land as it be all in the water and some of we up to the middle in shallow water we strive to draw she on land and despair to be ever able to go in she again we determine to fit she in such sort that she may serve our turn to cover we after the best manner that we can we break she into two part and of the great we make a shelter or cottage for thirteen of we and of the lesser a shed capable of five man under the which we enter cover they with part of our sail and with the rest and the cordage of the say pinnace we make continual fire to preserve our life now be utter destitute of all sustenance of meat and drink we go wander upon the sea shore where nature give we food to maintain life with certrine perewinckle or shellfish and barnacle and of these not as many nor when we will but in very small quantity and remove the snow in some place we find a certain herb which together with the snow we cast into the cauldron and when we think it be boil we eat it nor can we satisfy ourselves therewith and thus we live for thirteen day together with small charity among we by reason of the great scarcity of all thing and extreme famine lead rather a brutish life than the life of man continue in this rude and homely kind of life it happen that through the intolerable want four of our companion of the great retire place fail even where the afflict master be with those remedy and slender comfort for their soul and body so that you may think their body remain near unto we who be very weak have lose all our strength we be not able to remove they two yard out of sight and yet I will say more that we have no soon take the freeze or warm water in our mouth but present nature of itself cast it up again we not be able to abstain from it nor almost to stand on our foot great weakness the cold season of the year have bring we to such necessity that to warm we we stand close throng in such sort that we seem as it be to be sew together wherefore I enter under the sail which cover both our cottage round about down to the ground the smoke not be able to issue forth which proceed as I think from the pitch which be within certain piece of the pinnace which we burn so that our eye be swell that we can not see miserable cold nevertheless we endure all that we may be warm and our garment which we never put off be full of vermin and the louse swarm in such number that take they from our back we cast they by whole handful into the fire and they have enter into the flesh in such manner through the skin even to the bone that final they bring a young man of our company that be a notary even unto death so that he be never able to defend himself from so loathsome a little vermin abundance of louse a thing of most manifest example to abase and abate our pride and haughtiness of mind now concord sail among we every one use his own proper advice whereupon part of our company wander through the savage and un-inhabited place come to the knowledge of a solitary and ancient retire place make by the shepherd heretofore for the time of their abode and it be seat on the high part of the coast of the say island towards the west distant from we about a mile and a half unto the which six of the company of the number of those eight which be find in that first and great retire place determine to remove themselves to that new-found solitary habitation for their less inconvenience leave the other two their other companion alone in a abandon and forsake place as well because they be not able to travel as also for that we be altogether unable to conduct they it come to pass that those six through the gracious goodness and gift of God find a exceed great fish they find a Fish to the which I know not what name to give whether whale or por piss of the sea which we be to think be send from the divine and excellent bounty to feed we and consider that we see it cast up by the sea upon the shore dead fresh good and great and at the time of our so great necessity we render thanks unto our most gracious lord God who at that time will sustain our so weak and disease body with that food appease peradventure through the prayer of some vigilant and devout soul with this fish we feed ourselves for nine day sufficient and as it happen those very nine day be so tempestuous with wind rain and snow that by no mean the cruel storm will have suffer we to go one pace out of our cottage the miraculous fish be spend the furious tempest be somewhat assuage wherefore not have wherewith to maintain life like wolf that oppress with famine go to seek out other place of abode we arise out of the cottage and go wander through the desert rock to find any succour to sustain our life with perewinckle of the sea and barnacle with the which we be of necessity to be content although they be very little thing and so we maintain ourselves until the last of january 1431. and therefore we be lean pale afflict and but half alive 1432. in foreign account in which time find certain dung of ox scorch and dry with the cold and wind whereof we gather every day to make a fire we certain know that place to be frequent by ox which thing give we assure hope of some good end and through this persuasion we endure part of our grievous care and sorrow in the end the hour come wherein our benign creator and most gracious lord purpose to conduct his little flock so much afflict into the haven of their safety and it be in this manner two young heifer of a fisherman near unto this island within five mile be stray the former year from the place where he use to dwell i will of Rustene and never understand any news of they within the year nor have any hope to find they again on the very first day of February 1431. at night one of the son of the say fisherman of Rustene for so the say island be call be of the age of sixteen year dream that certain the two heifer be escape and go up to the island of saint distant from they where we be lodge at the point of the west part upon the which no man dare ever go at the low water whereupon the son who have such a vision or dream pray the father and a elder brother of he that they will accompany he to go to seek they and so all three in a fisher-boate take their way towards the say island and come to the point where we be and the say young man land there leave their father to look to the boat and have ascend a little upon the cliff they see a smoke arise in the air from their retire place which they have former use whereupon through fear and astonishment they marvel and that not a little how whence and by what mean it may come to pass wherefore they stand a long time much amaze and desire to know the cause they begin to talk one with another and although we perceive the noise and hear the voice yet we can not conceive whence it shall be but rather judge it to be the cry of crow than the voice of man and we be the rather induce thereunto because some few day before we have see upon the miserable carcase of our eight companion cast to the wind multitude of crow that rend the air with their croak feed themselves upon they whereupon we think it can be no other but continue from good to better the voice of the child of God send to save we we clear perceive that they be the voice of man and not the cry of fowl and at that instant Christophor^ Fioravanti arise out of the cottage and see the two young stripling cry with a loud voice come towards we say rejoice behold two come to seek we whereupon inflame with a earnest desire we raise ourselves on our foot go rather with the heart then with the foot and draw near unto they we perceive that through the sudden and extreme strangeness of the matter they be afraid and their countenance begin to wax pale but contrary we cheer ourselves and be comfort with a assure hope show with action and gesture of humility that we come not to offend they in any wise diverse thought come in our mind whether we shall detain one of they or both or whether one or two of we shall go with they the first determination be against we because we know not with who nor with how many we have to do for that we understand not they nor they we but be advise by the holy ghost we go down to their boat in the best and most amiable manner that we can where the father be who expect they and when he see we he also remain astonish and amaze in this mean space we look whether there be any thing in their boat to succour our necessity to maintain life but we find nothing there so they move through pity see we affamished by sign and action which we make unto they be content to carry with they Ghirardo da Lione a sewer and Cola di Otranto a mariner who have some knowledge and be able to speak the french and the high dutch leave we in great hope of present safety and help their boat come to Rustene with our two companion all the people flock together and see the countenance and habit of our companion astonish at so great and strange a matter they demand among themselves whence and how such like fellow as these appear or from what place they land and that they may be the better advertise they attempt to speak unto they in diverse language but in the end Almain priest of the order of the preacher a German Priest speak with one of the say companion in the high dutch and by that mean they be certify what we be from whence and how we have arrive there the which matter the morning follow which be the second day of February dedicate to the glorious mother of Christ the say priest publish to all the people of Rustene exhort they that through our misfortune they will be move to pity and to help we according to their ability in this mean space through the catholic remembrance of the Almain priest on the three day of February 1431. at the very instant of the day of saint Biagio the courteous and pitiful inhabitant of Rustene come unto we with great plenty of all sustenance which they use for their provision to feed we and preserve we be desirous to conduct we to their kind habitation to refresh our weak body and so we be guide and receive into Rustene upon the say day where we have great restorative which be rather hurtful for we through the exceed abundance thereof because we can never satisfy ourselves with eat and our weak stomach not be able to endure it it make our heart to grieve so that we think we shall have die there be remain in the first and great of our two retire place two of the company which be impotent and together they go with the priest sing psalm and hymn as well to bury those eight that be dead as to conduct to the haven of safety the two that be remain behind and arrive at the island of saint they sustenance and yet he be bring to Rustene with some little show of life where at the end of two day he depart this transitory life eleven of we be come to Rustene we land and go into the house of our guide host and lord as he and the rest desire whereinto our most prudent master master Piero Quirini enter use his wisdom and discretion perform a action of exceed great humility as soon as he see the companion of our conductor and sergeant Maior declare by semblance that he will acknowledge she to be the mistress of the house he cast himself down at her foot but she refuse and lift he up from the ground embrace he and bring he to the fire and with her own hand give he somewhat to eat in this island there be twelve little house with about one hundred and twenty person for the most part fisherman Rustene describe and they be by nature endue with understanding to know how to make boat bucket ton basket net of all sort and every other thing necessary for their use and trade and they be very courteous one towards another and serviceable desirous to please rather for love then for hope of any gift or good turn to be do they again fish call stockfish in all their payment and barter be use in stead of coin money and they be all as it be of one bigness and measure stockfish in stead of money of the which every year they dry a infinite number in the wind and in the time of may freight themselves with they carry they through the realm of Denmark that be to say Sweden Denmark and Norway be all subject to the king of dacia where they barter and exchange the say fish for leather clothes iron pulse and other thing whereof they have scarcity few other thing for maintenance of life be find there except fish yet at certain time they have some small quantity of beef and milk of cow of the which with rice and I know not what other mixture they make bread of a naughty taste their drink be sour milk their drink and bread displease unto they who have not be accustom thereunto they use also ale that be to say wine draw out of rye we eat of the plaice or fish which be exceed great halibut very great so that you will not believe it we see some of they somewhat long than six foot of the common venetian measure above two foot broad upon the chine and more than three quarter of a foot in thickness a wonderful thing to be speak they clothe the man with red hide and likewise black able to defend they from the water and they use clothes very course of azure red and ash-colour bring from Denmark of small price and estimation these country people use much to frequent the church because they be very devout and yield great reverence to the worship and service of God avarice be as it be altogether extinguish sincerity for they understand not in any sort nor know not what thing of another may become they but by barter and therefore they use not to lock door house nor window nor any chest for fear to be rob but only by reason of the wild beast the inhabitant of this place both young and old be of so great simplicity of heart simplicity thus the italian think in regard of their differ jealousy which scarce permit the grow son or brother to sleep under the same roof with the mother or sister and obedient to the commandment of God that they neither understand know nor imagine in any wise what fornication or adultery may be but use marriage according to God they return where he also and his wife sleep and successive in one bed near adjoin be their daughter and son of ripe age together near to the which bed we also sleep almost close adjoin to they so that when they go to sleep or when they arise or when they strip themselves naked and we in like manner we indifferent see one another and yet with that purity as if we have be little child but I will tell you more that for two day together our say host with his elder son arise to go a fish even at the time of the most delightful hour of sleep leave his wife and daughter in the bed with that security and purity as if he have proper leave they in the arm and embracement of the mother not return to his home in less time than the space of eight hour the inhabitant of this island especial the elder ^ort be find so unite in their will to the will of God that in every casualty of natural death which befall father mother husband Wife child or whatsoever other kinsman or friend when the hour of their passage unto another life appear present without any grief of heart and complain they assemble themselves together unto the cathedral church to thank and praise the heavenly creator who have permit such a one to live so many year and at that present as his creature vouchsafe to call he or she into his gracious favour and near unto he and at the appoint hour they cause they to be wash clean to have they pure and neat as they be bear whereupon rejoice and content themselves with his infallible will and pleasure they give he praise and glory not show any passion either in word or gesture as if proper they have but sleep sure we may say that from the three of February 1431. until the fourteen of may 1432. which amount to a hundred day and one we be within the circuit of paradise to the reproach and shame of the country of Italy there at the begin of may we see great variety and alteration first their woman use to go unto the bath which be very near and commodious as well for purity as for the custom they observe which they hold agreeable unto nature they use to come forth of their house stark naked as they come out of their mother womb go without any regard to their way carry only in their right hand a heap of grass in manner of a broom as they say to rub the sweat from their back and the left hand they hold upon their hip spread it as it be for a shadow to cover their hinder part that they shall not much appear where have twice see they we pass away by they as easy as their own people the country be so cold and the continual see of they that it cause we to make no account thereof on the contrary part these very woman be see on the sunday to enter into the church in long and comely garment and that they may not by any mean be see in the face they wear on their head a thing like a complete morion with a gorget which have a hole to see through at the end like the hole of a pipe through the which they behold within that no further off from their eye then the hole be long so that they seem to have it in their mouth to pipe and worse than that they can neither see nor speak unless they turn themselves a yard or more from the hearer I think good to note these two extreme variety as worthy to be understand from the twenty of November until the twenty of February the night continue and last there about one and twenty hour or more the moon never whole hide her body or her ray at least and from the twenty of May until the twenty of August either the whole sun be always see or else his beam never fail in this country there be infinite plenty of white bird in their language call Muxi but we call they cock of the sea which by nature converse and willing abide where man inhabit whether they find they in bark or on the Land and they be so domestical and tame as house-dove be with we in this island and in the country of Succia we see very white skin of bear as white as armelin much long than twelve venetian foot we abide in Rustene three month and eleven day expect a fit time to pass with our host into Sueden with his usual freight of stockfish which be in the time of May when these country people depart carry with they infinite plenty thereof through the realm of the aforesaid king of dacia on the fourteen day of May 1432. come the hour so much desire to turn our face towards our amiable and belove country as our mind and desire always be and leave the charitable place of Rustene which be the last succour and refresh to our misery so we take our leave of our domestical friend of the house and of our mistress and hostess to who in token of our love we leave not that whereunto we be in duty bind but what we have remain and that be certain small trifle thing of little value in our opinion as goblet girdle and small ring and likewise we take leave of the neighbour and the priest and general of all show they by sign and word as the interpeter may understand then that we acknowledge ourselves bind unto they all and have perform due salutation we enter into a bark of the burden of twenty ton or thereabouts lade with the say fish guide by our patron and host with three of his son and certain of their kindred and we depart on the say day bend our course towards bergie which be the first convenient and fit haven for the dispatch and riddance of such fish which place be distant from Rustene about some thousand mile so we conduct the say bark through certain direct and safe channel row most commodious and at ease token of the Skiffe drown but after we be about two hundred mile off from Rustene we find certain relic of the plank and rib of our Skiffe whereby we plain know that our companion which be in it be perish and drown the first night that they depart from we Trondon the nine and twenty of may 1432. we arrive with the say bark at Trondon upon the coast of Norway the princely seat of the king of Denmark where the honourable body of glorious saint Olaus rest saint Olaus there we stay ten day to wait for passage and a fit time for our voyage but not find it because we will lose no more time we take leave of our belove host his son and the rest to proceed on our journey by Land the nine of june we depart from Trondon travel on foot go towards Vastena a place subject to the king of Denmark Vastena within the province of Sweden where the cheekbone and part of the bone of the head of saint Bridget remain be there we understand by the venetian that the inhabitant for the reverence of their glorious king saint Olaus unto who as they well know our signiory of Venice do great favour in his go and return from his voyage to Jerusalem be dispose with deed to provide for we by their counsel help and money and first they advise we not to go the direct way into dacia by reason of the danger of wild beast which may befall we but to address ourselves to go direct to Stichimborgi to find out a valiant venetian knight call m. Giovan Francho from who we shall receive favour and help in plentiful manner for love of our country although the way be thirty day journey quite contrary to our direct way on the eighteen day we come to the court of the say Cavallier m. Giovan Francho a honourable baron and high esteem of the crown of dacia where with great joy we find our two straggle companion venetian knight the valorous knight be now inform of our come with a cheerful countenance declare well unto we how great the love of his country be and especial know the calamity and penury of we his countryman and be easy able to relieve it and therefore he can not sufficient satisfy himself in honour clothe and feed we but give we money for our necessity and furnish we afterward with good horse in his own proper person together with his only son m. Mapheo with a hundred and twenty horse of his own servant he accompany we many day journey through his territory travel always at his own charge afterwards upon his limit and bound we take our leave to depart thank he with the most reverend and kind speech that possible we can whereupon he be depart leave we for our guide his say son m. Mapheo with twenty servant on horseback who keep we company unto Vastena the place from whence about forty day before we have depart unto the which place for the avoid of two month travel we be fain to return so that on the thirty day of july we enter into Vastena where we abide until the second of August be always accompany and our charge bear by the say m. Mapheo on the second of August we take our leave of the aforesaid m. empire as the french do their dolphines the brother or elder son and more sufficient who have the great sway in peace and war but the Chans themselves perpetual depute and elect they but with the approbation of the tartar noble and if also any dissension or war be raise between the sultan or the Chan about the empire the turkish emperor neglect not to dispatch the sultan pledge with a army and standard into taurica or the Peninsula and it be sufficient for he to be prince the Chan and sultan be appease or force to go away by war for which cause he have always many janissary in taurica or the Peninsula election of the chan. the election of the Chans after the ancient custom of the nation do whilom consist in the free suffrage of the duke mursy and noble tartar furthermore for their frequent discord and hideous war which be occasion by the nogaien Tartar border on taurica or the Peninsula about the empire and be Chans over the tartar have by subtlety destroy the more noble and potent tartar and cast they into fetter begin absolute to domineer over the tartar and by force to draw the election to their posterity the emperor of the turk aid they but if the Chan will not constitute his brother Galga but his own son as it often fortune by reason of those discord and reciprocal butchery among themselves he circumuent crafty and subtle all the sultan brother and covert make they away yet most of they fly to the Turk of who they be bountiful entertain and comfort and receive a perpetual stipend of he the sultan young son of the Chans be educate and tutor by the that be fit be set over certain tartar troop and allure many voluntary tartar unto they notwithstanding they make leader of the nogaien tartar and remunerate with money and horse most of their parent and decency for they be so enrich by the lazy cowardice and especial by the irreligious impiety of the neighbour christian through make often inroad and get rich booty that the great noble of they in private wealth and domestic splendour wife and child be little inferior to the turk they may have as many woman by the mahometical law as they will and for the most part they buy wife of the petigoren which although they sustain and maintain not proud but very comely and civil according to the country guise but those by who they have issue very honourable and gorgeous Arabic letter they deliver their son in their infancy to be instruct in the Arabic letter but they keep not their daughter at home but commit they to the near in blood to be provide for they place their son grow to man age in the Chans or sultan service their marriageable daughter in wedlock to the more honourable and noble tartar or turk those tartar be mahometan and have priest and Mosches they use the chaldaic or Arabic letter mahometan religion which they have receive somewhat corrupt from the turk although before they come into taurica or the Peninsula they seem to have be a savage and brutish nation and of very savage condition which now also be very perspicuous by the rustic for they want then altogether those law rite letter and manner but the tartar be teach by the turk humanity and that false worship the more noble now general practice hospitality government and law the cadi and beg law or justice be administer in the town or city of the Chan and other sultan among the tartar after the mahometan Law there be always presbiterall cadi or judge in the village Begi or justice who hear and decide particular injury but cause of life blood theft which we call criminal or of land which we call civil or official the Chan himself decide with his counselor no attorney nor lawyer they plead their own cause in resolve of which they need no lawyer nor use trick of law calumny excusation nor procrastination the tartar or stranger of mean condition lie open themselves very free their wrong before the judge and Chan of who they be always hear and speedy discharge for at any time any may have access to he when he come in public man of the base degree be not exclude but be see of the Chan be examine to wit if they have any suit that they relate it for they do not only perform great obedience to the law they adore and venerate their prince in God steed all spiritual judge after Mahomet law be account among they for saint man of all equity and integrity fidelity and opinion great peaceableness to the shame of always law gospeler the prince and magistrate execute and dispatch whatsoever be bid or command sudden and faithful with alacrity promptness and great fear they be far from controversy crimination justice unnecessary and personal brawl envy hatred filthy excess luxury and ambition in their victual and array I abide their nine month neither hear I criminal or civil act to have happen among they or any composition by reason of enmity in the prince court they wear not nor at home sword neither bow nor any other weapon except wayfarer and traveller no daily use of weapon to who they be very courteous and friendly they be always secure from spoiler but except they keep perpetual watch they be less safe from high-way-theeve and night-robber who steal nothing from they but their horse although they have a rich soil yet very few gentleman or plebeian provide for the household estate for many neither till nor sow their ground they abound with horse camel ox cow sheep and flock of all cattle and thereof live yet the gentleman have bread flesh meat distil * * aquavitae meat and drink wine and metheglin but the rustic want bread but use stamp millet and macerate with milk and water which they vulgar call for meat and for drink they use mare milk and cheese they feed on camel horse and ox unprofitable for burden and kill they when they be about to die sometime eat sheep flesh the gentleman dwell not in the plain but in the village of taurica or the Peninsula they which be near wood live in they although many do not possess proper village yet they Regius and other in the vulgar tongue to the pastor who be ignorant of the latin as at that time almost all of they be and also send for fit and apt young man out of Iseland who he maintain in the haff^ian university at his own cost and give they charge over church and school king Woldemare as soon as they shall profess christian religion in Iseland ordain they two bishop one in scalholden in the east part and another in holen in the west two bishop in Iseland who successor at this day retain nothing but a shadow and a bare title for they have no other revenue but butter and Fish but when that reformation whereof I speak be make by king Christian in the church of Iseland one of the bishop in scalholden conspire with the people reject the doctrine of the gospel and make a rebellion they kill the king lieutenant the year follow which be 1535. the king send a noble man of the order of knighthood one Paul Hitfelt who I see a old man in Denmark furnish with a fleet soldier and munition into the island the seditious be slay he renew the reformation of the doctrine of the gospel and return into Denmark leave a certain noble man to take charge of the church and island the great man in Iseland at that time be one tadde bond he after the king army be depart tadde bonde conspire with the principal man who by his authority he draw to take his part revolt from his allegiance and persuade the rest of the islander to follow they meet together in a place call Waloe and conspire to rebel and cast off the king subjection Waloe they impart their counsel together and tadde have his poss^ssions not in one place and many retainer and for these cause he think they can not easy be suppress the bishop who dwell in the east have a special care to acquaint the king lieutenant with all that be do for the lieutenant be absent in the west part of that island and the bishop hate tadde a long time for in that first rebellion he have false accuse he to the lieutenant as guilty and author of the rebellion this accusation only bring great and extreme calamity upon he the lieutenant be certify what be do he persuade by fit instrument some of the complice of the faction to continue in their allegiance propound reward and punishment then many of they when they see the greatness of the danger leave he come humble to the lieutenant and beg pardon and obtain it tadde therefore be adjudge a enemy both of the king and of his country they promise therefore by a oath and give of their faith that they will pursue he then he through fear of the danger with a few of his domesticke which he have gather together keep himself at the foot of hekelueld but be circumvent they be all slay and he take they that take he bring he to the bishop to commit he to prison but he refuse to receive he therefore they draw he to another certain man of those who have the chief place in justice neither will he receive he fear the hatred of the people there be at that time there a certain Iselander jonas by name a man of courage I know say he to who I will commit he that will diligent keep he and forthwith he slay he and bury he and so the sedition be appease and from that time until this day the word of God be teach among barbarous man after the manner of the confession of Augusta the life and manner of the iselander in the whole island there be three sort of man who be hold in any reckon and account three sort of people for the common people by reason of the scarcity of ship wherewith they fish make themselves slave to the rich of those three sort the first be of they who they call loshmader that be to say man of justice for loch in their language signify Law these man administer justice and there be many of they but twelve of they only have the yearly charge of justice all man obey their judgement and decree twelve justice each year another sort be of they who be call Bonden they be in the place of noble and as every one of they be rich in ship and cattle so he have most fisher and follower this only power they know the three sort be of bishop and minister of the word of God of the which many be find every where throughout the whole island there be many of the iselander very proud and high mind especial by reason of the strength of body which they have strength I see a Iselander who easy put a hamburg tun full of ale to his mouth drink off it as if he have have but one small measure both sex in Iseland have the same habit so that by the garment you shall not easy discern whether it be man or woman they want flax except it be bring unto they by our countryman habit the womenkind there be very beautiful but ornament be want the whole nation of the islander be much give to superstition and they have spirit familiar serve they superstition and witchcraft for they only be fortunate in fish who be raise up by night of the devil to go a fish and although the minister of the gospel use all diligence in dissuade they from this impiety night raven yet this wickedness have take root and stick so deep in their mind and they be so bewitch of Satan that they can admit no sound doctrine and dehortation yea by the devil mean if you offer they money they promise a prosperous wind and perform it which I know as hereafter shall be speak the like Olaus Magnus write of the finlander in his three book they hold ship also by enchantment almost immovable and that in a prosperous wind and true it be a wonder that Satan so sport with they sweet sacrifice for the devil letice suitable his lip for he have show they a remedy in stay of their ship to wit the excrement of a maid be a virgin if they anoint the prow and certain plank of the ship he have teach they that the spirit be put to flight and drive away with this stink in the rest of the carriage of their life they thus behave themselves the parent teach their male child even from their childhood letter and the law of that island so that very few man be find throughout the whole island but they know letter and many woman use our letter learning and have also other character with the which they express some whole word of they which word can hardly be write with our letter they give themselves to hardness and fish from their infancy for all their life consist in fish they exercise not husbandry because they have no field and the great part of their food consist in fish unsavoury butter fiw and fish milk and cheese in stead of bread they have fish bruise with a stone their drink be water or whey drink so they live many year without medicine or physician many of they live till they be one hundred and fifty year old and I see a old man who say he have then live two hundred year a old man or a loud lie nay Olaus Magnus in his twenty book say that the iselander live three hundred year the great part of Iselanders have never see bread much less taste it if our man at any time sell they meal or corn Bread they mingle it with milk and lay it up for a long time as delicate for noble they call this sauce or mixture Drabbell the german that trade in Iseland have a place in the haven of Haffenefordt fence by nature where under tent they set their mercbandise to sale as shoe garment glass knife and such kind of merchandise of no price the iselander have oil melt out of the bowel of fish commodity know to our tanner and shoemaker they have fish Brimstone white fox skin butter and other thing they barter all these for our commodity nor be the bargain ratify before they be well stuff with our meat wine or beer together with their wife and child who they bring with they how many soever they have come into the haven they have their daughter with they which be marriage-able they after they have inquire of our company whore whether they have wife at home or not they promise a night lodging for bread biscuit or any other trifle thing sometime the parent yield their daughter free even for a whole month or as long as they stay if she prove with child by that lie with she the parent love their daughter better than before and the child be bear they bring it up some year while either the father return or they give it to their son in law that shall be for a dowry with their daughter who do not despise it because it be bear of the German blood if any virgin have familiarity with a German she be honour among they and therefore she be seek of many suitor and the time be before this that whoredom which be without the degree of consanguinity and affinity have no infamy and although preacher cry out against it and the offender be severe punish yet they hardly abstain drink and sing they lay not up wine and beer which they buy of our countryman but quaff it up house by house by course one with another and that free or for nothing while they drink they sing the heroical act of their ancestor not with any certain compose order or melody but as it come in every man head neither be it lawful for any one to rise from the table to make water but for this purpose the daughter of the house or another maid or woman attend always at the table watchful if any beckon to he that becken she give the chamber-pot under the table with her own hand the rest in the mean while grunt like swine lest any noise be hear the water be pour out he wash the basin and offer his service to he that be willing and he be account uncivil who abhor this fashion love worm lousy love they entertain they that come unto they with a kiss and they behold and look each on other if peradventure they may see louse creep on their garment which great trouble they for want of linen if thy see any each take they from the other and as often as he take away one so often do he thank he with his head discover and this they do one to the other as long as they see one by night the master of the house with all his family his wife and child lie in one room lodging cover with a cloth make of wool which they make and the like clothes they lap under they without straw or hay put under all of they make water in one chamber-pot with the which in the morning they wash their face mouth tooth and hand they allege many reason thereof to wit that this make a fair face maintain the strength confirm the sinew in the hand and preserve the tooth from putrefaction if cattle perish in the water or snow which often come to pass they say they be kill of God and be account among the delicate and it happen in the year 1564. in a place call ackermisse that in the month of january some cow stray in the dark and the fog be so great and the depth of snow that they can not be find in the month of April they be first find untainted and without any evil smell and be distribute among the neighbour some part be bring to the governor with who I live at that time which be not lawful for he to despise yet he command it to be give to the poor in the winter time before and after the when the sun decline and be in Sagitarius and Aquarius it depart from they long night neither do it ascend above the horizon while it touch therefore they have no light but of the moon and star in like manner about the summer when the sun ascend to Cancer and Leo it never go down under the horizon therefore at that time they have no night in the winter time they keep their bed many day and exercise themselves in the game of chess chess the invention whereof be due to Xerxes the philosopher the mean while the servant bring they their meat dress to their bed they keep lamp of the oil of fish continual burn other burn tallow candle in the month of February as soon as the sun ascend above the horizon by little and little the day grow long than they begin to fish whereof there be so great plenty that it be scarce credible for the fish which for three whole month swim in the dark as soon as they see a fish of tin fasten to a iron they run to it in schoale that they be not only draw up by the jaw but wheresoever the iron touch they have take they they pluck out the bone and lay up their bowel and make fat or oil of they they heap up their fish in the open air and the purity of the air be such there that they be harden only with the wind and sun without salt better sure than if they be corn with salt dry Fish and if they kill any beast they preserve the flesh without stink or putrefaction without salt harden only with the wind of the wonderful stand pool lake and fountain in Iseland in diverse place almost throughout the wh^le island be bath and scald fountain hot bath which flow out in great abundance this water as soon as it begin to cool have a sulphury substance in the top thereof in these scald water wherein I can scarce dip my finger red dive-doppers be see afar off if you come near they vanish if you depart they appear again so all day long if any please they play bo-peep with man dive-doppers whether they be dive-doppers indeed I leave it to other to decide at the west of this island there be a huge smoky lake and very cold which turn all thing that be cast into it into stone and that in few day stone-making water and which be worthy of great admiration if you put a stick upright into the bottom the low part which be stick into the earth have the resemblance and hardness of iron after two day that which be in the water have the hardness and show of a stone the upper part which remain above the water keep his wont form and I twice prove the truth of this thing note but when I put the low part which represent iron to the fire that it may melt it burn like a coal there be two fountain of most different quality in a place upon the sea coast which be call Turlocks haven the one cold the other hot these fountain by pipe be draw into one place and temper for bathe they make a most wholesome bath not far from these fountain there be a certain other fountain which bubble forth liquor like wax french disease which notable cure the french disease which be very common there not far from the haven Haffnefordt there be a cleave in a rock like to a fountain of unmeasurable depth if you look into it you can see the water but if you cast in a stone half a hour after you shall hear it fall as if it fall into brazen vessel and forthwith the water arise and it be fill to the top of the well brim and it be a most clear water which notwithstanding no man dare touch nor taste neither do it flow out but so long after as the stone which be cast in sink to the bottom there be another lake in the middle of the island which cast forth a pestiferous fume insomuch as it kill bird fly over it with the poison thereof of the wonderful mountain in island there be three mountain in island very admirable the one be call the mountain of the cross the other snevelsiockell these two pierce the cloud with their height who head or top no man ever see nor be they ever see without ice and snow in those lightning and horrible thunder be daily hear when nevertheless in the neighbour valley the air be fair and clear as in summer time the three mountain lie on the north of the island and not very high but it have burn very many year with what fire or matter it be unknown but see brimstone be dig out of the earth throughout the whole land it seem that the sulphury matter be sometime inflame this mountain be not far from the sea and the sea on one side beat upon it it be call Hecla sometime it cast forth flame sometime fiery water Hecla a burn Hill then black ash and Pumis stone in so great abundance that it darken the sun no man also can dwell near it by six mile neither be there any pasture about it sometime bold man and such as regard not their life cast stone into the hollow place for sometime there be a wonderful calm in the mountain especial when the western wind blow conceit of purgatory it cast back the stone fling into it with a horrible noise and sound the common people think the soul of the damn to be torment here it be certain that diverse and horrible spirit be observe in this mountain and about it for if a battle be fight in any place the islander especial they that sail and fish in the sea near to Hecla know the day of the battle fight although they know not where it be do for they see as they report wicked spirit go forth and return and bring soul with they and such a story be rep^rted all island over a fisherman sail by Hecla meet with another ship both have a prosperous wind and when after the manner of sailor he be demand who he be and of what place he answer that he have the bishop of breme in his ship collusion of man or illusion of devil a^ngim jonas a islander scoff at (@) as fabulous who he will convey to Hecla and it be know that the bishop die the same day which notwithstanding I will not set down for truth if any perish by sea or otherwise die sometime leave their friend and acquaintance they appear very heavy be demand whither they go and from whence they answer they be bring to Hecla under a cruel master the devil and so vanish and they be so bewitch of Satan that they think they the soul of the depart but because no man that be well in his wit will think that hell be in this mountain yet it may be demand whence the hill have this matter whereby it shall bring forth so many year flame so many ash and such abundance of Pumis stone for we see the most solid and firm body and all thing to be consume by fire and for that cause some think that it shall come to pass that these flame shall once be extingish for the cause fail they deny that any effect can follow but here what I think I will free speak yet save other man judgement it be manifest by watery meteor that there be a continual generation of water by the vapour gather together in the cavity of the earth which issue forth by fountain but the efficient and material cause abide perpetual the effect also continual remain so also in the bowel of the earth there be certain place which by their own nature draw unto they a hot and dry exhalation and that it resolve it into flame ash and Pumis stone which may easy be do in this mountain by reason of the sulphur matter which be find in island throughout the whole Land and as fountain send forth more abundance of water in the winter time then in the summer nay some of they be dry because matter fail so be it with this mountain for sometime matter fail it have neither flame nor smoke and all be quiet whereby it appear that the matter and efficient cause fail however it be I know this that no man may come to the foot of the mountain without danger and fear as hereafter shall be declare strange story the same year I be in island the nine and twenty of November about midnight in the sea near Hecla there appear a flame which give light to the whole island so that all of we astonish wonder and careful expect the issue thereof the elder sort and such as be skilful in this matter say that this light come from Hecla a hour after the whole island tremble as it shall have be move out of the place after the earthquake follow a horrible crack that if all warlike ordnance have be discharge it have be nothing to this terror it can be think much less express by word how horrible it be we think that the whole frame of the world will fall and that the last day be at hand but it be know afterward that the sea go back two league in that place and remain dry about the begin of july at a certain time of the year great store of ice sudden float to the island about Hecla and there go a rumour through the whole island nay it be believe that the damn soul be torment in this ice by course in the flame in the mountain and after in the ice this ice for three whole month swim only about Hecla another wonder if you take any part of this ice out of the sea and wrap it in a linen cloth and lay it up in a chest it remain so long unmelted as it swim in the sea but if the ice in the sea vanish which sudden in one night happen this appear not nor leave any sign of moisture in the linen cloth which be not a hard thing for Satan to do to take away the ice without moisture to increase their incredulity Olaus Magnus make mention of this ice in his eleven book but because I determine to search out all thing diligent I sail not without great fear unto this ice and I observe that this ice be violent cast against the rock by force of the wind and so make a mournful sound afar off as if miserable howl be hear there hereupon the islander think the soul of the damn be torment in this ice of the riches of the islander I have say that island be a rough and snowy country and beside it be full of rock and stone and so true that there be not a field in the whole island they have not so much as garden wherein they may have potherb or pulse they know no kind of corn nor apple pear nor cherry nor any fruit of tree and which be almost incredible they neither use bread nor salt yet they be well like and strong there be no city in the whole island no fruit they seldom have two or three dwelling together they have their cottage on the sea side for fish and under ground by reason of the fierce wind there be no lone of money among they for ware be change for ware brimstone grow on the south part and almost throughout the whole island Bartar Brimstone which be dig out in great abundance they sell this stuff purge for a small price mine of gold or silver nor of any other mettle they have none they use iron but such as be bring unto they you shall scarce find a man who have not iron nail in a bag wherewith horseshoe be fasten all their house be under ground for they have no matter for building there be not a tree in the whole island except the birch-tree and that in one place birch-tree which also exceed not the stature of a man in length and that by reason of the vehemency of the wind that it can grow high this birch-tree after the summer begin first to bud the leaf have a most sweet smell and of so fragrant a savour that the german put they in their tent and upon their meat for a singular delight yet sometime great abundance of firre-tree from Tartary or elsewhere carry by force of the wave and the ice arrive in island the chief use of they be in build cabin under the ground you shall scarce find a house out of the earth by reason of the strong wind which sometime overthrow horse and their rider they have great plenty of butter for the fatness of the grass for the island gras^e be so fat great wind that ox after a certain time be to be drive from the pasture lest they burst and it be of so please a scent that our man lay it up in their chest with singular care for their garment fat grass the most part for scarcity of vessel lay their butter aside in the corner of their house as we do lime or other matter and that without Salt they have domestical cattle as cow but many of they be without horn al their horse be ambler and very fit for carry of burden their cow horse and sheep dog of more price than child bear and fox white crow they have very great sheep they keep not a hog nor a hen for want of grain if fodder or hay fail they in the winter they feed their cattle with fish they have rough dog breed without tail and ear for their pleasure which they sell dear and great esteem when notwithstanding they offer their child to any that will ask they and that free beside this island have white fox and huge bear of the same colour they have no bird but the spaniard and portugal be also carry away in great number which thing be do while I be in island to my great profit island also have white partridge there be also every where through the whole travel by compass whale they that go from one part of the island to another by the continent have no way which they may follow for the solitariness thereof but as sailor in the sea so they by the help which be cover with snow and ice we find neither foot of man not any habitation nor fit port but the sea be close and fence on every side with craggy rock yet we meet with a great white bear which neither fear we a bear nor can be drive away with our cry but come full upon we as to his certain prey and when he come near unto we be twice shoot through with a gun he stand bolt upright with his fore-feet as a man stand till he be shoot through the three time and so fall down dead his skin be send to the king of Denmark we agree among ourselves before we go on shore if we find a fit harbour or else have need of their help that we shall pluck up our standard which we carry out with we for that purpose and that they if they will call we back shall signify the same with their ordnance a tempest arise in the mean while the master of the ship give we a sign to return by the discharge of a piece of ordnance and call we back unto the ship all of we therefore return with great labour after three day unto the ship with the bear skin we sail therefore to the other side of the island towards the north to the country of the pigmy or Zembla that by the mouth of the white sea we may come into the scythian or tartarian sea from whence they say there be a passage to the kingdom of China and cathay but be hinder by the ice we can not pass the mouth of that sea therefore without do flame of a green colour which have almost kill i with their sulphury and filthy stink so that I scarce escape to my forsake horse and companion upon that sudden astonishment I fall into a sickness and
