chap. 2 a commission for Ionas Poole our servant appoint master of a small bark call the Elizabeth of fifty ton burden for discovery to the northward of greenland give the last day of march 1610. in as much as it have please almighty God through the industry of yourself and other to discover unto our nation a land lie in eighty degree towards the north-pole Poole entertain by a certain stipend he be as I have hear miserable and base murder betwixt Ratcl^ffe and London after his return from this voyage we be desirous not only to discover far to the northward along the say land to find whether the same be a island or a main and which way the same do trend either to the eastward or to the westward of the pole as also whether the same be inhabit by any people or whether there be a open sea far northward than have be already discover for accomplish of all which our desire we have make choice of you and to that end have entertain you into our service for certain year upon a stipend certain not doubt but you will so carry yourself in the business for which you be so entertain as God may be glorify our country benefit yourself credit and we in our desire satisfy and for your better instruction to proceed in this your voyage we have think good to set down our opinion what course we think fit to be observe in the same which be that forasmuch as by your own report of the great store of whale in those sea we be at a extraordinary charge this year of set out a ship and man for that purpose which ship be call the marie Margaret of London in burden one hundred and fifty ton or thereabouts our meaning be that you do keep company with the say ship and not to leave she till God send you to the place where she may make her voyage which by your report shall be at a ^lace name by you the last year 1610. whale Bay and God send you to the say place we will have you to stay there the kill of a whale or two or three for your better experience hereafter to expedite that business if through extremity of the ice you shall be put from your discovery and in the mean time while you be stay about kill of the whale you may cause some of your people to be search the coast with their shallop for whale fin morse tooth ambergris or any other commodity that may be find upon that coast. and have thus stay a convenient time with the say great ship for the purpose above specify we will have you then to proceed on your discovery for the satisfy of our expectation former mention which be to discover further to the north Pole as far as possible you can and how the land already discover do trend further discovery to the north. and whether there be any inhabitant in the say land and whether there be a open sea to the northward beyond the say land and in this your coast the land we doubt not but you will endeavour with your shallop to gather up all the whale fin you can find and to kill the morse which you can come by on land and to reserve the tooth and blubber to the most advantage that may be the better to bear out the great charge which you know we be at in these discovery and to that end we have lade in you eleven ton of empty cask and have spend so much time in this your discovery and in gather up of such commodity as that coast will afford and as the season of the year will permit you than we will have you return for England and in your way homeward to touch at the place where you leave the Mary Margaret to see if she be not go and find she there and that the time of the year will permit we will have you melt your blubber into oil before your come from thence to avoid the great trouble and inconvenience you know we fall into the last year 1610. by bring the same hither in blubber but if the say ship shall chance to be full fish and so to be go before your come thither yet we will have you stay there or at island some small time to melt your blubber to which end we have appoint Thomas edge our servant in that ship to leave a copper and such necessary as shall serve your turn for the perform of that business Thomas edge see sup. l. 3 c. 2. behind he and have deliver he likewise advertisement at that place of their proceed in the voyage and of their intent what course they purpose to take together with their opinion what course they will have you take in these matter of discovery and uncertain voyage the variety of occurrence and sea danger be such as we can direct prescribe a course certain to be hold yet we hold it fit to set down our opinion of the needful which be that at your first departure out of England you keep counsel together and agree upon your place of meeting if by tempast of weather you chance to be separate still shape your course direct for cherry island where we will have you stay and if at your come thither you find the same clear of ice and that there be morse on shore than we will have you to work upon they as time and opportunity will permit always have respect to your intend voyage and have dispatch your business in that place we will have you depart in company together for the whale bay as aforesaid and to follow our instruction former set down to be do in that place and have perform what may be do in the part beyond island island and so return back again for England we hold it fit you make your rendezvous again at the say island and there to stay the one for the other and to be kill of the beast there till the last of August if need be and if it happen that one ship do arrive there before the other and no morse come on shore than we will have they spend the time in search for the lead or^ or any other mineral matter that may be like to be of worth upon the say Land and thus have stay at island till the last of August the one for the other and not meet together the ship so stay have make her voyage we will have she to return direct for England and to leave a note in write of the day of her departure this be our opinion notwithstanding if upon better ground you shall among yourselves find a course to be hold for the good of the voyage and the benefit of we the adventurer we leave it to yourselves to agree upon as time and opportunity shall serve and for the avoid of a objection heretofore use that the want of sufficient victual have be the cause of the overthrow of the voyage by speedy return home than otherwise they will we have think fit to set down the quantity of victual deliver aboard your ship in this our commission to the intent to clear ourselves and our agent of that imputation and to lay the blame on yourselves if by default the same be evil husband the particular be these beef 22. c 3. quarter 18li. bisquit 30. c beer 14. ton fish 200. of Haberdin and half a hundred ling cheese 300. c weight butter three Firkins oil three gallon pease ten bushel oatmeal five bushel candle six dozen aquavitae thirty gallon vinegar one rundlet of twenty gallon this proportion of victual will last you seven or eight month with good husbandry together with the help of fish fowl and beast that be to be have in abundance upon those coast so that we hope you shall have no cause to the contrary but cheerful to go forward in your business whereby not only the small bark you go in but the great ship may come home full lade with one commodity or other which we doubt not but by your diligence and good endeavour you may attain unto but if you shall chance by extremity of ice or otherwise to be put back from your discovery or from obtain commodity upon the coast of greenland whereby to lade both ship then we will have you stay at island or other land thereabouts so long time as possible you can and as the season of the year will permit you to finish the rest of your voyage and if there be lade between you both to lade the big ship we will have she to be dispatch from thence with all speed and you to stay there as long as you may convenient for the good of the voyage which the more beneficial it prove the more it will be for your credit and we will not be unthankful at your return we will have you at every place of meeting with the Mary Margaret to deliver to Thomas edge our servant a particular note of what good you have take into your ship and at your last lade place we will have you make a general invoyce of the whole Cargason of good lade in your ship and have sign the same to seal it up and direct the same to our agent resident in London and if you do c^ance to meet with the Mary Margaret at or after your last port of lade we will have you deliver a copy of the say invoyce to our servant Thomas edge for our better satisfaction what casualty soever may happen by the way and at any hand to have such a invoyce ever ready seal and for mortality sake put up in some sure place of custody we h^ld it fit that you jonas Poole shall be as grand pilot in this voyage to the northward and therefore we will have you to accompany the great ship and to bring she to the place of fish for the whale or to any other place which you out of your experience shall think fit to bring she for the good of the voyage and benefit of the adventurer and our will be that Steven Bennet master of the say great ship together with the rest of the company in that ship do follow the say jonas pool direction as they will answer the contrary upon their peril at their come home and for that heretofore the company have be abuse by lewd and bad people who have imbesele part of that which by our great charge and adventure have be obtain our mind and will be that you jonas Poole do make search in your own ship that none of our whale fin morse tooth oil or any other commodity gather at our charge be imbesele or carry away by any of the mariner who will look to have the uttermost of their wage pay they and to be feed with meat and drink sufficient and God send you into England we will have you suffer none of your people to go on shore unsearched neither will we have you to leave the ship till your come into the river of Thames that we give you order to the contrary and if you chance to be wind bind upon the coast you may send up one of your people with your letter but not to come yourself on shore till our far order as aforesaid the like order we will have Steven Bennet to use in his ship by virtue of this our commission which we have order to Thomas edge our servant to see perform according and in as much as we have agree here with a tanner for all the morse hide which we kill and bring into England and have send man of purpose for the flay salt and order of the same agreement with a tanner for morse hide whereof we have appoint one to go in your ship we will have you reserve the say hide and floor your ship therewith in stead of ballast and if you obtain a great quantity than you can bring away with you have always regard to commodity of more value which be oil tooth and whale fin that none of they be leave behind we will have you leave the say overplus of hide in some convenient place till the next year that we send more store of ship a commission for Thomas edge our servant appoint to go as our factor in the ship call the Mary Margaret of the burden of one hundred and fifty ton for the kill of the whale and morse upon the coast of greenland or any other place in the north ocean give the 31. of march 1611. you be not ignorant of our employ you heretofore in two several voyage to island the first whereof by reason of one dupper go thither together with certain man of Hull glut the say place prove to we a thousand pound loss of our principal as also in the second voyage adventure and loss in first discovery because you can not come to set foot upon the say island by reason of the abundance of ice lie round about the same sixteen league compass till the twenty eight of july by which occasion our whole charge of set out that year adventure have be lose if the refuge to lade our ship back again from saint Michael the archangel in Russia have not holpen we yet notwithstanding that help we lose by that voyage above five hundred pound we enter into due consideration of the premise do not impute the cause of these our loss unto you but to the accident then happen contrary to our expectation yet these loss grow upon we in the time of your employment we can do no less than put you in mind thereof to the intent to encourage and stir up your mind to do your uttermost endeavour to further the business in this your three employment that we may recover ourselves of the loss former sustain and for that end we have make choice of you again to go as our factor in the ship Mary Margaret of one hundred and fifty Tunnees the master be Steven Bennet for the kill of the whale and to that end as you well know have be at charge of procure of six me^ of saint John de luz accustom to that function who name be as follow juan de Bacoyne juan Martin de karre six biscainer procure for kill of the whale as I have hear by woodcock advice who have live and be employ with they in grand bay etc. Marsene de Horisada Domingo de Sarria and Adam de Bellocke which man we will have to be use very kind and friendly during this their voyage whereby be stranger and leave their own country to do we service they may have no just cause of complaint but rather to be encourage to do we service hereafter if there be cause and although it be our meaning they shall be encourage by all good and courteous usage to be ready to do we service yet we will have you together with our own people and mariner employ in this voyage to observe and diligent put in practice the execute of that business of strike the whale as well as they and likewise to know the better sort of whale from the worse whereby in their strike * * this be a conceit as if all place have choi^e of all kind which experience have since teach otherwise they may choose the good and leave the bad and to that end we do set you down here under the several sort of whale together with the difference of goodness between the one and the other as we have gather the same by information from man of excellency in that business who make know unto we that there be eight several kind of whale all differ the one from the other in quantity and quality which for your better instruction we have think good to set down in this our commission the first sort of whale be call the beard whale which be black in colour with a smooth skin and white under the chap which whale be the best of all the rest and the elder it be the more it do yield this sort of whale do yield usual four hundred and sometime five hundred fin and between one hundred and one hundred and twenty hogshead of oil the second sort of whale be call Sarda of the same colour and fashion as the former see of the kind of whale sup^ 471. I have add this to be compare with that for further light but somewhat less and the fin not above one fathom long and yield in oil according to his bigness sometime eighty sometime a hundred hogshead the three sort of whale be call Trumpa be as long as the first but not so thick of colour Grey have but one trunk in his head whereas the former have two he have in his mouth tooth of a span long and as thick as a man wrist but no sin who head be big than either of the two former and in proportion far big than his body in the head of this whale be the spermaceti which you be to keep in cask apart from your other oil you may put the oil you find in the head and the spermaceti altogether spermaceti or as the vulgar call it and mark it from the other oil and at your come home we will separate the oil from the spermeceti the like be to be do with the oil of this sort of whale which be to be keep apart from the oil of the other whale the reason be that the oil of this sort of whale be boil will be as hard and white as tallow which to be mingle with the other oil be liquid will make the same to show as footie oil and so consequent spoil both and be of little value you be therefore to be very careful to keep the oil of this sort of whale apart as well of the head as of the body for the reason before mention in this sort of whale be likewise find the ambergris lie in the entrail and gut of the same ambergris be of shape and colour like unto cow dung we will have you therefore yourself to be present at the open of this sort of whale and cause the residue of the say entrail to be put into small cask and bring they with you into England we will have the master also to be by at the open of this whale and to be make privy of the pack of those baril and although it be say that the ambergris be only in this whale and in none other yet we will not have you be absent at the open of any other but if you see cause to make a reservation of the entrail of every whale that you shall perceive to be cause of the least suspect to have any of the say ambergris be a matter as you know of good worth and therefore not slight to be regard the tooth likewise of this sort of whale we will have you cause to be reserve for a trial as also any other matter extraordinary that you shall observe in the same this whale be say to yield in oil forty hogshead beside the spermaceti the four sort etc. as sup. 471.472 and in as much as industry and diligence be two principal step to achieve great enterprise and negligence and idleness be enemy to the same we will have you in this charge commit unto you to embrace the one and to avoid the other and to show that example of pain take to the rest of the company of your ship in your own person as well in set they on work as in put your own hand to the business when need require as that there be no idle time spend but that every one be employ in some business or other in help to kill the whale or in search the bay along the coast for whale ambergris morse tooth or any other strange thing that may be find upon that coast or in kill the morse bear or any thing that may make profit towards our great charge touch direction for your keep company together with the Elizabeth and of the course we think fit for the master of that ship to observe we have set the same down at large in our commission deliver to jonas Poole a copy whereof we deliver you herewith for your better instruction to observe what be to be do on both your behalf for the good of the voyage which our commission we will have you strict observe unless upon some special occasion to we unknown and by the consent of the principal officer in both the ship you shall see just cause to the contrary you have with you a order set down by the lord of his majesty privy counsel for the maintain of our charter the rest as not so necessary to the public be omit which we will have you make know to any of our nation that you may chance to meet withal either at island or upon any of those coast and if any stranger do offer you violence or do disturb you in your trade you may both defend yourselves and maintain your trade to the uttermost of your power etc. chap. 3 a brief declaration of this my voyage of discovery to Greeneland and towards the west of it as follow be set forth by the right worshipful sir THOMAS smith governor of the right worshipful company of new trade etc. write by Ionas Poole we set sail at blackewall the eleven of April 1611. with four ship the one call the mary-margaret of burden one hundred and fifty tun with nine and forty man and boy the next the Elizabeth of burden sixty tun four ship with eighteen man and boy the three be call the amity of burden seventy ton with four and twenty man and boy the four be call the resolution with about sixteen man and boy the resolution be appoint to go to saint Nicholas in Russia in hope to make two voyage thither this year the amity be to go to Pich^ra or Novazembla there to see if they can make a voyage by way of trade see sup. l. 3. or by kill of mohorse etc. the mary-margaret be appoint to keep the Elizabeth company to Greeneland abovesaid there to kill the whale for which purpose we have six man of saint John de luz with all thing fit for that purpose the Elizabeth be appoint to see if it wear possible to pass from Greeneland towards the pole and to search in those Stas what likelihood of a passage that way etc. but before we be as far to the northwards as the latitude of sixty five we be all separate by reason of contrary wind the ship separate and foul weather the Elizabeth in which ship I be be stok^d that the water which be in she can not come to the pump but lay upon the ballast which be the cause we can bear no sail to keep the mary-margaret company yet by the thirteen day of may I come to island and the fourteen I speak with the amity the sixteen day I meet with the mary-margaret island which keep i company to Greeneland but in our passage thither we see a bank of ice to the east ward of we above forty league long the nine and twenty of May cross Rode we anchor in a place name by i the last year crossroad but before we get thither we be much trouble with ice and contrary wind and we find almost all the sound full of ice ice a hindrance to whale kill and discovery that the biscainer can not strike one whale although they see diverse which as they say be of the best kind of whale I stay there till the sixteen of june in which time we set up our shalop and range some part of the coast but find little by reason the beache be cover with snow and ice likewise in the same time I be put out of the road with ice and stand out west and by north into the sea about fourteen league where I find a bank of ice then I stand into the sound again and get off the Shalop which be in the road at which time which be about the eleven of june I stand to the sea again and have a storm at south which sink our Shalop and I see the ice lie close to the land in 80. degree then I go into cross road again and have a Shalop from the mary-margaret 80. degree and because I perceive the ice above say to lie close to the land and unpossible to pass that way there run very strong tide in the which it be dangerous deal with the ice I determine to stand to the southwards alongst the say ice to see if I can find the sea open that way and so get to the westward of the say ice and then proceed on my voyage but I find it to lie the next hand south south-west and south-west and by south and run alongst it about one hundred and twenty league new discovery at which time I suppose myself near greenland as it be lay down by Hudson and other and call hold with hope hold with hope I run near forty league to the west ward of the eastermost part of the say land as it be lay down and by my account I be to the southwards of it near the latitude 74. degree where I see abundance of whale by the side of the ice for I sail all this time sometime in and sometime by the say ice and sound most common each watch s^ore of whale but have no ground at 160.140.180 and 200. fathom then the wind come to the northwest and I perceive the ice to trend still to the southwards determine to stand to Greeneland from whence I come there to make my voyage and likewise to try the certainty concern the misplace of the land but the next day be about the seven and twenty of june the wind come to the north and I stand for island and come to it the nine and twenty of the same month where I find that place of my be when I suppose I shall have find land do bear from island west and by south above one hundred twenty five league island when I come to the island I see about three hundred morse on land but a storm come they go all into the Sea the twelve of july we slay above two hundred three hundred mo^ses and by the three and twenty day we have take all their fat hide and tooth which with the victual we have lade the ship then I determine to hale up a shalop to go to Greeneland to search if I can find any land or land that may prove beneficial the next year and likewise to search for tooth and whale fin the four and twenty and five and twenty day it be very much wind at north which cause the sea to go so high that we can not land yet at eight aclocke at night the wind cease and I go on land where I find certain of the marie Margaret^ man by number of thirty person be arrive on the south side in three boat and that they part from two boat in greenland with nine man in they immediate master edge and master Bennet come aboard and I weigh aforesaid and we do determine to kill at my arri^all assoon as the ship be moor we get out blubber and send it on land to be bring into oil and we follow our work till the seven of August at noon at which time have oil by the ship side we put out all the blubber which be in hold save two ton and a half suppose the ship have ballast enough in she for there be twelve ton of hide which be the chief cause of the loss of the ship and nine ton of oil and above seven ton of ballast a hogshead and a barrel of tooth beside half a ton of stone all which be about nine and twenty ton weight and to any unpartial man judgement sufficient to shift a bark of sixty ton but as the last but go out of she the ship begin to hold and with all a great many man go to leeward there be at that time above aboard then the hide which lay in hold slide to leeward and bring she altogether down than every man make shift to save his life and I be far from the hatch can not get up so soon as other do at which time I see death before my eye two way double danger one if I stay in hold I be sure to be drown the other if I go up the hatch I be in election to be slay for down at the hatch fall hogshead of beer and diverse other thing the least of they be sufficient to beat a man bone and in attempt to get up I be beat down twice and hurt but it be not the will of God to take my life from i then but to revive i to pluck i even from the jaw of death and by swim and crawl I get into the sea clear of the ship where a boat take i up and bless bee God no man perish at that so dangerous a accident we be all get into three boat go to the Hull ship where we find but small comfort for duke tell we plain we shall not come aboard his ship and cause pike and lance to be bring to keep we out then master edge and diverse other desire he to let i come aboard which he do and with much ado I get aboard have my head break to the skull and my brow that one may see the bare bone and by my ear I have a sore wound likewise the rib on my right side be all break and sore bruise and the collar bone of my left shoulder be break beside my back be so sore that I can not suffer any man to touch it that which follow be few place be all cover with snow but ere we go away the top of the high hill and the low plain appear green with moss and some little quantity of grass this country and likewise the sea in these part be subject to marvelous thick and misty weather especial when the sun with his most forcible heat melt the ice and snow who vapour obscure the light of the sun make small difference between the day there and the irksome night in other place we find in this country many fat dear which we kill with our piece and dog at our pleasure which be a great refresh to we in that uncouth place many white bear many fat deer white bear white grey and dun fox abundance of sundry fowl Allen a devour fowl with white grey and dun fox we find also abundance of fowl namely cul^idines sea pigeon white land partridge wild goose willocke and many other fowl among which I note the nature of one which we call a all^n who like to the great fish which eat up the small or like to some great man which devour all the labour of the poor when some small bird have get any thing than he leave not beat of they till they have cast up what they have eat which he lay hold of devour up and so with little meat in their gorge and few feather on their back he leave they to get more not for themselves but for he we find on the shore many huge morse there be great store of fresh water in every valley many huge morse which proceed most of the melt snow on every beech be great plenty of drift wood but never a bush nor tree grow in those quarter as far as we have hitherto discover chap. 4 a relation write by FOTHERBYE the ship Thomasine go down from black-wall to Woolwich the sixteen of April and from thence to Gravesend the three and twenty where she remain until the eight and twenty of the same and weigh from thence she anchor again in tilberie hope with ten ship more of good burden and two Pinnasses all of the greenland fleet set forth also at the charge of the say company under the command of master Benjamin joseph chief captain and general of the say Fleet. we set sail out of tilberie hope the four of May and come to a anchor the same day in Lee road where we stay till the next morning we go forth to Sea we meet with ice in 75. deg. 10. minute than we set sail again and go forth to sea before night we proceed in company of the fleet and meet with straggle ice the five and twenty of May in the latitude of 75. degree 10. minute through which we pass without danger hold on our course all tha^ day till time of midnight then we find the ice so close pack together that we be force to tack about and stand to the westward till we find more open passage we ply through it without any great danger till the eight and twenty day but then be in fight of land we pass among very much ice all the forenoon which lie in great abundance on both side of we but a desire as it seem to get through it draw we on to be the more entangle with it for about noon we can neither find a passage to go forward nor way to retire back again but be nine ship and two Pinnasses for the prosperous and the desire lose company through foul weather the one and twenty of May otherwise we have be thirteen sail we begin very sudden to be enclose and shut up with ice now every one wrought the best mean he can for the safety of his ship our master in the Thomasine cause a hauser and a grapnel to be carry forth and lay upon a great island of ice eleven sail fast in the ice m. th. sherwin and so we ride as at a anchor and by that mean we stay from forceable rush against other piece afterward we lay forth a anchor for sure hold and make ^enders of a old ca^le which be hang over the ship side to keep the ice from pierce of her plank we rid thus from the eight and twenty of May till the second of june still float as the wind drive we with our anchor hold island which now we account as the shore and make use thereof according for upon it our carpenter seal and trim our lesser shallop on the second of june we have a great homeme sea the wind be at northwest whereby we judge we be not far from a open sea to windward of we june there we resolve to make trial what we may do to free ourselves out of the ice in the afternoon about three a clock we get aboard our anchor let fall our fore topsail and put forth our mizzen and so drive a stern for a while till the float island give way then we fill out topsail and attempt diverse place where to pass but have repulse and fall asterne again notwithstanding at the length we prevail and with much ado we attain a open sea at a north and by west sun part very glad from these ill neighbour land we go clear off the ice which at our part from they give we or rather receive from we some knock but while we remain among they they seem much more perilous than they prove hurtful so we praise God for our safe deliverance wish that the rest of the ship which we leave in the ice be as clear out of it as be the Thomasine have attain the open sea to the westward we proceed to the northwards keep the ice still on our starboard side and meet with ^he Mary An-Sarah we meet with the Mary An-Sarah that get also free of the ice the same day that we come forth of it we keep company together till the next day when be as high as prince Charles land we both stand in for the shore the Mary An-Sarah go for bel-sound her assign harbour but we proceed to the fore-land where when we come the six of june we meet with two shallop that belong to the desire we come to the before land wherein be Cuthbert appleyard and William (@) harponier by who we understand that the prosperous and the desire have more desire prosper than all the rest of the fleet they escape the danger that all the rest fall into and come to the fore-land the three of june find the harbour open here be yet no work begin for they have not see one whale since their come into the harbour so that for we there be no cause of stay to be helpful unto they and therefore we proceed to the northward hope to find the shore still as free from ice we proceed to the northwards maudlin sound hackluyt head-land we anchore^ in maudlin sound as it be at this place but it fall out contrary to our expectation for be come as far as maudlin sound in the latitude of 79. degree 34. minute we meet with some straggle ice and from the main top we see much ice lie betwixt we and Hackluyt^ head-land which seem to be close to the shore therefore we send some man in a shallop to maudlin sound to see if it be open that we may harbour our ship there and search for a leak which we find her subject unto in foul weather the sound be open and we anchor in a good harbour but the ice be not go clear from the shore therefore we can not hale our ship aground but we carine she and set up our Biscaine shallop which we carry with we out of England in piece the next day after our come hither I go forth in a little shallop the other be then unset together to see how the ice lie at hackluyt head-land I go forth in a shallop and whether we may pass with our ship that way or no. be come forth of the harbour we perceive that it be very foul weather at sea notwithstanding I proceed into fair haven where the south harbour be then open but much ice lie then in the sound unbroken from shore to shore otherwise we may have pass that way to hackluyt head-land betwixt the island and the main land we stay here till the next morning than the weather begin to clear up and we put forth to sea again intend to go without the land but be out of the harbour we find the foul weather to be such we set sail out of maudlin sound and follow the ice as our little weak shallop be not able to endure therefore we return again to our ship into maudlin sound where we kill two female morse and take their tooth hide and blubber on the ten of june we set sail out of maulden sound and coast along to the northward till we be past hackluyt head-land but then we see the ice lie before we extend close to the shore so that for we to pass further that way it be not possible therefore we turn to the westward to see if we can find passage further from the shore we sail as the ice trend west and west south-west till the thirteen day and keep still alongst it prince Charles island in 78. degree 40. minute we stand again for shore eleven Holland ship we anchor in sir t. smith Bay we find it to trend near south and south south-west we proceed well thus far till we come under the latitude of prince Charles his island in 78. degree 40. minute be eight and twenty league from shore but then we alter our course and stand in for the fore-land to go and be helpful to the other ship there for the further of their voyage according to our instruction as some do understand they but contrary I be sure to some of our desire when we come near the fore-land we see eleven ship of hollander under sail ply to the southwards one of they come room towards we and strike her top-sail twice whereby we suppose they take we for some of their fleet which they want but we hold on our course still into sir Thomas smith bay where we come to a anchor the fifteen of june by the john-Anne-Francis and the desire the Mary Margaret be then under sail to go to the fore-land here be yet no need of any help^ that we can make they for they have hitherto neither kill nor see one whale since their first come in hither therefore we think it best not to stay here but rather go to fair haven where we shall be more ready to proceed on our discovery when the ice will give we leave and in the meantime we may be helpful to the two ship thither assign for the make of their voyage and so much the rather we haste because we understand that the hollander also set forth a ship on discovery we set sail the seven of june and meet with the prosperous that come from crosse-road and be go into sir Thomas smith bay we go forth of sir t. smith Bay there to get some brick and lime to mend their furnace as Nicholas woodcock the master tell we then we go forth to sea and be about four league from the shore the wind begin to blow so hard from the northwest that we be force back again to seek harbour and come to a anchor the nineteen of june in crosse-road here we stay two day we be drive back again into crosse-road much wind blow at the north north-east till the one and twenty of june and then in the afternoon the wind come to the east and by south and the weather be fair therefore at a north northwest sun we weigh and set sail again and so do the Thomas Bonaventure that come to a anchor by we this morning be also bind for fair haven we set sail out of crosse-road this next day in the afternoon we be thwart of maudlin sound and the weather be fair and calm we send a shallop to the northward to see what alteration there be among the ice and to seek out some good harbour for a ship and also to set up the king arm at hackluyt head-land or some other convenient place when master baffin be go from the ship in the foresay shallop I go present into the other shallop into maudlin sound one shallop to the northward the other into maudlin sound there to set up the king arm and also to see if there be any morse come ashore when I be within the sound I find no Beech bare for morse to come upon for ice and snow lie yet undissolue from the shore side but I go to the harbour and there cause a cross to be set up and the king arm to be nail thereon under which also I nail a piece of sheet lead whereon I set the moscovie company mark with the day of the month and year of our Lord then cut up a piece of earth which afterward I carry aboard our ship the king arm set up in Trinity harbour I take it into my hand and say in the hear of the man there present to this effect I take this piece of earth as a sign of lawful possession of this country of king james his new-land and of this particular place which I name Trinity harbour take on the behalf of the company of merchant call the merchant of new trade and discovery for the use of our sovereign lord james by the grace of God king of great Britain France and Ireland who royal arm be here set up Trinity harbour be under the parallel of 79. degree 34. minute we come to a anchor in fair haven to the end that all people who shall here arrive may take notice of his majesty right and title to this country and to every part thereof God save aforesaid island a storm and there make fast our shallop with a grapnel lay upon the icy shore use the best mean we can with our shallop sail to keep we from the extremity of so cold a harbour we stay here eight hour and the storm continue drive the ice still eastward in great abundance and with wonderful swiftness when the weather begin to clear I cause the man to row to leeward to another island a league distant which seem then to be a cape of the main land purpose there to set up the king arm but afterward we find it to be a island and to the main we can not come for break ice this stormy weather continue from Monday night till Friday morning during which time we have be but eleven league at the further from our ship yet go we so far as we can have go have the weather be never so fair for at four league distance from cape barren the ice lie firm and unbroken two or three mile from the shore and close again to it lay the shatter ice throng together with this present storm on Friday morning we come back again to hackluit headland julie and there I set the king arm in the like manner as at Trinity harbour from thence we row towards our ship and as we enter into faire-haven there come a whale that accompany we into the harbour leap and advance himself almost quite out of the water the whale begin now to come in fall headlong down again with great noise we haste aboard our ship and I send forth both our shallop to strike this whale if they can and tell master Mason of her come in who also go forth in his shallop but it seem the whale pass under the ice which lie yet unbroken betwixt the north harbour and the south harbour for they can not see she again the next day there come more whale in and Robert Hambleton two whale escape our master mate strike two which unlucky escape the first for want of help the gamaliel shallop being in chase of another whale and our own little shallop not able to row against a head-sea to assist the other so that at length the whale have tow the shallop forth to sea the harp iron come out the second be also strike within the sound and run under the ice which lie yet unbroken at the east end of the sound and draw the shallop upon therefore we ply that way when we have run seven or eight league more the ice lie so thick on every side that we be bar from proceed any further then we stand in towards the shore and be a little to the northwards of cape barren our shallop have sight of we and come row to we through the break ice master baffin tell we the shore to the eastward be much pester with ice and he have set up the king arm at the entrance of a fair sound about four league distant from cape barren now the weather be fair and calm master sherwin master baffin and I go in the shallop to the place where the king arm be set up purpose because the air be very clear to go upon some high mountain from whence we may see how the sea be pester with ice and what likelihood there be of further proceed according to this our intent we ascend a very high hill and from thence we see the ice lie upon the sea so far as we can discern so that the sea seem to be whole tour with ice save only to the eastward we think that we see the water beyond the ice which put we in some hope that we shall ere long get passage with our shallop along the shore if we can not pass with our ship be thus satisfy we return towards fair haven we return aboard our ship and ply towards fair haven advise among ourselves of the best course we can to further the business commit unto we we resolve to make our discovery along the shore with both our shallop and to carry with we our provision for the whale-killing we intend to discover in shallop conceive good hope beside of profit which the beache will afford we therefore we intend when our ship be bring safe into harbour again to go from she with both our shallop and to put in practice this our late resolution but the weather fall calm and a fog succeed which continue three day so that our ship come not into harbour till the twelve of july I go from she the eleven day intend to search the beache I go forth in the one shallop till master baffin come to i with the other shallop and then we to proceed both together but before he come I have go so far as that the ice will not suffer i to pass a boat length further and I have also search a very fair beach which be altogether fruitless master baffin come to i in the other shallop red-beach master baffin come to i at a place appoint the fourteen day of julie in the other shallop and we proceed both together to the eastward again and find passage among the ice about a league further than I have late be so that we come to the firm ice that lie almost two mile from the shore of red-beach unbroken up this year here we hale up our shallop out of the water lest the break ice which be carry to and fro with the wind may split they or bruise they then master baffin and I with four man more walk over the firm ice and go ashore on red-beach where we travel about the space of three mile by the shore side but find no commodity as we expect to have do for here have the hulman be in 1612. as we may know by fire that they have make we hail our shallop upon the ice and gather the fruit that many year before have bring forth thus as we can not find that which we desire to see so do we behold that which we wish have not be there to be see which be great abundance of ice that lie close to the shore and also off at sea so far as we can discern wherefore be thus satisfy and more weary to know that we can pass no further then with travail so far we return to our shallop and go aboard of our ship in fair haven on Sunday the seventeen of july we return to our shallop pass the near way betwixt the land and the main land for now the ice be break betwixt the south-harbor where we rid and the north harbour where the hollander rid the next day we send our shallop to the north-east side of fair haven there to lie for the come of blow right into the harbour so that we can not get forth and therefore we come to a anchor again where we ride before on the one and twenty of july our harponier kill a whale which split one of our each shallop think that now we shall find the ice break and clear go from the shore conceive some good hope to proceed and make some new discovery which be the chief occasion of our employment we pass although perhaps with much ado we may get about the point of the beach yet shall we still be pester with ice from proceed any further we resolve to walk over land to the other side of the beach where we see a hill about four mile distant from which we think we shall be satisfy how much further it be possible for we to proceed so thither we travail where when we come we see a very fair sound on the east side of the beach which be open within but there lay very much ice at the entrance of it we walk over red-beach which although it be extend more than half over sound yet we doubt not but if we continue fair and clear as now it be therefore we intend to make trial what we may do but before we return we go down to the point of the beach at the entrance of the sound and there set up a cross the point of red-beach and with many crooked wind among the ice at length we get over wiche sound for so it be now name as soon as we be over on the other side about two league from red-beach master baffin and I clamber up a very high hill from whence we see a point of land bear east north-east by the ordinary compass eighteen or twenty league distant as I suppose we likewise see another fair sound to the southwards of we which be much pester with ice but we can not see the end of it here upon the mountain we set up a warelocke and then come down again with less labour but more danger than discovery make in 1612. have not be upon this land to search the beache for in all other place where we have be heretofore we can find nothing at all now therefore we resolve to make further search the latitude which I find to be 79. degree 54. minute we see a shallop come row towards the extreme point of this shore we meet with the hearts-ease shallop therefore we hasten towards they to see who in company together the one may have be helpful to the other when need require and more easy it seem to save they both then be separate to keep either of they from wrack but God who in his wont mercy perfect health chap. 7 a true report of a voyage 1615. for discovery of sea land and land to the northwards as it be perform by ROBERT fotherrie in a pinnace of twenty ton call the Richard of London set forth at the charge of the right worshipful sir THOMAS smith knight my very good master and master richard wiche governor and the rest of the worshipful company of merchant call the merchant of new trade and discovery trade into Moscovia and king JAMES his new Land by the providence of almighty God I go forth of Harwich harbour in the foresay pinnace the twelve of May in the company of eight ship of the fleet for king james his new land who in foul weather out-fayled i in the latitude 71. degree or thereabouts so I proceed alone towards king james his new land and meet with ice in latitude 73. degree 30. minute I stand north-eastwards for the waist of king james his new land and have sundry conflict with the ice in rainy and wet foggy weather and have sight of land the eleven of june and on the nineteen of the same I anchor in fair haven here I stay till the three of july for the pinnace have receive some hurt among the ice which to amend I be fain to hale she aground beside diverse other thing necessary to be do which detain i long then willing I will have stay there from hence I sail northward but meet with ice in latitude 79. degree 50. minute be six league from hackluyt head-land hackluyt Headland than I coast the ice as it lay in point and bay to the westward and southwestward and be thirty league from the land in latitude 79. degree 10. minute I find it to trend northward and north-westward and coast it to the latitude of 79. degree 50. minute but then I be embay with ice and be fain to stand out again and sail above ten league before I get clear when I be out of this bay I proceed south westerly with the ice on the starboard to the latitude 78. degree 30. minute where be forty league from the shore I be again embay with the ice peril and escape and have have fair sunshine weather all the day which make i the bold to stand so near it the weather on a sudden fall foggy and the wind begin to blow hard at south which put we to great trouble and no small peril but the almighty power who have merciful deliver we heretofore out of as great danger preserve we also from this when we be get clear off the ice we have the sea much grow and the storm increase but be desirous still to keep the sea I stand close by the wind under a pair of corpse till the pinnace wax leak with bear too much sail and there be force to lie atry under a main coarse only and although she stem southeast and southeast by south yet be she hurry violent to the north-eastwards and by the merciful providence of God we fall right with the fore-land in latitude 79. degree than I stand over sir Thomas smith bay for harbour in crosse-road where I anchor the thirteen of july be Thursday I stay here four day in which time my man mend the sail and ship tackle that have receive hurt by the late storm and make a new main sail to serve in time of need and on the seventeen of july I weigh out of crosse-road and sail westward from thence come to ice again in latitude 78. degree 40. minute which I coast as it lie near south-west or more westerly but with many point and bay wherewith I be sometime entangle yet God be thank get clear again either by help of oar or sail without any hurt in this sort I proceed with good satisfaction although not with so good content till I come to the latitude of 76. degree be above one hundred league from point lookout but then be cross with a contrary storm from the south-west and south south-west which drive i to the south-eastward till I come in the latitude of 74. degree and then I make my way westward again so near as I can lie close by the wind and overranne the former suppose land of Groynland note error of Grouland which some have lay down in plait and extend to 75. degree when I come into the latitude of 73. degree I stand west and northwest and fall with ice again in latitude 73. degree 50. minute and think indeed at that time that I be near land by abundance of fowl which we see in great flock but such thick fog have continue for three or four day together fog that we may soon hear the land if anywere then see it and so do we first find this ice by hear the rut think till we see it that it have be land so that we be embay with it before we think that we have be near it then I stand out again and coast the ice still to the westward southerly but can see no land as I expect to have do until we come under the latitude of 71. degree thirty minute and then we espy a snowy hill very high in the cloud high Hill for this day be very clear at sea but the fog be not yet clear from the land so that we can see no part of it but only the top of a snowy mountain which appear very high although we be fourteen or fifteen league distant from it bear off we southeast and by south then I stand in for the shore suppose it have be part of the main of Groynland for the fog lie on each side of this mount as if there have be a great continent under it but it prove otherwise for as we come near to it the fog disperse more and more and when we be five league distant the land appear in form like a island when I come near the shore I can find no harbour to anchor in notwithstanding the weather be fair and calm I hoist out my boat and go ashore with three man more and set up the king arm then we search a sandie beach which be abundant store with drift wood drift wood but yield no other fruit that we can find worth the take up so I return aboard again and send ashore my boat to fetch some wood but before the man have lay into she the little quantity that she be able to carry they come aboard again for the wind begin to blow hard and the sea to go lofty so that here be no place for we to abide any long otherwise I be purpose to have search further alongst the shore but this gale of wind come northerly I stand from hence to the westward be desirous to see more land or find a more open Sea and have sail about fifteen or sixteen league I meet with ice again in latitude 71. degree and coast it eight or nine league further westward and southwestward as it lay but then the wind come to the south-west and we stand close by it a while to the southwards but find the gale to increase and consider that it be the most contrary wind which can blow against my further proceed for the ice as we find do ^^end near south-west and beside if there have be any high land within twenty league of we we may perfect have make it the weather be so fair and clear in these respect and for the reason follow I take the benefit of this wind to return to the north-eastwards again be now about two hundred league from king james his new land in latitude 71. degree note first I purpose to sail alongst the southeast side of the land that I have discover to be better satisfy what harbour there be and what likelihood of profit to ensue and from thence to proceed to the place where I first fall with ice in latitude 73. degree when I be drive to the south-eastwards with a westerly storm for I be yet very persuade that be there we be not far from land although we can not see it by reason of thick foggy weather then my further intent be if I find no good occasion to spend my time there for to coast the ice or try the open sea to the northwards betwixt 73. and 76. degree where former I have not receive desire satisfaction by reason of a storm that drive i off and then I purpose if time may seem convenient to proceed to the north coast of king james his new land to have see what hope be there to be have for passage northward or for compass of the land which be most like to be a island I stand away east and by south and be near the foresay island the wind come to the west and blow a very hard gale wherewith I pass alongst the southeast side of the island under a pair of corpse but without that satisfaction which I expect for the wind blow so stormy and the sea grow very great I be force to stand further from the shore then willing I will have do and beside there be a thick fog upon the land whereby I can not be satisfy what harbour or road be about it yet may we see three or four cape or headland as if there go in bay betwixt they I sail about it and then stand to the northward again and be now assure that it be a island I name it sir Thomas smith island sir t. smith island this island be about ten league in length and stretch north-east and south-west it be high land and at the north end of it there be a mountain of a wonderful height and bigness mount Hackluyt all cover with snow which I call mount Hackluyt the base or foot of it on the east side be almost four league long it have three such side at the base lie out to the sea and from the four side do the rest of the island extend itself towards the south-west which be also as it be a place fortify with castle and bulwark for on each side there be three or four high rock which stand out from the land appear like tower and fort it lie in the parallel of 71. degree where the needle vary from the true meridian westward eight degree the land be general so far as I have see rocky and very barren and worse than the land that I have see in king james his new land under eighty degree for there be no grass but moss and where I first land upon low ground all the stone be like unto a smith finder both in colour and form the sand be general mix with a corn like amber the beache be abundant store with drift wood and many stone light like Pumis which will swim on the water I see many trace of fox and the foot of bear but not any sign of deer or other live creature and very small store of fowl from hence I stand to the northward according to my former purpose but be cross with a contrary storm from the northwest which put i off to the eastward but as the wind shift I make my way to the north-westward all I can and come again to the ice in latitude 75. degree from whence I proceed towards king james his new land and have sight of the land the eighteen of August be in latitude 77. degree 30. minute and have a hard gale of wind then at northwest I stand close by it under a pair of corpse but can not weather prince Charles island and therefore I bear up intend to go into nick cove which be on the north side of ice-sound there to attend a fair wind and in the mean time to get ballast aboard the pinnace and all other thing necessary but come to enter into the harbour I think it not a place convenient because I can hardly have get out again with a southerly wind which will carry i to the northwards and therefore I stand over for green-harbor where I anchor at one a clock in the morning the nineteen of August here I cause my man to launch a shallop and to get ballast and water aboard the pinnace and before nine a clock at night I be ready to proceed northward with the first fair wind I stay here five day during which time it blow hard for the most part at north and northwest and on the four and twenty of August the wind come to the east north-east as we suppose till we be out of the harbour so I set sail to proceed northward and have the wind easterly out of ice-sound wherewith I stand northwest towards cape cold but be clear of the high land we find the wind to be at north north-east therefore I resolve of another course which be this have peruse hudsons journal write by his own hand in that voyage wherein he have sight of certain land hudsons hold-with-hope question as before also which he name hold-with-hope I find that by his own reckon it shall not be more than one hundred league distant from king james his new land and in the latitude of 72. degree 30. minute or thereabouts therefore see I can not proceed northward I purpose to go to the southwestward to have sight of this land and discover it if wind and weather will permit so I stand away south-west and sometime west south-west till I have run one hundred and thirty league and be by account in latitude 72. degree 30. minute where have the wind contrary to proceed further westward I stand eastward till I have run thirty league in which course I shall have see this land if credit may be give to hudsons journal but I see not any and have a hard gale of wind still northerly I conceive no course so good to be take at this time as to s^eed homeward and so stand to the southwards direct my course for England this be the eight and twenty of August after which time the wind continue northerly till the six day of September and then we be on the coast of Scotland in latitude 57 degree and on the eight day of September have sight of the land of England on the coast of Yorkshire thus by the great mercy of God have we escape many danger and after a cold summer have some taste of a warm autumn all glory therefore be to God the father the son and the holy ghost amen by this brief relation and by the plat wherein I have trace the ship way upon each several traverse it may plain appear how far the state of this sea be discover betwixt 80. and 71. degree of latitude make difference of longitude 26. degree from the meridian of hackluyt Headland now if any demand my opinion concern hope of a passage to be find in those sea I answer that it be true that I both hope and much desire to have pass further than I do but be hinder with ice wherein although I have not attain my desire yet forasmuch as it appear not yet to the contrary but that there be a spacious sea betwixt Groinland and king james his new-land although much pester with ice I will not seem to dissuade this worshipful company from the yearly adventure of 150. or 200. pound at the most till some further discovery be make of the say sea and land adjacent for which purpose no other vessel will I advise unto than this pinnace with ten man which I hold to be most convenient for that action although heretofore I conceive otherwise but now I speak after good experience have sail in she out and in above two thousand league ro. Fotherbie a letter of ROBERT Fotherbie to captain edge write in crosse-rode july 15. 1615. master edge by the mercy of God I come into crosse-road on Thursday last be drive from sea near shore by extreme tempest at the beginning of the storm I be unwitting embay with ice above forty league from land in latitude 78. degree and 30. minute but thanks be to God I get clear of it yet not without much trouble and great danger have ply under two corpse to and again so long till my pinnace be make leak with bear I try it under a main coarse and stem southeast and southeast and by south notwithstanding I be hurry to the northward and fall right with the foreland which by reason of the misty storm we can not set till we be within a league of it then I stand over the bay and come to a anchor here where I must be force to stay till our sail be mend and a new main coarse be make if not a fore coarse also then I purpose to go to sea again and to proceed in coast the ice to the westward if it hinder i to proceed northward I have already coast it from hackluyt Headland to the latitude aforesaid and intend to begin again so near as I can at the place where I be put off with the storm I come from fair haven the four of july and then have there be kill twelve whale beside one find dead and another bring in by fra. Birkes which he find at sea before he come into fair haven when I come in hither here be three ship and a pinnace of the king of Denmark ship of the king of Denmark they ride in deep water about a league and a half from the road but weigh from thence and the admiral come to a anchor close by i and send to entreat i to come aboard of he I go aboard and be courteous entertain by the general who question i of the country and ask i by what right the english merchant do resort and fish in this place I tell he by the king of England right who have grant a patent to the muscovie company of merchant whereby he authorize they and forbid all other to frequent these place then he entreat i to go with he to sir tho. smith bay to the two english ship there I tell he it will be loss of time to i because I have some business here to do and then to go forth present to sea again to prosecute my discovery he say that he will have i go with he to be witness what pass betwixt he and you for he have matter of importance to acquaint you withal which concern our king and they and therefore entreat i to give direction present to weigh and set sail for I must needs go with he I reply again that it will be a great loss unto i of time and I know not how to answer it but he tell i peremptory that I must go with he so see no remedy I bid the master be ready then he present weigh and keep i aboard he but afterward meet with the two captain that come from you he return and anchor again in crosse-road I receive very courteous entertainment of the admiral vide-admiral and of captain Killingham but captain Killingham be aboard of i go away as he seem discontent because I will not give he a young Morse I have aboard which I deny to do because I write to my master from fair haven that such a thing I have and will bring alive into England if I may when he go off aboard of i he say he will shoot down my flag and soon after there come a shot which slay over we out of the admiral and I expect another but soon after there come a man aboard of i out of the admiral to see if any of your man that come in the shallop will go with they into the bay and he swear unto i that the shot be make to call their boat aboard because they be ready to weigh as far as I can perceive their purpose be to see what grant the king of England have make unto the company for they seem to pretend that the right of this land belong to the king of Denmark and neither to english nor hollander thus with my hearty commendation to yourself and master Bredcake together with my prayer for your prosperous voyage I commit you to God chap. 8 diverse other voyage to greenland with letter of those which be there employ communicate to i by master WILLIAM HELEY an. 1616. edge island be discover decrow by William Heley in Portnick the 12. of August 1617. worshipful sir my duty remember may it please you to understand that through God blessing our voyage be perform in all the harbour in the country this year with a great overplus than our ship will carry so that in some place we must of force leave good store of oil and blubber behind for the next year we be all for the most part ready to set sail be full lade only I desire to see the coast clear of interloper whereby our provision may be leave in security we take a ship of Flushing call the Noah ark master John Verlile in horne-sound have out of he two hundred hogshead of blubber and two whale and a half to cut up a great copper and diverse other provision and send he away ballast with stone there be two more of they who be go lade with blubber before we can get thither have intelligence of our come there be also two dane who make one hundred and odd ton of oil and lade one ship for copenhaven the other with half the oil and fin for Amsterdam and leave the country about the six or seven of August and for master Cudner he ride in Portnick where he kill eleven whale and make some seventy and odd ton of oil which be lade aboard he and his fin in who if our ship have come together thither as I desire I will have lade forty or fifty ton of oil in he and displace his man and send he for England but bad weather hinder our ship get thither and his sudden departure after our come in with the pleasure she be lade and not sufficient fit to surprise he he escape but I send she away in company with he whereby he may not do any hurt in other place in the country I will have have he to have take in some oil for which I offer he freight so I may put some man into he to see to it and that it may be bring safe to London but he refuse yet protest he purpose to bring his ship and good to London his voyage be by the three so that his man will rather die then forgo that they have get the small ship John Ellis be return from the south eastward have make some further discovery and kill some eight hundred seamorse and lade the tooth and thirty ton of hide and the rest of his lade in oil he bring some sea-horse blubber with he he meet with Thomas Marmaduke of Hull in those part who have not do any thing when he see he towards make a voyage but go for hope island and no doubt but he will do much spoil there as for the bear she depart for hamborough the three of August out of crosse-road and the greyhound in company with she for England who I hope be safe arrive and by who I hope you understand of her proceed at full the whale kill this year in the country be about one hundred and fifty in number and the oil make will be about one thousand eight hundred and odd ton beside the blubber leave for want of cask the lade of this ship be one hundred and eighty ton as by the bill of lade here enclose thus have not further wherewith to acquaint your worship withal pray God to send all home in safety with a good passage I humble take my leave and do rest ready at your worship command in all dutiful service william HELEY a letter of master ROBERT salmon to master sherwin in sir THOMAS smith bay the 24. of june 1618. love friend master Sherwine I kind salute you wish you as much prosperity as unto myself etc. since our come into the bay we have be much trouble with ice and northerly wind so as we have not be two day free of ice we have a storm northerly which bring in much ice so as we be enclose withal eight day ther^ go such a sea in the ice that do beat our ship very much for four and twenty hour that I do think we shall have spoil our ship but I thank God we can perceive any hurt at all it have do to we also we have break two anchor with the ice we have kill thirteen whale but they yield but little in regard of the ice which have much hinder we in our work for in ten daye^ we can not do any work the bay be so full of ice the bay be full as low as fox no^e and now at this present the bay be full of shatter ice the wind hang northerly keep it in here be five sail of fleming which have fourteen and sixteen piece of ordnance in a ship and they do man out eighteen shallop so that with they and we here be thirty shallop in the bay too many for we to make a voyage there be at the least fifteen hundred ton of ship of the fleming we have reasonable good quarter with they for we be merry aboard of they and they of we they have good store of sack and be very kind to we proffer we any thing that we want I be very doubtful of make a voyage this year yet I hope crosse-road will help we for one ship the company must take another course the next year if they mean to make any benefit of this country they must send better ship that must beat these knave out of this country but as far as I can understand by they they mean to make a trade of continuance of it they have every one of they grave maurices commission under his hand and seal we will let they rest this year and let who will take care the next year for I hope not to trouble they I pray remember my duty to the captain and also to honest master thorn-bush and to John Martin master Smith do remember his love to you and to all the rest of his friend we be well at this present I thank God I pray let we hear from you when you have any conveyance I hope we shall go home in company together as we come out thus with my love once again remember to you beseech God to send we all a prosperous voyage and joyful to meet I rest a letter of master th. sherwin bell-sound this 29. of june 1618. master William Heley couple of hen and a bottle of canary wine but I pray be careful of yourself and keep you warm and take heed the do not pick out your eye but as for the fleming let they all go hang themselves and although you be not strong enough to meddle with they yet the worst word be too good for they the time may come you may be revenge on they again the captain wish they will come all into bell-sound and beat we out and carry we for Holland here be a great fleet of they in this country here come in two fleming but we handle they very honest but for fear of afterclap or have it be the latter part of the year we will have handle they better now they be go for horne-sound I will that they have all of they as good a pair of horn grow on their head as be in this country as concern our voyage master Salmon can certify you both in horne-sound and in our harbour my brother buss John Martin and I drink to you and wish you many a venison pasty we have so little to do we fear we shall all have the scurvy but we have pull down the flemish house and bring it near more fit for our turn thus pray you to remember my love to all at faire-haven I cease with my prayer to God to send you and we all a prosperous voyage with all your good health that we may go merry home together a letter of JAMES BEVERSHAM to master HELEY from faire-haven the 12. of july 1618. master Heley my commendation remember to yourself master salmon master Smith and master Beymond as also to master wilkenson mate Headland master Greene and the rest of our good friend with you wish all your health as my own I be very sorry to understand of the annoyance by the fleming both with you and other place as also of the small hope there be in make a voyage this year for our part we be and have be so pester with ice these twenty day that we have not be able to go out to sea with our shallop above twice in the time neither have we be able to do any good by reason of foul weather and fog nor have see any more than one whale in all that time which after she be kill turn we to much trouble by reason of foul weather and force we at last to leave she in the ice where the bear make a prey of she who I fear will spoil she before she be recover we have kill sixteen whale beside whereof the flemish biscainer steal one for which they have promise satisfaction but they be so shut up with ice that they be not able to stir either ship or shallop all the sea to the northward of hakluyt headland and both eastward and westward thereof be pack so full of ice that I fear it will overthrow our voyage and put our ship in much hazard the lord release we of that misery in due time I neither have nor will be slack to do my best endeavour for the good of the voyage the prosperity whereof I do much wish and desire both here and in all other place I pray remember my love to the captain by your next convoy to the southward with my commendation to all the rest of our friend thus for present wish your health I kind take my leave and rest your love friend I have think to have add a large discourse of occurrent betwixt the dutch and english in greenland this 1618. and have prepare it to the press but have already give some relation thereof from captain edge etc. and see the insolence of some of the dutch be intolerable to english spirit which then suffer or hereafter shall read they I choose rather to pass they by advise my countryman not to impute to that nation what some frothy spirit vomit from amid his drink but to honour the hollander worth and to acknowledge the glory of the confederate province howsoever they also have their sink and stink rewer too officious mouth such as some in this business of greenland beyond all name of impudence against his majesty and his liege people as other elsewhere have demean themselves who loathsomeness be not to be cast as a aspersion to that industrious and illustrious nation every body have its excrement every great house its vault or jakes every city some port exquiline and dunghill every camp the baggage the world itself a hell and so have every nation the retriment stumme dregs rascality intemper distemper spirit which not fear god nor reverence man spare not to spew out that to the dishonour of both which save the honour of both can scarce be relate after they a difference be to be make of relation and personal fault of which we have say enough in the HELEY bel-sound june 16. 1619. love and approve good friend master William Heley etc. I be force to write in tear unto you for the loss of our man by the most uncouth accident that ever befall unto poor man the thirteen of june last we be put ashore in the ice bay our shallop be not aboard but as soon as we hear of it terrible disaster we make what haste we can and hale our shallop upon the ice and go aboard our ship by that time we have be there a hour make what mean we can to get she out a main piece of the cliff fall the fearful sight that ever I behold be then aboard expect nothing else but death with all the rest that be in she but God of his great mercy and providence deliver we that be not then appoint to die that be pass all hope of life for the ice fall so high and so much that it carry away our foremast break our mainmast spring our bouldstrit and fetch such a career that she heave a piece of ordnance overboard from under our half deck have i over board among the ice in all the sea and yet I thank the lord I be never hurt with a piece of ice although it please God they be spoil and kill close by i thus have relate unto you the misery of this our voyage hope of your aid and assistance in what you may I shall be ever bind to pray for you the captain bid i write unto you for a five inch Haser which I pray you spare i and it be possible I have write the particular of our want in my brother sherwin letter which I pray you be a mean to further i in thus cease any further to trouble you I commit you unto the lord unto who I pray to bless and prosper you in this your present voyage with all the rest of your day the man that be kill be these my mate money Nicholas Greene and Allin the butcher there be many more hurt which I hope will recover it by the help of God and the mean of a good surgeon love friend master Heley I kind salute you etc. your letter I receive the five of this present wherein I understand of the backwardness of your voyage the which I be hearty sorry for but you must be content see it be the will of God it shall be so and that other harbour take neighbour fare with you our best hope of our voyage be upon you for of ourselves we do little in regard we be much trouble with ice and have be so this ten day which have make we hale ashore six or seven time for it we have have the wind at north-east and east north-east and at northwest which now keep in the ice we have kill ten whale whereof eight be make into oil which have make one hundred and eleven tun and a half the other two be kill the four of this present be very there be so much ice off of point look out that George can not get about this ice have put in young duke of Hull into horne-sound his ship be much tear with the ice his merchant be now aboard of we his name be medcafe who the captain do detain his voyage be utter overthrow for he have lose one shallop with six man and another shallop break with the ice his ruther iron be all break his steam break a way close to the wooding also George do meet with a Fleming of Flushing burden two hundred tun the which he think be cast away with ice for the ice do beat she very sore I understand by m. Kirgis Mutalla 7128. the three and twenty of September in the emperor dominion at Soldota a Cazacke of siberia call Euashko Pettlin do report be examine of his travel the last year past 7127. he say that the Boiaren and Simonowich koorockin send he from the castle of Tomo and his f^llow^ Andrashko to conduct the king altines ambassador as also to inquire or search the kingdom of Catay they go from the castle of Tomo about the nine of May and travel from Tomo to Kirgis with much expedition ten day and in Kirgis be a duke subject to the emperor majesty his name be who give they victual and post through this land of Kirgis they be half a day and come to the dominion of Mutalla to the Altine king who give they provision and post and dispatch they thence so they pass through his land five week to the country of Sheremugaly where reign a queen call Manchika who cause to have provision and post give they in this country of Sheromogula they travel four day q. Manchika and come into the dominion of Catay call crim where be a wall make of stone fifteen fathom high alongst the side of which wall they go ten day where they see petty town and village belong to (@) queen Manchika but in those ten day they see no people upon the wall at all at the end of these ten day wall of Catay the gate and guard they come to the gate wherein lie very great piece of ordnance shoot shoot as big as a man head and in the say gate stand in watch three thousand man and they come with their merchandize to traffic at the gate the Altine man also come to the gate with
