this manner they shoot at the seal or other great fish with their dart unto which they use to tie a bladder which do boy up the fish in such manner that by the say mean they catch they so come aboard our ship have leave certain trifle behind we in their tent and take nothing away with we within half a hour after our come aboard the savage to who we have give the knife with three other their come all the savage begin to sling stone at we yea they do sling so fierce that we can scarce stand on the hatch I see their brutish deal cause the gunner to shoot a falcon at they which light a little over they at which time they go to their boat and row away about one a clock in the afternoon they come again to we cry in their accustom manner yli^nt they be sixty three in number the shripper stone they whisper one with another begin to sling stone unto we they sling stone again I present shoot off a little pistol which I have for the gunner and the rest of the folk to discharge which indeed they do but whether they do hurt or kill any of they or not I can certain tell but they row all away make a howl and hideous noise go to the same point whereas in the forenoon they have be be no soon come on land but from the hill they do so assail we with stone with their sling that it be incredible to report in such sort that no man can stand upon the hatch till such time as I command for to lose sail and bonnet two man height to shield we from the force of the stone and also do hide we from their sight so that we do ply our musket and other piece such as we have at they but their subtlety be such that as soon as they do see fire give to the piece they will sudden duck down behind the cliff and when they be discharge then sling their stone fierce at we again thus have continue there till four a clock they depart away the nineteen day in the morning about four a clock it be calm I depart from this roadsted so cause our man to row alongst the shore till the tide of the ebb be so far and so long time as the time limit to i therefore I think it convenient to make a brief description of the same according as by my short experience I find the same to be the land of Groenland be a very high ragged and mountainous country be all alongst the coast break land make very goodly sound and harbour the description of the land of Groenland have also in the land very many good river and bay into some of which I enter sail up the same the space of ten or twelve english league find the same very navigable with great abundance of fish of sundry sort the land also in all place wheresoever I come seem to be very fertile of the fertility of the country according to the climate wherein it lie for between the mountain be most pleasant plain and valley in such sort as if I have not see the same I can not have believe that such a fertile land in show can be in these northern region there be also in the same great store of fowl as raven crow partridge pheasant sea-mewes gull with other sundry sort of beast I have not see any except black fox of which there be very many store of foul black fox also as I do suppose there be many deer because that come to certain place where the people have have their tent we find very many heart horn with the bone of other beast round about the same also go up into the land we see the foot and dung of diverse beast which we do suppose to be dear and other beast also the foot of one which we find to be eight inch over yet notwithstanding we do see none of they for go some two or three mile from the pinnace we return again to go aboard moreover in the river we find sundry sort of fish as seal whale salmon fish with other sort of fish in great abundance as concern the coast all alongst it be a very good and fair land have very fair shoald of the same for be three english league off the same of the coast. I find very fair shoald in fifteen fathom and come near than same fourteen twelve and ten fathom very fair sandy ground as concern the people of the people they be as I do suppose a kind of samoite or wander nation travel in the summer time in company together first to one place and have stay in that place a certain time in hunt and fish for dear and seal with other fish straight they remove themselves with their tent and baggage to another they be man of a reasonable stature be brown of colour the colour of the people the people very active very like to the people of the east and west indies they be very active and warlike as we do perceive in their skirmish with we in use their sling and dart very nimble they eat their meat raw or a little parboil either with blood oil or a little water which they do drink they apparel themselves in the skin of such beast as they kill they eat their meat most part raw of their apparel of their weapon but especial with seal skin and foul skin dress the skin very soft and smooth with the hair and feather on wear in winter the hair and feather side inward and in summer outward their weapon be sling dart arrow have their bow fast tie together with sinew their arrow have but two feather the head of the same be for the most part of bone make in manner and form of a harp iron as concern their dart they be of sundry sort and fashion what knowledge they have of God I can certain say but I suppose they to be idolater worship the sun the country as be aforesaid seem to be very fertile yet can I perceive or see no wood to grow thereon we can see no wood drift-wood we meet all alongst this coast much drift-wood but whence it come I know not for coast all this coast alongst from the latitude of 66. degree and a half until the latitude of 69. degree I find many goodly sound bay and river give name unto diverse of they and purpose to proceed further the folk in the pinnace with i do earnest entreat i to return to the ship again John knight with five more pass over to a great island where he and three of his company seem to have be intercept by the savage and he and Edward gorrell his mate and his brother and three more of our company take the boat carry with they four pistol three musket five sword and two half pike for to go over to a great island which be not above a mile from our ship to look if they can find any of the clock at night but can hear no news of they after their departure up into the top of the Hill their trumpettor then do the trumpettor sound two or three time and the other do discharge his rest of the company be when we come on shore they inquire for our master and the rest of our company but we can tell they no news of they after their departure out of the boat but that we do see they boatswain be who when they see he they shoot their arrow at he run towards he as fast as they can whereupon he discharge his musket at they and flee to our tent as fast as he can think they have beset we they be so many of they in sight the steward hear his musket go off come out of the ship and as he be come see the savage run to our shallop and cry out to we that be asleep in our tent to come to wit together we send two of our man back unto our tent our man expulse the savage the rest of we make towards they and shoot at they some three or four musket who when they see we shoot they stand in they see we march towards they so fierce our dog be foremost they run away above fifty savage in sight but we dare not pursue they any further for it be in the night and they be in sight above fifty man thus we recover our shallop then we send some more of our man to our tent to keep it and the rest follow towards the place whither they flee but before we can overtake they they be get into their boat and be row away through the ice very great boat of the savage which be so thick that they can not pass away but stick fast for their boat be very great we see they stick fast in the ice some set with oar and some row come so near they as we can and shoot at they some dozen shot before they can get clear which shoot cause they to cry out very sore one to another for their boat be full of man knight be write by Oliver Browne one of the company chap. 17 the four voyage of JAMES HALL. to Groeneland wherein he be set forth by english adventurer 1612. and slay by a Greenelander write by WILLIAM baffin WEdnesday the eight of july 1612. in the morning I perceive the sun and the moon both very fair above the horizon as I have do diverse time before at which time I purpose to find out the longitude of that place by the moon come to the meridian most part of this day I spend about find of the meridian line which I do upon a island near the sea hang at the extreme of my meridian line two thread with plummet at they instead of a index and sight Thursday the nine day very early in the morning I go on shore the island be a fair morning and observe till the moon come just upon the meridian at which very instant I observe the sun height and find it 8. degree 53. minute north in the elevation of the pole 65. degree 20. minute by the which work by the doctrine of spherical triangle have the three side give to wit the compliment of the pole elevation the compliment of the almecanter and the compliment of the sun declination to find out the quantity of the angle at the pole I say by this work I find it to be four of the clock 17. minute and 24. second which when I have do I find by my ephemerides that the moon come to the meridian at London that morning at four of the clock 25. minute 34. second which 17. minute 24. second substract from 25.34 leave 8.10 of time for the difference of longitude betwixt the meridian of London for which the ephemerides be make and the meridian pass by this place in Groenland now the moon motion that day be 12. degree 7. minute 60. degree 30. minute difference of longitude between the meridian of London and cockin sound in Groenland which convert into minute of time be 48. minute 29. second which work by the rule of proportion the work be thus if 48. minute 29. second the time that the moon come to the meridian soon that day than she do the day before give 360. the whole circumference of the earth what shall 8. minute 10. second give to wit 60. degree 30. minute or near there abvut which be the difference of longitude between the meridian of London and this place in Groenland call cockin sound lie to the westward of London this find of the longitude I confess be somewhat difficult and troublesome and there may be some small error but if it be careful look unto and exact wrought there will be no great error if your ephemerides be true but some will say that this kind of work be not for mariner objection because they be not acquaint to work proposition by the table of sign and a instrument be not precise enough to find out the hour minute and second for the loss of one minute of time be the loss of 7. degree of longitude I answer that although the most part be not use to this work answer yet I know some of the better sort which be able to work this and the like proposition exact and those which ye^ can and be desirous to learn may in short space attain to such knowledge as shall be sufficient for such thing and how necessary it be that the longitude of place shall be know I leave to the judgement of all skilful mariner and other that be learn in the mathematics this afternoon it be agree by the chief of our company that our master james hall shall go in the small ship far to the northward the foresay Thursday in the evening he depart out of the patience into the hearts-ease to get forth of the harbour which our master call cockins-ford in remembrance of alderman Cockin one of the adventurer cockin Ford in 65. deg. 20. which place be in the latitude of 65. degree 20 minute and the variation of the compass be 23. degree 58. minute to the westward that evening be very the lord be praise here I think it not amiss brief to relate the state and manner of the people of Groenland forasmuch as I can learn as also what likelihood there be of a pass into the sea which lie upon Tartary and China the northwest part of gronland be a exceed high land to the seaward and almost nothing but mountain which be wonderful high all within the land high mountain of stone very pure as far as we can perceive and they be all of stone some of one colour and some of another and all glister as though they be of rich value but indeed they be not worth any thing for our goldsmith james Carlisle try very much of the Vre no profitable Vre and find it to be nothing worth if there be any mettle it lie so low in the mountain that it can be well come by there be some rock in these mountain which be exceed pure stone fine and white than alabaster the side of these mountain continual be cover with snow for the most part and especial the north side and the noth side of the valley have a kind of moss and in some place grass with a little branch run all along the ground continual snow grass no tree ball river a grove of small wood bear a little black Berrie it run along the ground like three-leafed grass here in England there be few or no tree grow as far as we can perceive but in one place some forty mile within the land in a river which we call ball river there I see on the southside of a high mountain which we go up and find as it be a young grove of small wood some of it six or seven foot high like a coppice in England that have be some two or three year cut and this be the most wood that we see grow in this country be some of it a kind of willow juniper and such like we find in many place much Angelica we suppose the people eat the root thereof for some cause for we have see they have many of they in their Bo there be great store of fox in the land and in the main of sundry colour fox white hare dear and there be a kind of hare as white as snow with their fur or hair very long also there be dear but they be most common up within the main very far because the people do so much hunt they that come near the Sea I see at one time seven of they together which be all that we do see in the country but our man have buy diverse coat of the people make of deer skin and have buy of their horn also beside we have diverse time see the footstep of some beast these seem to be elke or lo^shes dog like wolf the pizzle of dog and fox^s be bone so also be the morse pizzle of which I have by i one of stone the great swiftness of their Bo their oar broad at both end who foot be big than the foot of a great ox furthermore the inhabitant have a kind of dog which they keep at their house and tent which dog be almost like unto wolf live by fish as the fox do but one thing be very strange as I think for the pizzle of both dog and fox be bone the people all the summer time use nothing but fish dry their fish and seal flesh upon the rock for their winter provision every one both man and woman have each of they a boat make with long small piece of firre-wood cover with seales skin very well dress and sew so well with sinew or gut that no water can pierce they through be some of they above twenty foot long and not past two foot or two foot and a half broad in form of a weaver shuttle and so light that a man may carry many of they at once for the weight in these boat they will row so swift that it be almost incredible for no ship in the world be able to keep way with they although she have never so good a gale of wind and yet they use but one oar who sit in the middle of their boat and hold their oar in the middle be broad at each end like our oar will at a instant go backward and forward as they please in these boat they catch the most part of their food be seal and salmon morse and other kind of fish salmon and morse etc. angle and line some they kill with their dart and other some with angle have a line make of small shiver of whale fin and a hook of some fish bone with which line and hook we also have catch very much fish also they have another kind of boat which be very long for we have see one of they thirty two foot in length their great boat 32. foot long open in the top like our boat have ten seat in it in which when they remove their dwelling they carry their good or householdstuff for they remove their dwelling very often as their fish do serve live in the summer time in tent make of seales skin and in winter in house somewhat in the ground we can not particular learn their rite or ceremony but general they worship the sun they worship the sun their salutation as chief author of their felicity at their first approach unto we they use with their hand to point up to the sun and to strike their hand upon their breast cry ilyont as who will say I mean no harm which they will do very often and will not come near you until you do the like and then they will come without any fear at all their burial they bury their dead in the out-iland near the seaside their manner of burial be this upon the top of the hill they gather a company of stone together and make thereof a hollow cave or grave of the length and breadth of the body which they intend to bury lay the stone somewhat close like a wall that neither fox nor other such beast may devour the body cover they with broad stone show afar off like a pile of stone and near unto this grave where the body lie be another wherein they bury his bow and arrow they burn the weapon and all other furniture of the dead with his dart and all his other provision which he use while he be live he be bury in all his apparel and the coldness of the climate do keep the body from smell and stink although it lie above the ground they eat all their food raw and use no fire to dress their victual as far as we can perceive also we have see they drink the salt-water at our ship side but whether it be usual or no I can tell although they dress not their meat with fire yet they use fire for other thing they use fire as to warm they etc. diverse of our man be of opinion that they be man-eater and will have devour we if they can have catch we but I do not think they will for if they have be so mind they may at one time have catch our cook and two other with he as they be fill of water at a island they be not man-eater a great way from our ship these three I say be in the ship boat without either musket or any other weapon when as a great company of the savage come row unto they with their dart and other furniture which they never go without nail and old iron great desire of the savage man be not to go among savage without the^r weapon and stand look into the boat for nail or any old iron which they so great desire while our man be in such a fear that they know not what to do at length our cook remember that he have some old iron in his pocket and give each of they some as far as it will go with his key of his chest. and present they all depart without offer any harm at all but this I speak not that I will have man to trust they or to go among they unprovided of weapon chap. 18 a true relation of such thing as happen in the four voyage for the discovery of the northwest passage perform in the year 1615. write by WILLIAM baffin after three sundry voyage towards the northwest to the great charge of the adventurer the first by Huds^^ in which he perish the second by sir Tho^a^ button the three by captain gibbins the last be under the command of captain gibbins in which be little or nothing perform yet the right worshipful sir Dudley digges knight master Wostenholme esquire master alderman jones with other being not therewith discourage this year 1615. again set forth the discovery a ship of fifty five ton or thereabouts which ship have be the three former voyage on the action the master be Robert bile a man well acquaint that way have be employ in the three former voyage myself being his mate and associate with fourteen other and two boy the sixteen we weigh anchor at saint Katherine and that tide come to Blackwall the wind be at south south-west the seventeen we go down to Gravesend and the eighteen to Lee where we anchor that night upon the six of May we see land on the coast of Groenland on the east side of cape farewell and that night we have a great storm Groenland cape farewell so we keep a southerly course to get about the ice which lie on that shore and then keep our course until the seventeen day of May all which forenoon we sail by many great land of ice some of which be above two hundred foot high above water as I prove by one short after which I find to be two hundred and forty foot high and if report of some man be true which affirm high icy land that there be but one seven part of the ice above water than the height of that piece of ice which I observe be one hundred and forty fathom or one thousand six hundred and eighty foot from the top to the bottom this proportion I know do hold in much ice but whether it do so in all I know not this seventeen of May about noon we be come to the firm ice as one will suppose be in the latitude of 61. degree 26. minute or thereabouts be the latitude of the sou^h part of the i will of resolution we come to this ice i will of resolution our master ask my opinion concern the put into the ice my judgement be it will be best for we to stand and ply it up to the northwards he answer we be on the north side of the south channel and much ice we must pass through and if that we can get some two or three league within the ice it will every tide open and we shall get some thing onward of our way have all the channel to the southward of we so with this resolution we put within the ice the wind be at east north-east this first entrance I like not very well scarce find any place to put in our ship head and be near thirty league from the shore towards evening we be fast among the ice but sometime each day the ice will a little open we make what way we can towards the northwest in for the shore till the two and twenty day have have the wind all southerly yet we plain see that we set to the southwards for all that we can do the two and twenty day the wind come up at north northwest then our master determine to stand forth again for if the wind shall have come to the north-east it will be unpossible for we to fetch any part of the channel see we drive so fast to the southwards with southerly wind and have so far into the shore not have see the Land our master be also determine to spend some twenty or four and twenty day in fretum davis to see what hope will be that way suppose there will be little good to be do in hudsons straits for this time limit then we ply to get to seaward and so by eight a clock at night the three and twenty day we be clear of the thick ice again the lord make we thankful the wind at northwest and by north fair weather but no soon be we forth of the ice but that our master change his opinion and be clear of this thick ice we stand to the northward as much as the ice and wind will give we leave run some thirteen league true north-east by north be in the latitude of 61. degree 50. minute the four and twenty day fair weather the five and twenty day also fair weather the wind at north and by west till six a clock we have make a north-east by north way about twelve league and a half our latitude at noon 62. degree 20. minute at six a clock the wind be at the north north-east the six and twenty day all the forenoon fair weather and cold but in the afternoon it blow very hard be close hasie weather that about two a clock this afternoon we take in our sail and hull with our ship till the next morning at four a clock all the time that we sail this day we pass through many ledge of ice have great quantity to the northward of we and have run about twenty one league true upon a west course and note where I put this word true I mean the true course the variation of the compass and other accident allow the seven and twenty day close foggy weather with much snow freeze on our shrowd and tackle the like we have not all this year before but towards four so much ice that we can do but little good with a fair wind the wind continue all this day and night a stiff gale no night this night or rather evening because it be not dark at all we be set within the point of the island so that now we be within the straits the one and thirty day also fair weather the wind for the most part at north northwest the afternoon be clear we see the point of the south country and so God blessing you with all expedition to make your return home again chap. 19 to the right worshipful master JOHN WOSTENHOLME esquire one of the chief adventurer for the discovery of a passage to the northwest worthy sir there need no fill a journal or short discourse with preamble compliment or circumstance and therefore I will only tell you I be proud of any remembrance when I expose your worth to my conceit and glad of any good fortune when I can avoid the imputation of ingratitude by acknowledge your many favour and see it be not unknown to your worship in what estate the business concern the northwest have be heretofore and how the only hope be in search of fretum davis which if yourself have not be the more forward the action have well nigh be leave off now it remain for your worship to know what have be perform this year wherefore I entreat you to admit of my custom and pardon i if I take the plain highway in relate the particular without use any refine phrase and eloquent speech therefore brief and as it be in the forefront I intend to show you the whole proceed of the voyage in a word as namely there be no passage nor hope of passage in the north of davis straits we have coast all or near all the circumference thereof and find it to be no other than a great bay as the map here place do true show wherefore I can but much admire the work of the almighty when I consider how vain the best and chief hope of man be in thing uncertain howsoever the passage this way be embay yet that former discovery of sir tho. button then by he keep secret for some intent of his be both more probable and to the most judicious more than probable and that by that tide argument from the west as in master his map and note appear and to speak of no other matter then of the hopeful passage to the northwest how many of the best sort of man have set their whole endeavour to prove a passage that way and not only in conference but also in write and publish to the world yea what great sum of money have be spend about that action as your worship have costly experience off neither will the vainglorious Spaniard have scatter abroad so many false map and journal if they have not be confident of a passage this way that if it have please God a passage have be find they may have eclipse the worthy praise of the adventurer and true discoverer and for my own part I will hardly have believe the contrary until my eye become witness of that I desire not to have find still take occasion of hope on every little likelihood till such time as we have almost coast the circumference of this great Bay neither be master davis to be blame in his report and great hope if he have anchor about hope Sanderson to have take notice of the tide for to that place which be in ever studious to supply my other want by my best endeavour and ever rest at your worship command WILLIAM baffin a brief and true relation or journal contain such accident as happen in the five voyage with other in the good ship call the discovery of London Robert bile master and myself pilot perform in the year of our lord 1616. in the name of God amen the forename ship be in full readiness upon the fifteen day of April be clear of Dartmouth we be force the next day to put into Plymouth the nineteen day we set sail from thence and the twenty in the morning we pass between the land end and silly with a fair wind continue our course as in the brief table or journal be set down with every particular from noon to noon that here I need not make a tedious repetition nothing worthy of note happen but that we have a good passage and the first land we see be in fretum davis on the coast of Groinland in the latitude of 65. degree 20. minute on the fourteen of May in the forenoon Groinland than six of the people be a fish come to we to who we give small piece of iron they keep we company be very joyful suppose we have intend to come to anchor but when they see we stand off from shore they follow we a while and then go away discontent to our seem we prosecute our voyage be loath to come to anchor as yet although the wind be contrary but still ply to the northward until we come into 70. degree 20. minute then we come to anchor in a fair sound near the place master davis call London coast. the twenty of May at evening the people espy we flee away in their boat get on rock wonder and gaze at we but after this night we see they no more man and dog leave many dog run to and fro on the island at this place we stay two day in which time we take in fresh water and other necessary here we have some dislike of the passage because the tide be so small as not arise above eight or nine foot and keep no certain course but the near time of high water on the change day be at a quarter of a hour past nine and the flood come from the south the two and twenty day at a north sun we set sail and ply still northward the wind be right against we as we stand off and on upon the six and twenty day in the afternoon we find a dead whale about six and twenty league from shore dead whale have all her fin then make our ship fast we use the best mean we can to get they and with much toil get a hundred and sixty that evening the next morning the sea go very high and the wind arise the whale break from we and we be force to leave she and set sail and have not stand past three or four league northwestward come to the ice than we tack and stand to the shoareward a sore storm ensue by the thirty day in the afternoon we come fair by hope Sanderson hope Sanderson the far land master davis be at lie between 72. and 73. degree and that evening by a north sun we come to much ice which we put into ply all the next day to get through it the first of june we be clear of the ice before name and not far from shore the wind blow very hard at north north-east than we put in among diverse land tent man and woman the people see we flee away in all haste leave their tent behind and upon a small rock they hide two young maid or woman our ship ride not far off we espy they to who our master with some other of our company go in the boat they make sign to be carry to the island where their tent be close adjoin when they come thither they find two old woman more the one very old to our esteemation little less than fourscore the other not so old the next time we go on shore there be another woman with a child at her back who have hide herself among the rock till the other have tell she how well we have use they in give they piece of iron and such like which they high esteem in change thereof they give we seal skin other riches they have none save dead seal and fat of seal some of which fat or blubber afterward we carry aboard the poor woman be very diligent to carry it to the water side to put into our cask make show that the man be over at the main and at a other small island something more eastward then make sign to they that we will show they our ship and set they where the man be the four young come into our boat when they be aboard they much wonder to see our ship and furniture we give they of our meat which they taste will not eat then two of they we set on the island where they suppose the man to be the other two be carry to their tent again those that go to seek the man can not find they but come as near the ship as they can and at evening we set they over to the other this place we call woman land it lie in the latitude of 72. degree 45. minute woman land here the flood come from the southward at nep tide the water arise but six or seven foot and a south southeast moon make a full Sea the inhabitant very poor live chief on the flesh of seal dry which they eat raw with the skin they clothe themselves the people describe woman and also make cover for their tent and boat which they dress very well the woman in their apparel be different from the man and be mark in the face with diverse black stroke or line the skin be raze with some sharp instrument when they be young and black colour put therein that by no mean it will be get forth concern their religion I can little say religion only they have a kind of worship or adoration to the sun which continual they will point unto and strike their hand on their breast cry ily^nt their dead they bury on the side of the hill where they live which be common on small land make a pile of stone over they yet not so close but that we may see the dead body the air be so pierce that it keep they from much stink savour burial of man and dog so likewise I have see their dog bury in the same manner upon the four day we set sail from thence have very fair weather although the wind be contrary and ply to and fro between the ice and the land be as it be a channel of seven or eight league broad then on the nine day be in the latitude of 74. degree 4. minute and much pester with ice near unto three small land lie eight mile fromth shore we come to anchor near one of they these land be use to be frequent with people in the latter part of the year as it seem by the house and place where the tent have stand but this year as yet they be not come here the tide be very small especial the flood which arise not above five or six foot yet the ebb run with a indifferent stream the cause thereof in my opinion be the great abundance of snow melt on the land all this part of the year the ten day we set sail from thence and stand through much ice to the westward to try if that further from the shore we may proceed but this attempt be soon quail for the more ice we go through the thick it be till we can see no place to put in the ship head see that as yet we can not proceed we determine to stand in for the shore there to abide some few day till such time as the ice be more waste and go for we plain see that it consume very fast with this resolution we stand in and come to anchor among many land in the latitude of 73. degree 45. minute on the twelve day at night here we continue two day without show or sign of any people till on the fifteen day in the morning about one a clock than come two and forty of the inhabitant in their boat or canoas and give we seal skin 42. inhabitant and many piece of the bone or horn of the sea unicorn and show we diverse piece of sea tooth unicorn horn make sign that to the northward be many of they in exchange thereof we give they small piece of iron glass bead and such like at four several time the people come to we and at each time bring we of the aforesaid commodity by reason thereof we call this place Horn sound horn sound here we stay six day and on the eighteen day at night we set sail have very little wind and be at sea make the best way we can to the northward although the wind have be contrary for the most part this month but it be strange to see the ice so much consume in so little space for now we may come to the three land before name and stand off to the westward almost twenty league without let of ice until we be more north as to 74. degree 30. minute than we put among much scatter ice and ply to and fro all this month still in the sight of shore and many time fast in the ice yet every day we get something on our way nothing worthy of note happen but that at diverse time we see of the fish with long horn they see many sea unicorn many and often which we call the sea unicorn and here to write particular of the weather it will be superfluous or needless because it be so variable few day without snow and often freeze in so much that on midsummer day our shrowd rope and sail be so freeze sharp frost on midsummer day that we can scarce handle they yet the cold be not so extreme but it may well be endure the first of july we be come into a open sea in the latitude of 75. degree 40. minute which a new reviue our hope of a passage and because the wind be contrary we stand off twenty league from the shore before we meet the ice then stand in again when we be near the land we let fall a anchor to see what tide go but in that we find small comfort short after the wind come to the southeast and blow very hard with foul weather thick and foggy then we set sail and run along by the land this be on the second day at night the next morning we pass by a fair cape or head land which we call sir Dudley digges cape sir Dudley dig his cape it be in the latitude of 76. degree 35. minute and have a small island close adjoin to it the wind still increase we pass by a fair sound twelve league distant from the former cape have a island in the midst which make two entrance under this island we come to anchor and have not rid past two hour but our ship drive although we have two anchor at the ground than be we force to set sail and stand forth this sound we call Wostenholme sound it have many inlet or small sound in it Wostenholme sound and be a fit place for the kill of whale the four day at one a clock in the morning the storm begin again at west and by south so vehement that it blow away our forecourse and be not able to bear any sail we lay a drift till about eight a clock than it clear up a little and we see ourselves embay in a great sound then we set sail and stand over to the southeast side where in a little cove or bay we let fall a anchor which we lose with cable and all the wind blow so extreme from the top of the hill that we can get no place to anchor in but be force to stand to and fro in the sound the bottom be all freeze over towards two a clock it begin to be less wind than we stand forth whale sound in this sound we see great number of whale therefore we call it whale sound and doubtless if we have be provide for kill of they we may have strike very many it lie in the latitude of 77. degree 30. minute all the five day it be very fair weather and we keep along by the land till eight a clock in the evening by which time we be come to a great bank of ice it be back with land which we see determine to stand back some eight league to a island we call hackluit isle it lie between two great sound the one whale sound and the other sir Thomas smith sound this last run to the north of seventy eight degree and be admirable in one respect sir Thomas smith sound in 78. deg because in it be the great variation of the compass of any part of the world know for by diverse good observation I find it to be above five point or fifty six degree vary to the westward so that a north-east and by east be true north and so of the rest also this sound seem to be good for the kill of whale variation of the compass 56. degree to the west which may make questionable d. gilbert rule tom. 1 l. 2. c. 1. that where more earth be more attraction of the compass happen by variation towards it now the know continent of Asia etc. must be unspeakable more than here there can be and yet here be more variation then about japan or brasil Peru etc. carry land it be the great and large in all this Bay the cause wherefore we mind to stand to this island be to see if we can find any fin or such like on the shore and so indeed this night we come to anchor but with such foul weather that our boat can not land the next day we be force to set sail the sea be grow so high and the wind come more outward two day we spend and can get no good place to anchor in then on the eight day it clear up and we see (@) company of land lie off from the shore twelve or thirteen league we mind to go to they to see if there we can anchor when we be something near the wind take we short and be loath to spend more time we take opportunity of the wind ^nd leave the search of these land which we call careyes land all which sound and land the map * * this map of the author for this and the former voyage with the table of his journal and sail be somewhat then to have stand in again but this prove quite contrary to our expectation for we be force to run above threescore league through very much ice and many time so fast that we can go no way although we can come to anchor to make trial of the tide but the ice lead we into the latitude of 65. degree 40. minute then we leave off seek to the west shore because we be in the indraft of cumberland isle therefore we determine to go for the coast of Groineland to see if we can get some refresh for our man master Hubert and two more have keep their cabin above eight day beside our cook Richard Waynam which die the day before be the twenty six of july and diverse more of our company so weak that they can do but little labour so the wind favour we we come to anchor in the latitude of 65. degree 45. brief discourse of the probability of a passage to the western or south sea illustrate with testimony and a brief treatise and map by master BRIGGES I think good to add somewhat to this relation of master baffin that learned-unlearned mariner and mathematician who want art of word so real employ himself to those industry whereof here you see so evident fruit his map and table will have much illustrate his voyage if trouble and cost and his own despair of passage that way have not make we willing to content ourselves with that map follow of that thrice learned and in this argument three time thrice industrious mathematician master Brigges famous for his read in both university and this honourable city that I make no further voyage of discovery to find and follow the remote passage and extent of his name master baffin tell i that they suppose the tide from the northwest about digges island be misreport by mistake the hour eight for eleven and that he will if he may get employment search the passage from japan by the coast of Asia or any way he can but in the indies he die in the late Ormus business baffins death slay in fight with a shot as he be try his mathematical project and conclusion now for that discovery of sir Thomas button I have solicit he for his note and receive of he gentle entertainment and kind promise but be then force to stay in the city upon necessary and urgent affair he will at his return home seek and impart they since I hear that weighty occasion have detain he out of England and I can communicate that which I can not receive which if I do receive I purpose rather to give thou out of due place than not at all once he be very confident in conference with i of a passage that way and say that he have therein satisfy his majesty the king satisfy touch the passage who from his discourse in private infer the necessity thereof and the main argument be the course of the tide for winter in port nelson see the follow map he find the tide rise every twelve hour fifteen foot whereas in the bottom of hudsons bay it be but two foot and in the bottom of fretum davis discover by baffin but one yea and a west wind equal the nep tide to the spring tide plain argue the neighbourhood of the sea which be on the west side of America the summer follow he find about the latitude of 60. degree a strong race of a tide run sometime eastward sometime westward whereupon josias hubbard in his plat call that place Hubbarts hope as in the map appear now if any make scruple because this discovery be not pursue by sir Thomas button Hubbarts hope let he consider that be prince Henry servant and partly by he employ whence I think he name the country new Wales the untimely death of that prince put all out of joint nor be he so open that other shall have the glory of his discovery and if any man think that the passage be so far as the map use to express America run out into the west it be easy answer that either of negligence or overbusy diligence map by portugal in the east and spaniard in the west have be false project hence that fabulous strait of anian as before by Francis gaul testimony and navigation be evident and hence the portugal to bring in the Moluccas to that moiety of the world agree upon betwixt the spaniard and they be think to have much curtal Asia and the longitude of those land give few degree to they then in just longitude be requisite so the old map of America make the land from the Magelane strait to the south sea run much west when as they rather be contract somewhat easterly from the north. the like be just suppose of their false place Quivira and I know not nor they neither what country they make in America to run so far northwestward which sir Francis drake voyage in that sea his * * this easy appear in observe his voyage and compare that before of (@) Gaul therewith Albion be little further westward than Aquatulco plain evince to be otherwise yea the late map of california find to be a island the savage discourse in all the country northwards and westward from Virginia fame whereof fill my friend master dermer with so much confidence that hear of strange ship which come thither for a kind of Vre or earth the man use fork in their diet with caldron to dress their meat etc. thing nothing suitable to any part of America he suppose they to come from the east near to China or japan and therefore he make a voyage purposely to discover but cross with diverse disaster he return to Virginia frustrate of accomplishment that year but full of confidence as in a letter from Virginia he signify to i where death end that his design soon after but how often be the usual chart reject by experience in these navigation in this work record painter and poet be not always the best oracle for further proof of a passage about those part into the west sea or south as it be call from the first discovery thereof to the south from the part of new Spain whence it be passage of when I be at Venice in April 1596. happy arrive there a old man about threescore year of age call common juan de Fuca but name proper Apostolos Valerianos of nation a greek bear in the hand Cefalonia of profession a mariner and a ancient pilot of ship this man be come late out of Spain arrive first at Ligorno and go thence to Florence in Italy where he find one John Dowglas a Englishman a famous mariner ready come for Venice to be pilot of a venetian ship name Ragasona for England in who company they come both together to Venice and John Dowglas be well acquaint with (@) before he give i knowledge of this greek pilot and bring he to my speech and in long talk and conference between we in presence of John Dowglas this greek pilot declare in the italian and spanish language thus much in effect as follow first he say that he have be in the west indies of Spain by the space of forty year and have sail to and from many place thereof as mariner and pilot in the service of the spaniard also he say that he be in the spanish ship which in return from the land and China towards Spania be rob and take at the cape california by captain Candish Englishman captain Candish whereby he lose sixty thousand ducat of his own good also he say that he be pilot of three small ship which the vizeroy of Mexico send from Mexico arm with one hundred man soldier under a captain spaniard to discover the strait of anian along the coast of the south-sea and to fortify in that straight to resist the passage and proceed of the english nation which be fear to pass through those strait into the south Sea and that by reason of a mutiny which happen among the soldier for the sodomy of their captain that voyage be overthrow and the ship return back from california coast to Spania without any effect of thing do in that voyage and that after their return the captain be at Mexico punish by justice also he say that short after the say voyage be so ill end the say viceroy of Mexico send he out again 1592. with a small and a pinnace arm with mariner only to follow the say voyage for discovery of the same strait of anian and the passage thereof into the sea which they call the north sea which be our northwest Sea and that he follow his course in that voyage west and northwest in the south sea all alongst the coast of Spania and california and the indies now call north America all which voyage he signify to i in a great map land trend in 47. degree and a sea-card of my own which I lay before he until he come to the latitude of forty seven degree and that there find that the land trend north and north-east with a broad inlet of sea between 47. and 48. degree of latitude he enter thereinto sail therein more than twenty day and find that land trend still sometime northwest and north-east and north and also east and south-eastward and very much broad sea than be at the say entrance and that he pass by diverse land in that sail and that at the entrance of this say straight there be on the northwest coast thereof a great Hedland or island with a exceed high pinnacle or spire rock like a pillar thereupon also he say that he go on land in diverse place and that he see some people on land clad in beast skin and that the land be very fruitful and rich of gold silver pearl and other thing like Spania and also he say that he be enter thus far into the say strait and be come into the north sea already and find the sea wide enough every where and to be about thirty or forty league wide in the mouth of the strait the mouth of the straight where he enter 30. or 40. league broad where he enter he think he have now well discharge his office and do the thing which he be send to do and that he not be arm to resist the force of the savage people that may happen he therefore set sail and return homeward again towards Spania where he arrive at acapulco 1592. hope to be reward great of the viceroy for this service do in this say voyage also he say that after his come to Mexico he be great welcome by the viceroy and have great promise of great reward but that have sue there two year time and obtain nothing to his content the viceroy tell he that he shall be reward in Spain of the king himself very great and will he therefore to go into Spain which voyage he do perform also he say that when he be come into Spain he be great welcome there at the king court in word after the spanish manner but after long time of suit there also he can not get any reward there neither to his content and that therefore at the length he steal away out of Spain and come into Italy to go home again and live among his own kindred and countryman he be very old also he say that he think the cause of his ill reward have of the spaniard to be for that they do understand very well that the english nation have now give over all their voyage for discovery of the northwest passage wherefore they need not fear they any more to come that way into the south sea and therefore they need not his service therein any more also he say that in regard of this ill reward have of the spaniard and understand of the noble mind of the queen of England and of her war maintain so valiant against the spaniard and hope that her majesty will do he justice for his good lose by captain Candish he will be content to go into England and serve her majesty in that voyage don John Pacheco duke of Escalona chap. 2 observation gather out of the first second three and four book of JOSEPHUS acosta a learned jesuite touch the natural history of the heaven air water and earth at the west indies also of their beast fish fowl plant and other remarkable rarity of nature @. i. of the fashion and form of heaven at the new-found world and of the air and windes lib. 1. cap. 5. many in Europe demand of what form and fashion heaven be in the southern part for that there be no certainty find in ancient book who although they grant there be a heaven on this other part of the world yet come they not to any knowledge of the form thereof although in truth they make mention of a goodly great star see in those part which they call Canopus those which of late day have sail into these part plin. lib. ^ c. 22. have accustom to write strange thing of this heaven that it be very bright have many goodly star and in effect thing which come far be common describe with increase but it seem contrary unto i hold it for certain that in our region of the north there be a great number and big star find no star in these part which exceed the fisher or the chariot in bigness it be true that the cross in these part be very fair and please to behold see (@) voyage we call the cross four notable and apparent star which make the form of a cross set equal and with proportion the ignorant suppose this cross to be the southern pole for that they see the navigator take their height thereby as we be accustom to do by the north star but they be deceive and the reason why sailor do it in this sort be for that in the south part there be no fix star that mark the pole as the north star do to our Pole and therefore they take their height by the star at the foot of the cross distant from the true and fix Pole antarctic thirty degree as the north star be distant from the pole Arctic three degree or little more and so it be more difficult to take the height in those part for that the say star at the foot of the cross must be right the which chance but in one hour of the night which be in diverse season of the year in diverse hour and oftentimes it appear not in the whole night so as it be very difficult to take the height and therefore the most expert pilot regard not the cross take the height of the sun by the astrolabe height take by the sun by which they know in what height they be wherein common the Portugal be more expert as a nation that have more discourse in the art of navigation than any other there be also other star in these southern part which in some sort resemble those of the north. that which they call the milken way be large and more resplendent in the south part appear therein those admirable black spot whereof we have make mention consider with myself oftentimes what shall cause the equinoctial to be so moist as I have say show the reason why the sun without the tropic cause great quantity of water when it be far off and contrariwise within they it breed most when it be near l. 2. chap. 7. to refute the opinion of the ancient I find no other reason but the great force of the sun in those part whereby it draw unto it a great abundance of vapour from out of the ocean which in those part be very great and spacious and have draw unto it this great abundance of vapour do sudden dissolve they into rain and it be approve by many try experience that the rain and great storm from heaven proceed from the violent heat of the sun first as we have say before it rain in those country when as the sun cast his beam direct upon the earth at which time he have most force but when the sun retire the heat be moderate and then there fall no rain whereby we may conclude that the force and heat of the sun be the cause of rain in those country moreover we observe both in Peru new Spain and in all the burn zone that the rain do usual fall in the afternoon when as the sun beam be in their great force be strange to see it rain in the morning and therefore traveller foresee it begin their journey early that they may end and rest before noon for they hold that common it rain after noon such as have frequent and travel those country can sufficient speak thereof and there be that have make some abode there say that the great abundance of rain be when the moon be at the full but to say the truth I can never make sufficient proof thereof although I have observe it moreover the day the year and the month show the truth hereof that the violent hea^e of the sun cause the rain in the burn zone experience teach we the like in artificial thing as in a limbeck wherein they draw water from herb and flower for the vehemency of the fire force and drive up a abundance of vapour which be press and find no issue be convert into liquor and water the like we see in gold and silver which we refine with quicksilver the fire be small and slow we draw out almost nothing of the quicksilver but if it be quick and violent it do great evaporate the quicksilver which encounter the head above do present turn into liquor and begin to drop down even so the violent heat of the sun produce these two effect when it find matter dispose that be to draw up the vapour on high and to dissolve they present and turn they into rain when there be any obstacle to consume they and although these thing seem contrary that one sun within the burn zone be near shall cause rain and without the zone afar off shall breed the like effect so it be that all well consider there be no contrariety a thousand effect in natural cause proceed of contrary thing by diverse mean we dry linen by the fire and in the air and yet the one heat and the other cool pasture be dry and harden by the sun and with the frost moderate exercise provoke sleep be too violent it hinder if you lay no wood on the fire it die if you lay on too much it likewise quench for the only proportion entertain and make it to continue to well discern a thing it must not be too near the eye nor too far off but in a reasonable distance proportionable be too far off from any thing we lose the sight and too near likewise we can see it if the sun beam be weak they draw up no fog from the river if they be violent have draw up the vapour they present dissolve and consume they but if the heat be moderate it draw up and preserve it for this reason the vapour rise not common in the night nor at noon but in the morning when as the sun begin to enter into his force there be a thousand example of natural cause upon this subject which we see do often grow from contrary thing whereby we must not wonder if the sun be near engender rain and be far off work the like effect but be of a moderate and proportionable distance cause none at all yet there remain one doubt why the nearness of the sun cause the rain under the burn zone and without when it be far off in my opinion the reason be that in winter without the tropic the sun have not force sufficient to consume the vapour which rise from the land and sea for these vapour grow in great abundance in the cold region of the air where they be congeal and thicken by the extremity of the cold and after be press they dissolve and turn into water therefore in winter when the sun be far off the day short and the night long his heat have small force but when the sun approach which be in the summer time his force be such as it draw up the vapour and sudden consume and disperse they for the heat and the length of the day grow through the nearness of the sun but within the tropic under the burn zone the far distance of the sun work the same effect that the nearness do without the tropic by reason whereof it rain no more under the burn zone when the sun be far off then without the tropic when it be near for that in this approach and retire the sun remain always in one distance whence proceed this effect of clearness but when the sun be in the period of his force in the burn zone and that he cast his beam direct upon the inhabitant head there be neither clearness nor dryness as it seem there shall be but rather great and strange shower for that by this violent heat he draw up sudden a great abundance of vapour from the earth and ocean which be so thick as the wind not able easy to disperse they they melt into water which breed the cold rain in so great abundance for the excessive heat may soon draw up many vapour the which be not so soon dissolve and be gather together through their great abundance they melt and dissolve into water the which we may easy discern by this familiar example roast a piece of pork mutton or veal if the fire be violent and the meat near we see the fat melt sudden and drop away the reason be that the violent heat draw forth the humour and fat from the meat and be in great abundance can dissolve it and so it distil more away but when the fire be moderate and the meat in a equal distance we see that it roast handsome and the fat drop not too sudden for that the moderate heat draw out the moistness which it consume sudden and therefore cook make a moderate fire and lay not their meat too near nor too far off lest it melt away the like may be see in anooth experience in candle of tallow or wax if the wick be great it melt the tallow or the wax for that the heat can consume the moistness which rise but if the flame be proportionable the wax melt nor drop not for that the flame do waste it by little and little as it rise but this be not to hinder the exception which nature have give to this rule exception to general rule make some region of the burn zone extreme dry the which be report of Ethiopia and we have see it in a great part of Peru where all that land or coast which they call plain want rain yea land water except some valley where river fall from the mountain the rest be a sandy and barren soil where you shall hardly find any spring but some deep well but with the help of God we will show the reason why it rain not in these plain the which many demand for now I only pretend to show that there be many exception to natural rule whereby it may happen that in some part of the burn zone it rain not when the sun be near but be far off although unto this day I have neither see nor hear of it but if it be so we must attribute it to the particular quality of the earth and also if sometime the contrary do chance we must have regard that in natural thing there happen many contrariety and let whereby they change and dissolve one another for example it may be the sun will cause rain and that the wind will hinder it or else cause more abundance than have be usual when I pass to the indies I will tell what chance unto i have read what poet and philosopher write of the burn zone the author experience I persuade that in one season of the year and in place of one height and distance from the pole and equinoctial we find so great diversity that some be environ with heat some with cold and other temper with a it appear that there be matter in it second cause to temper the violence of the heat to this I will add a other reason which deserve to be know not only for this matter but for many other for although bottom thrust on with the violence and currant of the flood hold themselves fast in their canoe or bark and although in fall they be turn topsy-turvy and both they and their canoe plunge into the deep yet by their care and industry they recover themselves again and in this sort the whole army escape except some few that be drown golden thirst and that which be more admirable they carry themselves so cunning that they neither lose their powder nor munition in their return have suffer many trouble and danger they be force in the end to pass back that same way mount by one of those high rock stick their poniard in the rock captain Peter make another entry by the same river who be dead in the same voyage and the soldier mutiny other captain follow the enterprise by a arm that come into the be not of that greatness and yet be equal yea they surpass the great of Europe as that of magdalaine near to saint marthe call the great river and that of alvarado in new Spain and a infinite number of other of the south side on the mountain of Peru the river be not usual so great for that their current be not long and that many water can join together but they be very swift descend from the mountain and have sudden fall by reason whereof they be very dangerous and many man have perish there they increase and overflow most in the time of heat I have go over twenty and seven river upon that coast yet do I never pass any one by a ford how they pass their river the indian use a thousand device to pass their river in some place they have a long cord that run from one side to the other and thereon hang a basket into the which he put himself that mean to pass and then they draw it from the bank with another cord so as he pass in this basket in other place the indian pass as it be on horseback upon a bottle of straw and behind he he that desire to pass and so row with a piece of a board carry he over in other place they make a float of gourd or pompion upon which they set man with their stuff to carry over and the indian have cord fasten to they go swim before and draw this float of pompion after they as horse do a coach other go behind thrust it forward have pass they take their bark of pompion upon their back and return swim this they do in the river of saint at Peru. we pass that of alvarado in new Spain upon a table which the indian carry upon their shoulder and when they lose their foot they swim these device with a thousand other wherewith they use to pass their river breed a terror in the beholder help themselves with such weak and unsure mean and yet they be very confident hair and straw Bridges they do use no other bridge but of hair or of straw there be now upon some river bridge of stone build by the diligence of some governor but many few than be needful in such a country where so many man be drown by default thereof and the which yield so much silver as not only Spain but also other strange country make sumptuous building therewith the indian do draw from these flood that run from the mountain to the valley and plain many and great brook to water their land which they usual do with such industry as there be no better in Murcia nor at Milan whole mountain of these sand as also for the marsh which grow by reason of the water that fall from the mountain which find no issue in these flat and low land drown they and make they unprofitable the mountain which be fifty common league although in some place as at Chachapayas it be broad this part of the world which we call Peru be very remarkable and contain in it strange property which serve as a exception to the general rule of the indies one wind only the first be that upon all the coast it blow continual with one only wind which be south and south-west contrary to that which do usual blow under the burn zone the second be that this wind be by nature the most violent tempestuous and unhealthful of all other yet in this region it be marvelous please healthful and agreeable so as we may attribute the habitation of that part thereunto without the which it will be troublesome and inhabitable by reason of the heat if it be not refresh with the wind the three property be that it never rain thunder snow nor hail in all this coast which be a matter worthy of admiration four that a little distance from the coast it rain and snow terrible five that there be two ridge of mountain which run the one as the other and in one altitude notwithstanding on the one there be great forest and it rain the great part of the year be very hot and the other be all naked and bare and very cold so as winter and summer be divide on those two mountain and rain and clearness itself for the better understanding hereof we must consider that Peru be divide as it be into three part long which breed a amazement to think upon it so great be the desire of silver that for the gain thereof man endure any pain and true it be not without reason that Pliny treat of this subject exclaim and perform work more than giant make hole and cave in the depth of the earth pierce mountain so deep by the light of candle whereas the day and the night be alike and in many month they see no day so as often the wall of their mine fall smother many of they that labour therein and afterward he add they pierce the hard rock with hammer of iron weigh one hundred and fifty pound and draw out the metal upon their shoulder labour day and night one deliver his charge to another and all in darkness only the last see the light with wedge and hammer they break the flint how hard and strong soever for the hunger of gold be yet more sharp and strong the vein as I have say where they find silver run betwixt two rock how they refine the metal of silver chap. 9 which they call the chase whereof the one be common as hard as flint and the other soft and easy to break this metal be not always equal and of the same bounty for you shall find in one and the same vein one sort of metal very rich which they call Cacilla or Tacana from which they draw much silver and another be poor from whence they draw little the most rich metal of this mountain be of the colour of amber and the next be that which incline to black there be other somewhat red and other of the colour of ash final of diverse and sundry colour which seem to such as know they not to be sin of no value but the miner do present know his quality and perfection by certain sign and small vein they find in they they carry all this metal they draw out of these mine upon indian sheep which serve they as ass to carry it to the mill the rich metal be refine by melt in those small furnace which they call Guayras for that be most leadie by reason whereof it be most subject to melt and for the better melt thereof the indian cast in a matter they call soroche which be a metal full of lead the metal be in these furnace the filth and earthy dross through the force of the fire remain in the bottom and the silver and lead melt so as the silver swim upon the lead until it be purify then after they refine the silver many time after this manner of melt they have usual draw out of one quintal of metal thirty forty and fifty piece of silver and yet I have see some most excellent that have be show i where they have draw in the melt two hundred yea two hundred and fifty piece of silver of a quintal of metal a rare wealth and almost incredible if we have not see the trial thereof by fire but such metal be very rare the poor metal be that which yield two three five or six piece or little more this metal have common little lead but be dry and therefore they can refine it with fire and for this reason in Potozi there be great store of these poor metal whereof they make no great account but be reject like straw and as the scum of the good metal until they find mean to refine it by quicksilver whereby the scum they call Oquiache be of great profit for the quicksilver by a strange and wonderful property purify the silver and be apt for these metal which be dry and poor wherein they consume less quicksilver then in the rich for the rich they be the more need of quicksilver they have at this day the most usual manner of refine in Potozi be by quicksilver as also in the mine of Cacatecas and other of new Spain there be in old time upon the side and top of Potozi above six thousand Guayras which be small furnace where they melt their metal the which be place like light a pleasant sight to behold by night cast a light afar off like a flame of fire but at this day there be not above two thousand for that as I have say they use little melt but refine it by quicksilver the which be the great profit and for that the property of quicksilver be admirable and that this manner of refine of silver be remarkable I will discourse of quicksilver of the mine and work and what be requisite for that subject quicksilver so call by the latin for that it run and slide sudden from place to place among all other metal have great and wonderful virtue the first be although it be a true metal yet be it not hard neither have it any certain form nor subsistence like to other metal but be liquid not like unto gold and silver melt but of his own proper nature and although it be a liquor yet be it more heavy than any other metal and therefore all other swim above and sink not to the bottom be more light I have see two pound of iron put into a barrel of quicksilver the which do swim about like unto wood or cork upon the water plin. l. 33. c. 6. Pliny give a exception hereunto say that gold alone do sink and not swim above it I have not see the experience but it may be this grow by reason that quicksilver by nature do environ gold and cover it which be one of the most important property it have sympathy with gold for it join with gold in a strange manner it seek it where it lie and environ it in such sort as it do distinguish and separate it from any other body or metal wherewith it be mix for this reason such take gold as will preserve themselves from the danger and discommodity of quicksilver they have use a remedy to those in who ear they have put quicksilver to cause they to die secret to put little plate of gold into their ear for that gold have the virtue to draw out Mercury and after they draw out these plate all white with the quicksilver it do stick unto they be one day at Madril I go to see the exquisite work which a rare workman of Milan make for saint Laurence the royal it be my hap to be there one day when as they gild certain piece of a countertable of brass which be do with quicksilver and for that the fume of Mercury be mortal he tell i that the workman preserve themselves from this venom by swallow a double ducat of gold roll up the which be in the stomach draw unto it all the quicksilver that enter in fume by the ear eye nostril and mouth and by this mean free themselves from the danger of quicksilver which the gold gather in the stomach and after cast out by the excrement a thing true worthy of admiration after the quicksilver have purify and purge gold from all other metal and mixture he be likewise separate from the gold his friend by the heat of the fire the which purify it from all quicksilver plin. l. 33. c. 6 Pliny say that by a certain art and invention they do separate gold from quicksilver it seem to i the ancient have no knowledge to refine silver by quicksilver which at this day be the great use and chief profit of quicksilver for that he say plain that quicksilver join with no other metal but with gold and when he make mention of refine of silver he speak only but of the manner of melt whereby we may infer that the ancient have no knowledge of this secret in truth though there be a league and sympathy betwixt gold and quicksilver yet where as the Mercury find no gold it join with silver though not in the like manner as with gold but in the end it do cleanse and purge it from earth copper and lead among the which the silver grow without any need of fire to melt it yet must they use fire to separate it from the silver as I will show hereafter quicksilver hold no account of other metal but of gold and silver but contrariwise it do corrupt they force and consume they and fly from they as much as may be the which be likewise admirable and for this cause they put it in earthen vessel or in beast skin for if it be put in vessel of copper of iron or other metal it present pierce and corrupt they and therefore Pliny call it the poison of all thing for that it consume and spoil all we find quicksilver in the grave of dead man which after it have consume the body come forth pure and whole there have be likewise find in the bone and marrow of man and beast who have receive it in fume by the mouth and nostril congeal within they and pierce even unto the bone therefore it be a dangerous thing to frequent so perilous and mortal a creature it have another property which be to run and make a hundred thousand small drop whereof not one be lose be they never so little but they return every way to their liquor it be almost incorruptible have nothing in a manner that may consume it and therefore Pliny call it the eternal sweat it have yet another property that although it do separate gold from copper and all other metal yet they that will gild copper brass or silver use quicksilver as the mean of this union for with the help thereof they gild metal among all the wonder of this strange liquor that seem to i most worthy observation that although it be the weighty thing in the world yet be it convert into the light of the world which be smoke and sudden the same smoke which be so light a thing turn again into so heavy a substance as be the proper liquor of quicksilver whereinto it be dissolve for this smoke encounter the metal on high be a solid body or come into a cold region sudden it thicken and be convert into quicksilver and if you set he once again to the fire he do likewise return into smoke to be resolve again into quicksilver quicksilver be find in a kind of stone which do likewise yield vermillion which the ancient call Minium of the place where they find quicksilver and how they discover these rich mine in Guancavilca chap. 11. and at this day they call the image of crystal Miniades which be paint with thereof almost like unto a moor target or buckler then do they dry it and this be the bread they eat it have no taste but be healthful and of good nourishment for this reason we say be at saint wheat why it grow not in those part which be saint Dominicke Cuba port and some other thereabouts for that the soil of these land will neither bear wheat nor may for when as they sow wheat it come up well and be present green but so unequal as they can gather it for of the seed sow at one instant some be spindle some be in the ear and some do but bud one be great and another little one be in the grass and another in the grain and although they have carry labourer thither to see if there be any tillage or art to be use yet can they find no remedy for the quality of the earth they carry meal from new Spain or the canary which be so moist that hardly can they make any profitable bread or of good taste the wafer-cake wherewith they say mass do bend like to wet paper by reason of the extreme humidity and heat which be joint in that country there be another extreme contrary to this which hinder the grow of may or wheat in some part of the indies as on the height of the Sierre of Peru and the province which they call of Colao which be the great part of this realm where the climate be so cold and dry as it will not suffer any of these seed to grow instead thereof the indian use another kind of root which they call Papas these root be like to ground nut they be small root which cast out many leaf Papas and Chuno they gather this Papas and dry it well in the sun then beat it they make that which they call Chuno which keep many day and serve for bread in this realm there be great traffic of Chuno the which they carry to the mine of Potozi they likewise eat of these Papas boil or roast there be one sweet of these kind which grow in hot place whereof they do make certain sauce and mince meat which they call Locro to conclude these root be the bread of that land so as when the year be good they rejoice much for that oftentimes they freeze in the earth so great be the cold of that region they carry may from the valley or sea-coast and the spaniard which be dainty carry these have they very great and cool but in truth there be no more comparison nor resemblance of the one with the other then there be as the proverb say betwixt a egg and a chestnut for first the ancient plane carry no fruit at the least they make no account thereof but the chief reason why they esteem it be for the shadow for that there be no more sun under a plane than under a roof and contrariwise the reason why they shall regard it at the indies yea make great account thereof be by reason of this fruit which be very good for they have little shade moreover the ancient plane have the body so big and the bough so spread that Pliny report of one Licinius a roman captain who with eighteen of his companion dine at ease in the hollow of one of these plane plin. lib. 2. cap. 1. and
