the earth out of the which spring many and sundry scion and sprig divide and not join together these sprig grow big every one make a small tree apart and in grow they cast forth these leaf which be of a fine green smooth and great as I have say when it be grow to the height of a and a half or two it put forth one only bough of fruit whereon sometime there be great number of this fruit and sometime less I have tell upon some of these bough three hundred whereof every one be a span long more or less and two or three finger big yet be there much difference herein betwixt some and other they take away the rind and all the rest be a firm kernel and tender good to eat and nourish this fruit incline more to cold than heat they be accustom to gather the bough or cluster as I have say be green and put they into vessel where they ripen be well cover especial when there be a certain herb mingle with it which serve for this effect if they suffer they to ripen on the tree they have a better taste and a very good smell like to camoiss or sweet apple they last almost all the year for that there be always young one that grow out of this stock so as when one end another begin to yield his fruit the one be half ripe and the other begin to bud anew so as one succeed another and the fruit continue the whole year in gather the cluster they cut the sprig or stalk for that it bear but one and Yguanas be a better meat but more horrible to the eye Yguanas for they be like to the very lizardes of Spain although they be of a doubtful kind for that they go to the water and come to land they Chinchilles which be find on the Sierre of Peru where there be likewise a small beast very common which they call cuye and which the indian hold for a very good meat cuye and they be accustom often to of vicugne and tarugne of Peru chap 40. lib. 3. the partib animal c. 2. lib. 10. c. 7^ the vicugne be wild and the sheep be tame some think that the vicugne be those which Aristotle Pliny and other author call which be wild goat and in truth they have some resemblance for the lightness they have in the wood and mountain but yet they be no goat for the vicugne have no horn as those have whereof Aristotle make mention neither be they the goat of the east indies from who they draw the bezoar stone for if they be of that kind it be a diverse one as in the race of dog the mastiff be diverse from the greyhound the vicugne of Peru be not those beast which carry the bezoar stone in the province of new Spain which there they call bezaar for that they be a kind of stag and venison yet do I not know in any part of the world there be any of these beast but in Peru and in Chille which be country join one to another these vicugne be great than goat and less than calf their hair be of the colour of dry rose somewhat clear they have no horn like stag and goat they feed upon the high top of the mountain which they call the snow nor frost do not offend they but contrariwise they seem to delight in it they go in troop and run most light when they meet with any traveller or beast they fly away seem very fearful and in fly they drive their young one before they they do not find that they multiply much and therefore the king ing^as do defend the hunt of vicugne if it be not for their feast or by their commandment some complain that since the spaniard enter there they have give too much liberty to hunt the vicugne and by this mean they be much diminish the manner the indian use in their hunt they assemble many man together Indian hunt to the number of a thousand or two thousand yea more and environ a great circuit of wood they hunt their game until they have compass it in on all part and by this mean they common take three or four hundred and so choose what they lift they let go the rest especial the female for breed they be accustom to sheer these beast and of their fleece to make cover and rug of great value for that this wool be like to white silk which last long and as the colour be natural and not die so be it perpetual the stuff that be make of this wool be very fresh and good in summer and they hold they profitable for the inflammation of the reins and other part temper the excessive heat this wool have the like virtue when it be make in quilt and therefore some use it to that end for the trial they have make thereof they say moreover that this wool or cover make thereof be physical for other indisposition as for the gout yet do I not know that they have make any certain trial thereof the flesh of these vicugne be not good although the indian eat it and dry it for the effect of physic I will say what I have see upon the Sierre of Peru come one night into a tambo or inn be much afflict with pain in my eye think they will fall out the which do common happen in those part for that they pass through place cover with snow which be the cause of this accident experiment for the eye be trouble with this pain and out of patience there come a indian woman which say to i father lay this to thy eye and thou shall be cure it be a piece of the flesh of vicugne new kill and all bloody I use this medicine and present the pain cease and soon after go quite away beside these chaco which be the most common manner of hunt at the indies they have use another more private to take they which be that come near they do cast certain line with plummet of lead which entangle their leg so as they can run and by this mean they take the vicugne the chief reason why this beast be esteem be by reason of the bezoar stone they find in they whereof we will entreat virtue of Pacos guanaco and indian mutton chap. 41. there be nothing at Peru of great riches and profit then the cattle of the country which our man call indian sheep and the indian in their general language call they lama for all thing well consider it be a beast of the great profit and least charge of any that I know from they they draw meat and clothing as from the sheep of Spain moreover they have the benefit to carry all thing they have need of use they to bear their burden and they have no need either of shoe or saddle nor yet of oat but he serve his master for nought feed on the grass he find in the field so as God have furnish they of sheep and mare and all in one beast and as it be a poor nation so will he in this point free they from charge for that there be much pasture upon the Sierre and this kind of cattle have no need of any other charge two kind there be two kind of these sheep or lamas the one they call Pacos or sheep bear wool and the other be bare and have little wool so be they better for burden they be big than great sheep and less than calf they have a very long neck like to a camel whereof they have good need for be high of stature they have need of a long neck else shall they be deform they be of diverse colour some all white other all black some grey and some spot which they call Moromoro the indian have great superstition in choose the beast for sacrifice of what colour they shall be according to the diversity of season and sacrifice their flesh be good although it be hard but that of their lamb be the better and the most delicate that can be eat yet they eat not many for that the chief fruit and profit they yield be their wool to make clothes and their service to carry burden the indian make stuff of this wool wherewith they clothe themselves the one be gross and common which they call Hanaca and the other fine and delicate which they call Cumbi they make carpet and cover and other exquisite work which last long and have a very fair lustre like half silk and that which be most rare be their manner of weave their work be both side alike so as you shall not find any end in a whole piece the Ingua king of Peru have many chief workman to make this work of Cumbi and the which for the most part be resident in the province of join to the great lake of they die this wool into diverse fine colour with sundry kind of herb whereof they make many sort of work both course and fine all the indian both man and woman work in the Sierre and have their loom in their house have no need to buy any stuff for their necessary use of the flesh of these sheep they make Cuscharg^i or dry flesh the which will last very long whereof they make great account they be accustom to drive troop of these sheep with burden and to go in band three hundred five hundred yea a thousand in a company with wine may Coca Chuno quicksilver and all other kind of merchandise and of silver which be the best of all they carry bar of silver from Potozi to Ariqua which be three score and ten league I have often wonder to see these troop of sheep lade with a thousand or two thousand bar of silver and much more which be above three hundred thousand ducat without any other guard or resort then some indian which serve only to guide these sheep and to lade and unlade they or at the most some few spaniard and they sleep all night in the midst of the field without other guard and yet in so long a way and so weak a guard they never find want or loss of any thing in so great a treasure of silver so safe be the way in Peru. the burden which one of these sheep do common carry be of four or six arrobe six arobe be a hundred and fifty pound weight when their voyage be long they go not above two three or four league at the most on a day those that guide those troop have their ordinary lodging where they be assure to have water and pasture and there they unlade and set up their tent make fire and dress their meat which be not painful although it be a phlegmatic and slow manner of travel when there be but one day journey one of these sheep will bear eight arrobe in weight or more and bear this burden eight or ten league in a day as the poor soldier be wont to do when they march through Peru. this kind of cattle delight most in a cold air and for this cause they live upon the Sierre and die in the by reason of the heat sometime these sheep be all cover with ice and frost and yet they continue sound and well the bare sheep be pleasant to behold for they will stay upon the way raise up their neck and will look upon any one very wistly and so they remain a long time without move or any show of fear which give occasion of laughter see they thus to stand and yet sometime they do grow amaze sudden and run away with their burden even to the high rock so as not be able to come unto they they be constrain to kill they with a harquebus lest they shall lose their bar of silver which they sometime carry the Pacos will grow reastie under their burden lie down and will endure to be cut in a thousand piece before they will rise when this humour take they whereof the proverb grow in Peru to say that one be reastie to signify he be obstinate for that when any of these beast be moody it be with excess the remedy they have be to stay and sit down by the Paco make much on he until the fit be past and that he rise and sometime they be force to stay two or three hour they have a disease like to scab which they call whereof they common die the ancient have a remedy to bury they quick that have the lest they shall infect the rest be a very contagious disease and go from one to another a indian that have one or two of these sheep be not repute poor for one of they be worth six or seven piece of assay and more according to the time and all beast that engender it chaw the cuid and common feed upon the snow and rock the indian report and teach by tradition from their father and ancient that in the province of Xaura and in other province of Peru there be many herb and venomous beast which poison the water and the pasture where they eat and drink and where they breathe amidst which venomous herb there be one very well know of of this herb the stone be compound in the stomach whence it draw all the virtue against poison and other wonderful effect this be the opinion and tradition of the indian discover by man of great gold and the manner of work in they this particular of the mine of gold be a thing great to be note and I may much better speak hereof then any other man forasmuch as there be now twelve year past since I serve in the place of the surveyor of the melt shop pertain to the gold mine of the firm land and be the governor of the mine of the catholic king don Ferdinando after whole departure from this life I serve long in the same room in the name of your majesty the i or vein which ought to be follow aught to be in a place which may stand to save much of the charge of the labourer and for the administration of other necessary thing that the charge may be recompense with gain the great part of the wrought gold which the indian have be base gold of indian base and hold somewhat of copper of this they make bracelet and chain and in the same they close their jewel which their woman be accustom to wear and esteem more than all the riches of the World the manner how gold be gather be this either of such as be find in Zavana that be to say in the plain and river of the champain country be without tree whether the earth be with grass or without or of such as be sometime find on the land without the river in place where tree grow so that to come by the same it shall be requisite to cut down many and great tree but after which soever of these two manner it be find manner of mine and search for gold either in the river or breach of water or else in the earth I will show how it be find in both these place and how it be separate and purge therefore when the mine or vein be discover this chance by search and prove in such place as by certain sign and token do appear to skilful man apt for the generation of gold and to hold gold and when they have find it they follow the i and labour it whether it be in the river or in the plain as I have say and if it be find on the plain first they make the place very clean where they intend to dig than they dig eight or ten foot in length and as much in breadth but they go no deep than a span or two or more as shall seem best to the master of the i dig equal gold in mine than they wash all the earth which they have take out of the say space and if herein they find any gold they follow it and if not they dig a span deep and wash the earth as they do before and if then also they find nothing they continue in dig and wash the earth as before until they come to the hard rock or stone and if in fine they find no gold there they follow no further to seek gold in that place but go to another part and it be to be understand that when they have find the i they follow it in dig in the same measure in level and depth until they have make a end of all the mine which that place contain spanish custom for usage of mine if it appear to be rich this i ought to consist of certain foot or pase in length or breadth according to certain order determine and within that compass of earth it be not lawful for any other to dig for gold and where as end the my of he that first find the gold immediate it be lawful for any other man that will with a staff to assign himself a place by the side of the same enclose it with stake or pale as his own these mine of Zavana that be such as be find in the plain ought ever to be seek near to some river or brook or spring of water or dike or stand pool to the end that the gold may be wash for the which purpose they use the labour of certain indian water a good neighbour as they do other in dig of the i and when they have dig out the mine they fill certain trey with that earth which other indian have the charge immediate to receive at their hand and to carry those trey of earth to the water where it may be wash yet do not they that bring it wash it but deliver it to other put it out of their own trey into they which they have ready in their hand to receive it these washer for the most part be the indian woman because this work be of less pain and travel then any other woman gold-washer these woman when they wash be accustom to fit by the water side with their leg in the water even up to the knee or less as the place serve their purpose and thus hold the trey with earth in their hand by the handle thereof and put the same into the water they move they round about after the manner of sift with a certain aptness in such sort that there enter no more water into the trey then serve their turn and with the self same apt move of their trey in the water they ever avoid the foul water with the earth out of the one side of the vessel and receive in clean water on the other side thereof so that by this mean by little and little the water wash the earth as the light substance of the trey and the gold as the heavy matter rest in the bottom of the same be round and hollow in the midst like unto a barber basin and when all the earth be avoid and the gold gather together in the bottom of the trey they put it a part and return to take more earth which they wash continual as before furthermore it be to be note that for every two indian that wash other labourer it be requisite that two other serve they to bring earth from the mine and other two to break the same small and fill their trey therewith also beside these labourer it be necessary that there be other people in the place where they work and rest in the night these be such as make their bread and provide for victual and other necessary so that to conclude there be in all five person ordinary assign to every trey of washer five to a trey there be another manner of work the mine in river or brook of run water and this be that in avoid the water of his course after that the bed of the river be dry and utter empty they find gold among the breach cliff and rift of stone and among all that be in the bottom of the channel and where natural the river run of great force so that it chance sometime that when the bed of the river be good and rich gold in Rivers or powder they find in it great quantity of Gold and therefore your majesty ought to understand for a general rule as it appear in fact that all gold be engender in the top and high place of the mountain gold engender on hill top and incontinuance of time be by little and little bring down to the vale and plain by shower of rain and the fall of spring Rivers and brook have their original in the mountain and descend from the same notwithstanding it be oftentimes find in the plain far from the mountain but when it chance to be find in great quantity it be for the most part among the mountain and in the river or their branch more than in any other part of the plain and in these two manner it be common find most abundant and for the better prose that gold be engender on high and be bring down into the low place I have one great token thereof which cause i to believe it for certain and this be to consider that coal never putrify nor corrupt under the ground if they be make of strong wood whereby it chance that dig the earth by the fold or indent place of the mountain or on the side his reason and break a mine in the earth where it have be break before and have now dig one or two or three pole in measure the miner find certain coal of wood under the same level where they find gold and this I say in the earth which be take for a virgin that be to say such as have not before be open for any mine the which coal can not natural be engender there or enter in by any mean but when the superficial part of the earth be equal with the level where the coal be find it be like that the coal be leave there by some occasion of fire and that they fasten there in time and that afterward in long continuance of time they be by little and little cover with the earth which the often shower of rain wash from the mountain so that by the course of year the earth overgrew the coal unto the say level and measure which have before time be the superficial part of the earth where the coal and gold be find together some may think that coal shell and other natural grow there whereby it may appear that the gold be no more engender there then be the coal but bring thither from the mountain by the fall of water as we have say forasmuch as the mountain be the and bowel of all rich metal further and beside this I say that in how much more the gold be go far from the natural place of this generation to the place where it be find it be so much the more purify and fine and of a better carat and the near that it be find to his proper mine or vein where it be engender it be so much the base foul and more crude and of a base allay and carat and do waste so much the more in melt and remain more brickle sometime there be find grain of gold of great quantity gold in grain one huge piece of gold and of great weight above the earth and sometime also under the earth and the great of all other that be find to this day in the indies be that which be lose in the sea about the island which weigh three thousand and two hundred of castellan of God which be in value four thousand a hundred thirty and eight ducat of gold which weigh one Arrova and seven pound or thirty and two pound after twelve ounce to the pound which make threescore and four mark of Gold a mark be a pound of 8. ounce 16. pound weight eight ounce (@) 12. ounce to the pound indian gild and I see in the year 1515. in the hand of Michael Passamonte treasurer to your majesty two grain of the which one weigh seven pound which be fourteen mark and be in value about three score and five ducat of gold every mark the other be of ten mark which be five pound of like value and of very good gold of two and twenty carat and better the^e be also find many other great grain although not equal unto these in bigness and forasmuch as I have speak of gold I have think good to declare somewhat how the indian can very excellent gild such vessel of copper and base gold as they make for they can give they so fair and flourish a colour that all the mass which they gild appear as though it be gold of two and twenty carat and better this colour they give with a certain herb as though it be wrought by the art of any goldsmith of Spain or Italy and will of they be esteem as a thing of great riches and a secret manner of gild for the desire that our man have to gold they nothing esteem the copper although there may great commodity and profit be have thereby and also by other metal which they nothing regard except silver which be find abundant in that part of the firm land which be call new Spain of the manner of fish for pearl the indian exercise this kind of fish for the most part in the coast of the north in Cubagua and cumana and many of they which dwell in the house of certain particular lord in the land of San Dominico and johannis resort to the island of Cubagua for this purpose their custom be to go five six or seven or more in one of their canoas or bark early in the morning to some place in the sea thereabouts where it appear unto they that there shall be great plenty of those shell fish which some call muscle and some oyster wherein pearl be engender and there they plunge themselves under the water even unto the bottom save one that remain in the Canoa or boat which he keep still in one place as near as he can look for their return out of the water and when one of they have be a good while under the water he rise up and come swim to the boat enter into the same and leave there all the oyster which he have take and bring with he for in these be the pearl find and when he have there rest himself a while and eat part of the oyster he return again to the water where he remain as long as he can endure and then rise again and swim to the boat with his prey where he rest he as before and thus continue course by course as do all the other in like manner be all most expert swimmer and diverse and when the night draw near they return to the island to their house and present all the oyster to the master or steward of the house of their lord who have the charge of the say indian and when he have give they somewhat to eat he lay up the oyster in safe custody until he have a great quantity thereof than he cause the same fisherman to open they and they find in every of they pearl other great or small two or three or four and sometime five or six and many small grain according to the liberality of nature they save the pearl both small and great which they have find and either eat the oyster if they will or cast they away have so great a quantity thereof that they in manner abhor they these oyster be of hard flesh and not so pleasant in eat as be we of Spain this island of Cubagua where this manner of fish be exercise be in the north coast and be no big than the island of Zealand oftentimes the sea increase great and much more than the fisher for pearl will because whereas the place be very deep a man can natural rest at the bottom by reason of the abundance of airy substance which be in he as I have oftentimes prove for although he may by violence and force descend to the bottom yet be his foot lift up again so that he can continue no time there and therefore where the sea be very deep as I have say in the chapter of the beast call Bardati that those beast may be the original and document to imbarbe horse even so the first invention of music may seem by the hear of this beast to return again to the selfsame song and do this only in the night and not in the day by reason whereof and also because of her evil sight I think she to be a night beast and the friend of darkness sometime the christian man find these beast and bring they home to their house where also they creep all about with their natural slowness insomuch that neither for threaten or prick they will move any fast than their natural and accustom pace and if they find any tree they creep thither immediate and mount to the top of the high branch thereof where they remain continual for the space of eight or ten or twenty day without eat of any thing as far as any man can judge and whereas I myself have keep they in my house I can never perceive other but that they live only of air and of the same opinion be in manner all man of those region because they have never see they eat any thing but ever turn their head and mouth towards that part where the wind blow most whereby may be consider that they take most pleasure in the air they bite not nor yet can bite have very little mouth they be not venomous or noyous any way but altogether brutish and utter unprofitable and without commodity yet know to man save only to move their mind to contemplate the infinite power of God who delight in the variety of creature whereby appear the power of his incomprehensible wisdom and majesty so far to exceed the capacity of man understanding in these region there be likewise find certain fowl or bird which the indian call alcatraz these be much big than goose fowl and bird alcatraz the great part of their feather be of russet colour and in some part yellow their bill or beak be of two span in length and very large near to the head and grow small towards the point they have great and large throat and be much like to a fowl which I see in Flanders in Brussels in your majesty palace which the fleming call Haina and I remember that when your majesty dine one day in your great hall there be bring to your majesty presence a cauldron of water with certain fish alive which the say fowl do eat up whole and I think very that that fowl be a foul of the sea because she have foot like fowl of the water as have also these Alcatrazi which be likewise fowl of the sea and of such greatness that I have see a whole coat of a man put into the throat of one of they in panama in the year 1521. and forasmuch as in that coast of Pama there pass and fly a great multitude of these Alcatrazi be a thing very notable panama I will declare the manner hereof as not only I but also diverse other now present in your majesty court have oftentimes see your majesty shall therefore understand that in this place as I have say before the sea of sur rise and fall two league and more from six hour to six hour so that when it increase the water of the sea arrive so near to the house of panama as do our sea call mare mediterraneum in Barzalona or in Naples and when the say increase of the sea come there come also therewith such a multitude of small fish call sardines that it be so marvelous a thing to behold that no man will believe it that have not see it insomuch that the cacique that be the king of that land pilchard at such time as I dwell there be bind daily as he be command by your majesty governor to bring ordinary three canoas or bark full of the say sardines and to unlade the same in the market place which be afterward by the ruler of the city divide among the christian man without any cost or charge to any of they insomuch that if the people have be a much great multitude than they be and as many as be at this present in Toledo or more and have none other thing to live by they may have be sufficient sustain by these sardines beside the overplus which shall have remain but to return to the fowl whereof we have speak as the sea come and the sardines with the same even so likewise come the say Alcatrazzi therewith and fly continual over it in such a multitude that they appear to cover the upper part or floor of the water and thus continue in mount and fall from the air to the water and from the water to the air during all the time of their fish and assoon as they have take any of these sardines they fly above the water and eat they incontinent and sudden return again to the water for more continue thus course by course without cease in like manner when the sea fall they follow their fish as I have say there go also in the company of these fowl another kind of fowl call Coda inforcata that be the fork tail whereof I have make mention before and assoon as the alcatraz mount from the water with her prey of the sardines sudden this Coda inforcata give she so many stroke and so persecute she that she cause she to let fall the sardines which she have in her mouth the which assoon as they be fall and before they yet touch the water the Coda inforcata catch they even in the fall in such sort that it be a great pleasure to behold the combat between they all the day long the number of these Alcatrazzi be such that the christian man be accustom to send to certain land and rock which be near about panama with their boat or bark to take these Alcatrazzi while they be yet young and can fly and kill as many of they with staff as they will until they have therewith lade their bark or canoas these young one be so fat and well feed that they can be eat and be take for none other intent but only to make grease for candle to burn in the night for the which purpose it serve very well and give a clear light and burn easy after this manner and for this purpose innumerable of they be kill and yet it seem that the number of they that fish for Sardines do daily increase there be other fowl call that be simple sparowe these be somewhat less than seamewes and have their foot like unto great malards and stand in the water sometime and when the ship sail fifty or a hundred league about the land these fowl behold the ship come towards they break their flight and fall down upon the sail yard mast and cable thereof and be so simple and foolish that they tarry until they may easy be take with man hand and be therefore call of the mariner simple sparrow they be black and upon their black have their head and shoulder of feather of a dark russet colour they be not good to be eat although the mariner have sometime be enforce to eat they there be another kind of bird in the firm land bird with bill heavy than body which the christian call because they have very great beak in respect of the littleness of their body for their beak be very heavy and weigh more than their whole body beside these bird be no big than quail but have a much great ambushment of feather insomuch that their feather be more than their body their feather be very fair and of many variable colour their beak be a quarter of a yard in length or more and bend down towards the earth and three finger broad near unto the head their tongue be very quill wherewith they make a great hiss they make hole in tree with their beak in the which they make their nest and sure these bird be marvelous to behold for the great difference which they have from all other bird that I have see aswell for their tongue which be quill as I have say as also for the strangeness of their sight and disproportion of their great beak in respect of the rest of their body there be no bird find that provide better for the safeguard of their young in the time of their breed to be without danger of wild cat that they enter not into their nest to destroy their egg or young and this aswell by the strange manner of build their nest as also by their own defence and therefore when they perceive that the cat approach towards they they enter into their nest and hold their beak towards the entrance of the same stand at their defence and so vex the cat that they cause they to leave their enterprise there be also other bird or sparrow which the christian by contrary effect call Matti that be fool whereas nevertheless there be no bird that show more wit and craft in defend her young from peril foolish sparowe wise provident these bird be little and in manner black and somewhat big than our thrush they have certain white feather in their neck and the like sagacity or sharpness of sense as have the bird or pie call Gazzuole they seldom time light upon the earth they make their nest in tree separate from other because the monkey be accustom to leap from tree to tree not descend to the ground for fear of other beast except when they be enforce by thirst to come down to drink at such time as they be sure not to be molest and for this cause do not these bird make their nest but in tree far divide from other they make they of a cubit in length or more after the manner of bag or little sack large at the bottom and grow narrow and narrow towards the mouth whereby they be fasten have the hole whereat they enter into the sack of such bigness as may only suffice to receive they and to the end that the monkey may not devour their young if they chance to mount upon the tree where they have their nest they use another craft which be to make their nest in thick branch of tree and to defend the same with sharp and strong thorn implicate and set in such order that no man be able to make the like so that the monkey can by no mean put their leg into the hole of the nest to take out the young bird aswell for the sharpness of the thorn as also for the depth of the nest in the bottom whereof the young bird rest without danger of their enemy for some of their nest be three or four span in length the leg of the monkey can reach to the bottom thereof they use also another policy which be to make many of their nest in one tree the which they do for one of these two cause that be that either of their own natural disposition they be accustom to go in great multitude and rejoice in the company of their own generation as do the bird which we call stare or else to the intent that if it shall so chance that the monkey shall climb the tree where they make their nest they may be a great company to resist and molest the monkey at who approach they make a fearful and terrible cry whereby the monkey be put to flight furthermore in the firm land and in the land there be certain bird call Piche or Gazzuole somewhat like unto those which we call wood-wal Gazzuole or wood-peckes be less than we of Spain these be altogether black and go hop and leap their beak be also black and of the same fashion as be the popinjay beak they have long tail and be somewhat big than stare there be other bird call pintadelli which be like unto certain green bird pintadelli which the Itrlians call and be of seven colour these bird for fear of the monkey be ever wont to make their nest over the bank of river or the sea where the branch of tree so reach over the water that with a little weight they may bow down to the water their nest be make so near the top of the branch that when the monkey come thereon the branch bend towards the water and the monkey turn back again for fear of fall for although no beast in the world be more malicious than this yet whereas the most part of beast be natural incline to swim this monkey have no manner of aptness thereunto and be therefore soon drown or strangle in the water and by a privy sense of nature fear the danger which he can escape these bird make their nest in such sort that although they be wet and fill with water yet do they so sudden rise up again that the young bird be not thereby hurt or drown there be also many nightingale and other bird which sing marvellous with great melody and difference in sing these bird be of marvelous diverse colour the one from the other some be altogether yellow and some other of so excellent delectable and high a colour as it be a ruby other be also of diverse and variable colour some of few colour and other some all of one colour be all so fair and beautiful that in brightness and shine they excel all that be in Spain or Italy or other province of Europe many of these be take with net lime-twig and spring of diverse sort great fowl diverse other sort of great fowl like unto eagle and such other as live of prey be find in the firm land of such diversity that it be in manner impossible to describe they all particular and forasmuch as I have more large entreat hereof in my general history of the indies I think it not requisite here to make any further mention of the same of tree fruit and plant there be both in the firm land and the land a certain world insomuch that in the moment when it pass the palate of the mouth and begin to go down the throat it seem that from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there be no part of the body but that feel great comfort thereby as it be doubtless one of the most excellent thing that may be taste upon the earth and such as I be not able by writing or tongue to express and to proceed yet further I say that when the meat of this fruit be take from the vessel thereof the vessel remain as fair and neat as though it be polish good against the wind and stone colic and be without of colour incline towards black and shine or glister very fair and be within of no less delicateness such as have accustom to drink in these vessel and have be trouble with the disease call the fret of the gut say that tree find of diverse sort and difference as sweet cedar tree black date tree and many other of the which some be so heavy that they can float about the water but sink immediate to the bottom and other further to other thing I will declare the manner how the indian kindle fire kindle of fire without fire only with wood and without fire the manner whereof be this they take a piece of wood of two span in length as biggea the least finger of a man hand or as a arrow well polish and of a strong kind of wood which they keep only for this purpose and where they intend to kindle any fire they take two other piece of wood of the dry and light that they can find and bind they fast together one with another as close as two finger join in the midst or between these they put the point of the first little staff make of hard and strong wood which they hold in their hand by the top thereof and turn or rub it round about continual in one place between the two piece of wood which lie bind together upon the earth which by that uncessant rub and chase be in short space kindle and take fire putrify wood shine in the night I have also think good here to speak somewhat of such thing as come to my remembrance of certain tree which be find in this land and sometime also the like have be see in Spain these be certain putrify trunk which have l^en so long rot on the earth that they be very white and shine in the night like burn firebrand and when the spaniard find any of this wood and intend privy in the night to make war and invade any province when case so require that it shall be necessary to go in the night in such place where they know not the way the foremost christian man which guide the way associate with a indian to direct he therein take a little star of the say wood which he put in his cap hang behind on his shoulder by the light whereof he that follow next to he direct his journey who also in like manner bear another star behind he by the shine whereof the three follow the same way and in like manner do all the rest so that by this mean none be lose or straggle out of the way and for as much as this light be not see very far it be the better policy for the christian because they be not thereby disclose before they invade their enemy furthermore as touch the nature of tree one particular thing seem worthy to be note whereof Pliny make mention in his natural history Pliny where he say that there be certain tree which continue ever green and never loose their leaf as the bay-tree the cedar the orange-tree and the olive-tree with such other of the which in altogether he name not past five or six to this purpose I say that in the land of these indies and also in the firm land almost ^ll indian tree continue ever green it be a thing of much difficulty to find two tree that lose or cast their leaf at any time for although I have diligent search to know the truth hereof yet have I not see any that lose their leaf either of they which we have bring out of Spain into these region as orange-tree lemon cedar palm or date-tree and pomegranate-tree Cassia or of any other in these region except only cassia which lose his leaf earth hot low than a fathom a secret thing radical moisture and have a great thing appropriate to itself only which be that whereas all other tree and plant of India spread their root no deep in the earth than the depth of a man height or somewhat more not descend any further into the ground by reason of the great heat which be find beneath that depth yet do Cassia pierce further into the ground until it find water which by the philosopher opinion shall be the cause of a thin and watery radical moisture to such thing as draw their nourishment thereof as fat and unctuous ground with temperate heat yield a fast and firm moisture to such thing as grow in they which be the cause that such tree lose not their leaf as the say thin and waterish moisture be cause of the contrary as appear by the say effect which be see only in cassia and none other tree or plant in all these part of reed or cane in the firm land there be many sort of reed so that in many place they make their house thereof cover they with the top of the same and make their wall of they in like manner as I have say before and among these kind of reed there be one so great that the cane thereof be as big as a man leg in the knee and three span in length from joint to joint or more in so much that every of they be of capacity to contain a little bucket of water in this kind there be find some great and some less of the which some they use to make quiver for arrow there be find another kind which sure be marvelous reed-spring or fountain of water be little big than a javelin the cane whereof be long than two span these reed grow one far from another as sometime twenty or thirty pace and sometime also two or three league they grow in manner in all province in the indies and grow near to very high tree whereunto they lean and creep up to the top of their branch which they embrace and descend again down to the earth their cane be full of most clear water without any manner of taste or savour either of the cane or of any other thing and such as if it be take out of the fresh spring in the world nor yet be it know that ever it hurt any that drink thereof for it have oftentimes so chance that as the christian man have travail in these region in desolate way where for lack of water they have be in great danger to die with thirst they have escape that peril by reason that they find the say reed of the water of who cane they have drink a great quantity without any hurt thereof ensue therefore when they find these in any place they make water vessel of the cane thereof and carry as many of they full of water as may suffice for one day journey and sometime they carry so many that they take for every man two or three quart of water which may serve they for many day because it do not corrupt but remain still fresh and good or there be also certain plant which the christian call they be as high as tree and become as big in the trunk as the knee of a man or more from the foot to the top they bear certain long and large leaf be more than three span in largeness and about ten or twelve in length the which when they be break of the wind the stalk remain whole in the midst in the midst of this plant in the high part they grow they have a rind not very thick and easy to be break be within altogether full of a substance like unto the marry of the bone of a ox as it appear when the rind or bark be take from the same be a very good fruit and when it be open and the rind take off there be find within it many good dry fig fig which be roast or stew in a oven in a close pot or some such other thing be of pleasant which satisfy present necessity this trunk or sprig which bring forth the say cluster be a whole year in grow and bring forth fruit in which time it have put forth round about in ten or twelve sprig as big as the first or principal and multiply no less than the principal in bring forth of cluster with fruit likewise at their time and also in bring forth other and many sprig as be say before from forth of the sea as I have say this fish be very excellent and wholesome to be eat and of good taste the second of the three fish whereof I have speak be the Tiburon this be a very great fish tiburon of we these indian give great honour and reverence to their cacique that be their king and ruler the principal cacique the king be bear on man back have twelve of his most strong indian appoint to bear he when he remove to any place or go abroad for his pleasure two of they carry he sit upon a long piece of wood which be natural as light as they can find the other ten follow next unto he as footman they keep continual a trot pace with he on their shoulder when the two that carry he be weary other two come in their place without any disturbance or stay and thus if the way be plain they carry he in this manner for the space of fifteen or twenty league in one day the indian that be assign to this office be for the most part slave or Naborit^ that be such as be bind to continual service I have also note that when the indian perceive themselves to be trouble with too much blood let of blood they let themselves blood in the calf of their leg and brawn of their arm this do they with a very sharp stone and sometime with the small tooth of a viper or with a sharp reed or thorn all the indian be common without beard in so much that it be in a manner a marvel to see any of they either man or woman to have any down or hair on their face they have no beard or other part of their body albeit I see the cacique of the province of Catarapa who have hair on his face and other part of his body as have also his wife in such place as woman be accustom to have this cacique have a great part of his body paint with a black colour which never fade and be much like unto that wherewith the moor paint themselves in Barbary in token of nobility they paint their body but the moor be paint special on their visage and throat and certain other part likewise the principal indian use these paint on their arm and breast but not on their visage because among they the slave be so mark when the indian of certain province go to the battle especial the cannibal archer they carry certain shell of great welke of the sea the cannibal trumpet which they blow and make therewith great sound much like the noise of horn they carry also certain timbrel which they use in the stead of drum also very fair plume of feather and certain armour of gold armour of gold especial great and round piece on their breast and splint on their arm likewise other piece which they put on their head and other part of their body for they esteem nothing so much as to appear gallant in the war their gallantness in the war their jewel and to go in most comely order that they can devise glister with precious stone jewel gold and feather of the least of these welke or perewincle they make certain little bead of diverse sort and colour they make also little bracelet which they mingle with gande of gold these they roll about their arm from the elbow to the wrest of the hand the like also do they on their leg from the knee to the sole of their foot in token of nobility especial their noble woman in diverse province be accustom to wear such jewel and have their neck in manner lade therewith these bead and jewel and such other trinket they call Caquiras beside these also they wear certain ring of gold at their ear and nostril which they bear full of hole on both side so that the ring hang upon their lip some of these indian be poulde and round albeit common both the man and woman take it for a decent thing to wear long hair which the woman wear to the midst of their shoulder and cut it equal especial above their brow this do they with certain hard stone which they keep for the same purpose the principal woman when their teat fall or become loose how the woman bear up their teat with bar of Gold bear they up with bar of gold of the length of a span and a half well wrought and of such bigness that some of they weigh more than two hundred castelan or ducade of gold these bar have hole at both the end whereat they tie two small cord make of Cotton at every end of the bar one of these cord go over the shoulder and the other under the arm hole where they tie both together so that by this mean the bar bear up their teat some of these chief woman go to the battle with their husband or when they themselves be regent in any province in the which they have all thing at commandment and execute the office of general captain and cause themselves to be carry on man back in like manner as do the cacique of who I have speak before these indian of the firm land be much of the same stature and colour as be they of the land the stature and colour of the indian the indian call the island of giant jucatos they be for the most part of the colour of a olive if there be any other difference it be more in bigness then otherwise and especial they that be call be strong and big than any other that I have see in these part except those of the island of giant which be on the south side of the island of hispaniola near unto the coast of the firm land and likewise certain other which they call jucatos which be on the north side all which chief although they be no giant yet be they doubtless the big of the indian that be know to this day and common big than the fleming and especial many of they as well woman as man be of very high stature and be all archer both man and woman these inhabit thirty league in length by these coast from the point of Canoa to the great river which they call Guadalchiber near unto as I traverse by those coast I fill a butt of fresh water of that river six league in the sea from the mouth thereof where it fall into the Sea they be call that be crown because their hair be cut round by their ear and poulde lower a great compass about the crown much like the friar of saint Augustine order and because I have speak of their manner of wear their hair here come to my remembrance a thing which I have oftentimes note in these indian and this be that they have the bone of the skull of their head four time thick and much strong than we so that in come to handstroake with they the skull of indian head it shall be requisite not to strike they on the head with sword for so have many sword be break on their head with little hurt do of the chief land hispaniola and Cuba the indian which at this present inhabit the island of hispaniola be but few in number and the christian not so many as they ought to be for as much as many of they that be in this island be go to other land and to the firm Land for be for the most part young man unmarried and desirous daily to see new thing man be desirous of new thing wherein man nature delight they be not willing to continue long in one place especial see daily other new land discover where they think they may soon fill their purse by be present at the first spoil wherein nevertheless their hope deceive many of they and especial such as have house and habitation in this island for I certain believe confirm myself herein with the judgement of many other that if any one prince have no more seignory then only this island it shall in short time be such as not to give place either to Sicily or England the commodity of hispaniola England and Sicily whereas even at this present there be nothing wherefore it will malice their prosperity not be inferior to they in any felicity that in manner the heaven can grant to any land be furthermore such as may enrich many province and kingdom by reason of many rich gold mine that be in it of the best gold that be find to this day in the world gold mines and in great quantity in this island nature of herself bring forth such abundance of Cotton Cotton that if it be wrought and maintain there shall be more and better then in any part of the world there be so great plenty of excellent cassia Cassia that a great quantity be bring from thence into Spain from whencee it be carry to diverse part of the world etc. in this island furthermore be many sheep and a great number of hog of the which as also of the cow many be become wild and and give a great light in so much that when the man of the island go any journey in the night they bear some of these worm make fast about their foot and head in such sort that he that shall see they a far and ignorant of the thing will be great astonish thereat by the light of these also the woman work in their house in the night these worm they call ciena their light last for the space of three in Cuba be a certain kind of partridge be very little with their feather much of the colour of turtle dove but be of much better taste to be eat partridge they be take in great number and be bring meat that ever I have eat but to let pass many other thing that may be here say and to speak of two marvelous thing which be in this island of Cuba whereof the one be that a valley contain two or three league in length between two mountain be full of a kind of very hard stone of such perfect roundness and like unto pellet of gun bullet for gun wrought by nature that no art can make better or more exact polish of these some be as small as pellet for handgunne and other so increase bigge^ and big from that quantity that they may serve for all sort of artillery although they be of bigness to mine which they dig and take out such as they need of all sort the other marvelous thing of this island be this a fountain of th^ pitch of bitumen that far from the sea there issue out of a mountain a certain liquor much like the clay of Babylon call bitumen or like unto pitch in great quantity and such as be very commodious for the calk of ship this fall continual from the rock and run into sea in such abundance that it be see float above the water on every side of the sea thereabouts as it be drive from place to place by the wind or course of the water Curtius write in his history Curtius that repose the same with the ancestor which before have be so deal with this be their best book of heraldry to recount the name and several descent in that pedigree if any die in battle or so that they ignorant that see the intercourse of spaniard by letter they think that letter can speak and be very cautelous in their carriage of they lest the letter may accuse they of ill demeanour by the way that have not something in they good and worthy of commendation nor commonweal so well order that have not something blame-worthy and to be control if therefore there be no other fruit in the history and narration of the deed and gest of the indian but this common utility to be a relation or history of thing the which in the effect of truth have happen it deserve to be receive as a profitable thing neither ought it to be reject for that it concern the indian as we see that those author that treat of natural thing write not only of generous beast notable and rare plant and of precious stone but also of wild beast common herb and base and vulgar stone for that there be always in they some property worthy observation if therefore there be nothing else in this discourse but that it be a history and no fable nor fiction it be no unworthy subject to be write or read there be yet another more particular reason which be that we ought herein to esteem that which be worthy of memory both for that it be a nation little esteem and also a subject different from that of our Europe as these nation be wherein we shall take most pleasure and content to understand the ground of their beginning their manner of life with their happy and unhappy adventure and this subject be not only pleasant and agreeable but also profitable especial to such as have the charge to rule and govern they for the knowledge of their act invite we to give credit and do partly teach how they ought to be entreat yea it take away much of that common and foolish contempt wherein they of Europe hold they I of the ancient inhabitant of new Spain and of the six lineage of the Navatlacas of the mexican and adventure by the way the foundation of Mexico their first king and tribute the aneient and first inhabitant of those province which we call new Spain be man very barbarous and savage l. 7. c. 2. which live only by hunt for this reason they be call Chichimecas they do neither sow nor till the ground neither live they together Chichimecas their savage course of life for all their exercise be to hunt wherein they be very expert they live in the rough part of the mountain beastlike without any policy and they go all naked they hunt wild beast hare coney weasel mole wild cat and bird yea unclean beast as snake lizard locust and worm whereon they feed with some herb and root they sleep in the mountain in cave and in bush and the wife likewise go a hunt with their husband leave their young child in a little of reed tie to the bough of a tree which desire not to suck until they be return from hunt they have no superior nor do acknowledge or worship any god neither have any manner of ceremony or religion there be yet to this day in new Spain of this kind of people which live by their bow and arrow the which be very hurtful for that they gather together in troop to do mischief and to rob neither can the spaniard by force or cunning reduce they to any policy or obedience for have no town nor place of residence to fight with they be proper to hunt after savage beast which scatter and hide themselves in the most rough and cover place of the mountain such be their manner of live even to this day in many province of the indies those in new Spain which they call ottomy be of this sort ottomy be common poor indian inhabit a rough and barren land and yet they be in good number and live together with some order and such as do know they find they no less apt and capable of matter of christian religion than other which be hold to be more rich and better govern come therefore to our subject the Chichimeca^ and ottomy which be the first inhabitant of new Spain for that they do neither till nor sow the land leave the best and most fertile of the country unpeople which nation that come from far do possess who they call Navatalcas for that it be a more civil and politic nation this word signify a people that speak well in respect of other barbarous nation without reason these second peopler Navatalcas come from other far country which lie towards the north where now they have discover a kingdom they call new Mexico new Mexico there be two province in this country the one call Aztlan Aztlan tuculhuacan which be to say a place of heron the other tuculhuacan which signify a land of such who grandfather be divine the inhabitant of these province have their house their land till god custom and ceremony with like order and government to the Navatalcas and be divide into seven tribe or nation and for that they have a custom in this province that every one of these lineage have his place and private territory the Navatalcas paint their beginning and first territory in figure of a cave and say that they come forth of seven cave to come and people the land of Mexico whereof they make mention in their history where they paint seven cave and man come forth of they by the supputation of their book their beginning 900. year ago A.D. 720. it be above eight hundred year since these Navatalcas come forth of their country reduce which to our account be about the year of our lord 720. when they leave their country to come to Mexico they stay fourscore year upon the way and the cause of this their long stay in their voyage be that their god which without doubt be devil and speak visible unto they have persuade they to seek new land that have certain sign and therefore they come discover the whole land to search for these token which their idol have give they and in place where they find any good dwelling they people it and labour the land and as they discover better country they leave those which they have first people leave still some especial the age sick folk and the weary yea they do plant and build there whereof we see the remainder at this day in the way where they pass they spend fourscore year in this manner of leisurely travel the which they may have do in a month by this mean they enter the land of Mexico in the year 902. after our computation these seven lineage I have speak of come not forth altogether how the six lineage of Navatalcas people the land of Mexico chap. 3. suchimilcos Chalchas tepanecans Azcapuzalco Culhua the first be the suchimilcos which signify a nation of the seed of flower those people the bank of the great lake of Mexico towards the south and do build a city of their name and many village long time after come they of the second lineage call Chalcas which signify people of mouth who also build a city of their name divide their limit and territory with the suchimilcos the three be the tepanecans which signify people of the bridge they do inhabit upon the bank of the lake towards the west and they increase so as they call the chief and metropolitan of their province Axcapuzalco which be to say a aunt nest and they continue long time mighty after they come those that people tescuco which be those of Culhua which be to say a crooked people for that in their country there be a mountain much bend and in this sort this lake be environ with these four nation these inhabit on the east and the Tepanecas on the north. these of Tescuco be hold for great courtier for their tongue and pronunciation be very sweet and pleasant then arrive the tlalluicans which signify man of the Sierre or mountain those be the most rude and gross of all the rest Tlalluicans who find all the plain about the lake possess even unto the Sierre they pass to the other side of the mountain where they find a very fertile spacious and warm country where they build many great village call the metropolitan of their province Quahunachua Quabunachua which be as much to say as a place that sound the voice of a eagle which our common people call by corruption Queruavaca and at this day they call this province the marquisate those of the six generation which be the tlascaltecan which be to say man of bread pass the mountain towards the east cross all the Sierre or mountain of Menade tlascaltecans where that famous Vulcan be betwixt Mexico and the city of angel where they do find a good country make many building they build many town and city whereof the metropolitan be call by their name tlascala this be the nation which favour the spaniard at their entry by who help they do win this country and therefore to this day they pay no tribute but enjoy a general exemption when all these nation people these country the chinchimecans be the ancient inhabitant make no resistance but flee and as people amaze they hide themselves in the most obscure of the rock but those that inhabit on the other side of the mountain where the tlascaltecan have plant themselves do not suffer they in quiet as the rest of the chichimecans have do but they put themselves in defence to preserve their country and be giant as the history report giant they seek to expel the last comer but they be vanquish by the policy of the tlascaltecan who counterfeit a peace with they invite they to a great banquet and when they be busy in their drunkenness there be some lay in ambush who secret steal away their weapon which be great club target sword of wood and other such arm then do they sudden set upon they and the chichimecans seek to defend themselves they do want their arm so as they flee to the mountain and forest adjoin where they pull down tree as if they have be stalk of lettuce but in the end the tlascaltecan be arm and march in order they defeat all the giant not leave one alive note of giant we must not hold this of the giant to be strange or a fable for at this day we find dead man bone of a incredible bigness when I be in Mexico in the year 1586. they find one of those giant bury in one of our farm which we call jesus du of who they bring a tooth to be see which without augment be as big as the fist of a man and according to this all the rest be proportionable which I see and admire at his deform greatness the tlascaltecan by this victory remain peaceable and so do the rest of the lineage these six lineage do always entertain amity together marry their child one with another and divide their limit quiet then they study with a emulation to increase and beautify their commonweal the barbarous chichimecans see what pass begin to use some government and to apparel themselves beginning of civility be ashamed of what have pass for till then they have no shame and have abandon fear by their communication with these other people they begin to learn many thing of they build small cottage have some policy and government they do also choose lord who they do acknowledge for their superior by mean whereof they do in a manner quite abandon this brutish life yet do they always continue in the mountain divide from the rest of the mexican departure of their journey and people the province of mechovacan ch. 4. three hundred and two year after the former two lineage have leave their country to inhabit new Spain the country be now well practise at this day in many place in the time of our October the twelve and last month be call Aymara wherein they do likewise sacrifice a hundred sheep and make the feast call Raymicantara Raquis in this month which answer to our November they prepare what be necessary for the child that shall be make novice the month follow the child with the old man make a certain show with round and turn and this feast be call Ituraymi which common they make when it rain too much or too little or when there be a plague among the extraordinary feast which be very many the most famous be that which they call Ytu this feast Ytu have no prefix time nor season but in time of necessity to prepare themselves thereunto all the people fast two day during the which they do neither company with their wife nor eat any meat with salt or garlic nor drink any Chica all do assemble together in one place where no stranger be admit nor any beast they have garment and ornament which serve only for this feast they march very quiet in procession their head cover with their ve^les sound of drum without speak one to another this continue a day and a night then the day follow they dance and make good cheer for two day and two night together say that their prayer be accept and although that this feast be not use at this day with all this ancient ceremony yet common they make another which be very like which they call Ayma with garment that serve only to that end and they make this kind of procession with their drum have fast before then after they make good cheer which they usual do in their urgent necessity and although the indian forbear to sacrifice beast or other thing public which can be hide from the spaniard yet do they still use many ceremony that have their beginning from these feast and ancient upon the even of this feast the nobleman come to the temple bring a new garment like unto that of the idol the which the priest put upon he have first take off his other garment which they keep with as much or more reverence than we do our ornament there be in the coffer of the idol many ornament jewel earring and other riches as bracelet and precious feather which serve to no other use but to be there and be worship as their god itself beside the garment wherewith they worship the idol that day they put upon he certain ensign of feather with fan shadow and other thing be thus attire and furnish they draw the curtayn or veil from before the door to the end he may be see of all man then come forth one of the chief of the temple attire like to the idol carry flower in his hand and a flute of earth have a very sharp sound and turn towards the east he sound it and then look to the west north and south he do the like and after he have thus sound towards the four part of the world show that both they that be present and absent do hear he he put his finger into the ai^e and then gather up earth which he put in his mouth and do eat it in sign of adoration the like do all they that be present and weep they fall flat to the ground invocate the darkness of the night and the wind entreat they not to leave they nor to forget they or else to take away their life and free they from the labour they endure therein thief adulterer and murderer and all other offender have great fear and heaviness while this flute sound so as some can not dissemble nor hide their offence by this mean they all demand no other thing of their god but to have their offence conceal pour forth many tear with great repentance and sorrow offer great store of incense to appease their god the courageous and valiant man and all the old soldier that follow the art of war hear this flute demand with great devotion of God the creator of the lord for who we live of the sun and of other their god that they will give they victory against their enemy and strength to take many captive there with to honour their sacrifice this ceremony be do ten day before the feast during which ten day the priest do sound this flute to the end that all may do this worship in eat of earth and demand of their idol what they please they every day make their prayer with their eye lift up to heaven and with sigh and groan as man that be grieve for their sin and offence although this contrition be only for fear of the corporal punishment that be give they and not for any fear of the eternal for they certain believe there be no such severe punishment in the other life no fear but of temporal punishment and therefore they offer themselves voluntary to death hold opinion that it be to all man a assure rest the first day of the feast of this idol Tezcalipuca be come all they of the city assemble together in a court to celebrate likewise the feast of the calendar whereof we have already speak which be call toxcoalth which signify a dry thing which feast be not make to any other end but to demand rain in the same manner that we solemnize the rogation and this feast be always in May which be the time that they have most need of rain in those country they begin to celebrate it the nine of May end the nineteen the last day of the feast the priest draw forth a litter well furnish with curtain and pendant of diverse fashion this litter have so many arm to hold by as there be minister to carry it all which come forth besmear with black and long hair half in tress with white string and attire in the livery of the idol upon this litter they set the personage of the idol appoint for this feast which they call the resemblance of their god Tezcalipuca and take it upon their shoulder that day to serve the idol and therefore such as have make this vow come by the point of day offer themselves to the deputy of the temple that they may command they what they will have do the which manner forty day before the merchant buy a slave well proportion without any fault or blemish either of sickness or of hurt which they do attire with the ornament of the idol that he may represent it forty day before his clothing they do cleanse he wash he twice in a lake which they call the lake of the god and be purify they attire he like the idol during these forty day he be much respect for his sake who he represent by night they do imprison he as have be say lest he shall fly and in the morning they take he out of prison set he upon a eminent place where they serve he give he exquisite superstition in this manner they present take the sacrifice razor the which they wash and cleanse from the blood of man which remain of the former sacrifice of this wash they make a drink mingle with another liquor make of Cacao give it he to drink they say that this will make he forget what have be say unto he and will make he in a manner insensible return to his former dance and mirth they say moreover that he will offer himself cheerful to death be enchant with this drink the cause why they seek to take from he this heaviness be for that they hold it for a ill augur and a foretell of some great harm the day of the feast be come after they have do he much honour sing and give he incense the sacrificer take he about midnight and do sacrifice he as have be say offer his heart unto the feast end the which be usual do in their principal feast chap. 5 civil custom and art of the indian take out of acostas 6. book I will first show in what sort the mexican count and divide their year their month of the supputation of time and the kalende^^h mexican use cha. 2. their calendar their computation their world and age they divide the year into eighteen month to which they give twenty day wherein the three hundred and threescore day be accomplish not comprehend in any of these month the five day that remain and make the year perfect mexican year and 18. month but they do reckon they apart and call they the day of nothing during the which the people do not any thing neither go they to their temple but occupy themselves only in visit one another and so spend the time the sacrificer of the temple do likewise cease their sacrifice these five day be past they begin the computation of the year whereof the first month and beginning be in march when the leaf begin to grow green new year day their calendar although they take three day of the month of February for the first day of their year be as it be the six and twenty day of February as appear by their calendar within the which we be likewise comprehend and contain with a very ingenious art which be make by the ancient indian that know the first spaniard I have see this calendar and have it yet in my custody which well deserve the sight to understand the discourse and industry the mexican indian have every one of these eighteen month have his proper name and his proper picture the which be common take of the principal feast that be make in that month or from the diversity of time which the year cause in that month they have in this calendar certain day mark and distinguish for their feast and they account their week by thirteen day mark the day with a or cipher which they multiply unto thirteen week of 13. day or year see this in the mexican chronicle in their own figure and then begin to count one two etc. they do likewise mark the year of these wheel with four sign or figure attribute to every year a peculiar sign whereof one be of a house another of a coney the three of a reed and the four of a flint they paint they in this sort note by those figure the year that do run say of so many house of so many flint of such a wheel happen such a thing for we must understand that their wheel which be a age contain four week of year every week contain thirteen year which in all make fifty two year in the midst of this wheel they paint a sun from the which go four beam or line in cross to the circumference of the wheel and they make their course even as the circumference be divide into four equal part every one with his line have a distinct colour from the rest and the four colour be Greene blue red and yellow every portion of these four have thirteen separation which have all their sign or particular figure of a house a coney a reed or a flint note by every sign a year and upon the head of this sign they paint what have happen that year and therefore I do see in the calendar mention the year when the spaniard enter Mexico mark by the picture of a man clad in red after our manner for such be the habit of the first Spaniard who Fernando Cortes send at the end of the two and fifty year which finish the wheel they use a pleasant ceremony which be the last night they do break all their vessel and stuff and put out their fire and all the light say that the world shall end at the finish of one of these wheel and it may be at that time for say they see the world must then end what need be there to provide meat to eat and therefore they have no further need of vessel nor fire upon this conceit they pass the night in great fear say it may happen there will be no more day and they watch very careful for the day when they see the day begin to break they present beat many drum and sound cornet flute and other instrument of joy and gladness say that God do yet prolong the time with another age which be fifty two year and then begin another wheel the first day and beginning of this age they take new fire new age. and buy new vessel to dress their meat and all go to the high priest for this new fire have first make a solemn sacrifice and give thanks for the come of the day and prolongation of another age this be their manner of account their year month week and age how the king account the year and month although this supputation of time practise among the mexican be ingenious enough and certain for man that have no learning yet in my opinion they want discourse and consideration have not ground their computation according unto the course of the moon nor distribute their month according wherein those of Peru have far surpass they for they divide their year into as many day perfect accomplish as we do here and into twelve month or moon better computation of time in Peru. in the which they employ and consume the eleven day that remain of the moon as polo write to make the computation of their year sure and certain they use this industry upon the mountain which be about the city of cusco where the king hold their court be the great sanctuary of those realm and as we shall say another Rome there be twelve pillar set in order and in such distance the one from the other as every month one of these pillar do note the rise and set of the sun they call they Succanga by mean whereof they teach and show the feast 12. pillar of the sun and the season fit to sow and reap and to do other thing they do certain sacrifice to these pillar of the sun every month have his proper name and peculiar feast they begin the year by januarie as we do but since a king call Pachacuto which signify a reformer of the temple begin their year by
